records.title: Get started
records.text: Get started. Pick a quickstart for AWS, GCP, Azure, or Hetzner, and go from a new account to a running Kubernetes cluster.

records.title: Get started
records.text:
Alethia designs, deploys, and runs Kubernetes clusters in your own cloud account. Each quickstart
below takes you from a new account to a running cluster on one cloud, and then removes the cluster
again. They use the console in your browser, and end with the same steps from a terminal.

records.title: Get started
records.heading: Pick your cloud
records.text:
Connect an AWS account with an IAM role, and deploy an Amazon EKS cluster.
 
 
 Connect a Google Cloud project with Workload Identity Federation, and deploy a GKE cluster.
 
 
 Connect an Azure subscription with a managed identity, and deploy an AKS cluster.
 
 
 Connect a Hetzner Cloud project with an API token, and deploy a Talos Linux cluster.
 
 

AWS, GCP, and Azure connect without keys: Alethia signs in with short-lived tokens that your cloud
account trusts. Hetzner Cloud has no identity federation, so it connects with an API token that
Alethia stores encrypted. For the security model, see [Security](/concepts/security).

records.title: Get started
records.heading: Every quickstart has the same six steps
records.text:
1. **Sign up** and create an organization.
2. **Connect** your cloud account.
3. **Design** a project from a starting point.
4. **Deploy** it, after you read the plan.
5. **See the cluster running**, and get a kubeconfig for it.
6. **Destroy** the environment, so that nothing is left billing in your account.

records.title: Get started
records.heading: More ways in
records.text:
- [Installation](/get-started/install-the-cli): install the `alethia` CLI.
- [The console](/get-started/the-console): the pages of the web console.
- [The CLI](/get-started/the-cli): the same work from a terminal, declared in an `alethia.yaml` file.
- [Connect a Git provider](/guides/connectors/git-providers): GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket, for projects that start from a repository.
- [Deploy Online Boutique to three environments](/tutorials/online-boutique): a longer tutorial, from the terminal.
- [Limits](/reference/limits): the ceilings on sign-up, trials, AI use, jobs, and scans.
- [Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting): what to do when a step fails.

records.title: Installation
records.text: Installation. Install the Alethia CLI via Homebrew, Scoop, an install script, a Linux package, Docker, a binary download, or from source.

records.title: Installation
records.text:
The `alethia` CLI ships for **macOS, Linux, and Windows** (amd64 + arm64). Pick whichever
method fits your platform. Every method installs the same released binary.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: alethia update
records.text:
Update the CLI. One command regardless of how you installed it:

alethia update

Alethia checks the release published by your control plane. It delegates Homebrew and Scoop
installs to those package managers. It downloads and checksum-verifies a writable standalone
installation before replacing it. For Linux packages and Docker images, it prints the exact native
update command instead of changing the package database or host from inside a container.

Alethia never invokes `sudo` or opens a User Account Control prompt. If the binary is not writable,
the command stops and tells you how to rerun the installer with administrator privileges.

Interactive commands check for a new release at most once per day. Set
`ALETHIA_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to disable these automatic notices. Explicit `alethia version` and
`alethia update` checks still contact the control plane.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Homebrew (recommended)
records.text:
One line, no prior setup:

brew install alethialabs-io/tap/alethia

Or tap once, then install (and reinstall) by the short name:

brew tap alethialabs-io/tap
brew install alethia

`alethia update` runs `brew update` and upgrades this formula. You can also run
`brew upgrade alethialabs-io/tap/alethia` directly. (The literal tap-free `brew install alethia` requires
[Homebrew core](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/homebrew-core.md) — a future adoption milestone.)

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Install script
records.text:
No Homebrew? Pipe the installer — it detects your OS/arch, verifies the SHA-256 checksum, and
drops the binary in `~/.local/bin`:

curl -fsSL https://get.alethialabs.io sh

Pin a version or change the install dir with env vars:

curl -fsSL https://get.alethialabs.io ALETHIA_VERSION=0.3.0 sh
curl -fsSL https://get.alethialabs.io ALETHIA_INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin sh

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Linux packages (.deb / .rpm / .apk)
records.text:
Every release attaches Debian, RPM, and Alpine packages. Download the one for your arch from the
[latest release](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-cli/releases) and install it:

bash

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Debian / Ubuntu
records.text: sudo dpkg -i alethia_*_linux_amd64.deb

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Fedora / RHEL
records.text: sudo rpm -i alethia_*_linux_amd64.rpm

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Alpine
records.text: sudo apk add --allow-untrusted alethia_*_linux_amd64.apk

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Scoop (recommended)
records.text:
scoop bucket add alethia https://github.com/alethialabs-io/scoop-bucket
scoop install alethia

`alethia update` delegates to `scoop update alethia`.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Install script
records.text:
irm https://get.alethialabs.io/install.ps1 iex

Honors `$env:ALETHIA_VERSION` and `$env:ALETHIA_INSTALL_DIR`; installs to
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Alethia\bin` and adds it to your user `PATH`.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Docker
records.text:
docker run --rm ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/alethia --version

Images are published to GHCR for every release (`:latest` and `:X.Y.Z`, amd64 + arm64).

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Binary download
records.text:
Pre-built archives are on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-cli/releases)
for every tagged version:

 Platform Architecture Archive 
 ---------- ------------- --------- 
 macOS Intel (amd64) `alethia_Darwin_x86_64.tar.gz` 
 macOS Apple Silicon (arm64) `alethia_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz` 
 Linux amd64 `alethia_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz` 
 Linux arm64 `alethia_Linux_arm64.tar.gz` 
 Windows amd64 `alethia_Windows_x86_64.zip` 
 Windows arm64 `alethia_Windows_arm64.zip` 

tar xzf alethia_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz
mv alethia /usr/local/bin/
alethia --version

Each release also ships `checksums.txt` — verify with `sha256sum -c` (Linux) or
`shasum -a 256 -c` (macOS) before installing.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: From source
records.text:
Requires Go 1.27+:

cd apps/cli
go build -o alethia .
./alethia --version

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Build system
records.text:
Alethia releases are built by [GoReleaser](https://goreleaser.com/) via GitHub Actions on each
`cli-v*` tag. See [Release System](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/release-system.md) for the full pipeline.

The GoReleaser config (`apps/cli/.goreleaser.yml`) produces:
- binaries for macOS / Linux / Windows × amd64 / arm64 (CGO disabled), archived with checksums
- Linux packages (`.deb` / `.rpm` / `.apk`) and Docker images (GHCR)
- the Homebrew formula (`alethialabs-io/tap`) and Scoop manifest (`alethialabs-io/scoop-bucket`), updated automatically

The binary's default control plane is `https://alethialabs.io`. It is a constant in the source, not a
build variable. To use another control plane, run `alethia init` or set the `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN`
environment variable.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.text: Quickstart: AWS. Sign up, connect an AWS account, deploy a Kubernetes cluster to it, see the cluster running, and destroy it again.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.text:
This quickstart takes you from a new Alethia account to a running Kubernetes cluster in
your AWS account, and then removes the cluster. It has six steps: sign up, connect, design, deploy, see the
cluster running, and destroy. Plan for about an hour. Most of that time is the cloud creating the
cluster.

 
The deploy step creates real resources in your AWS account, and AWS bills you for them while they
exist. The last step destroys them. Do not skip it.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- An AWS account where you can create IAM roles and an IAM OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider. The setup script creates both.
- A web browser. You do not need the Alethia CLI for this quickstart.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Sign up
records.text:
1. Open [alethialabs.io/signup](https://alethialabs.io/signup).
2. Select **Continue with email**, or sign up with GitHub, Google, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
 The email path sends a 6-digit code to your address. Enter it on the **Enter your code** screen.
3. On **Create your organization**, keep the **Hobby** plan.
 Hobby is free and is enough for this quickstart. The **Pro** tile says whether a trial is open to you.
4. Enter a name in **Organization name**.
5. Select **Create organization**.

The console opens the **New project** screen. You come back to it in the design step.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Connect AWS
records.text:
1. Select **Connectors** in the sidebar.
2. On the card for AWS, select **Connect**. A setup sheet opens on the **AWS CLI / CloudShell** tab.
3. Under **Run the setup in AWS CloudShell**, copy the setup command.
4. Select **Open CloudShell**. AWS CloudShell opens in your browser.
5. Paste the command into CloudShell and run it.
 The script creates an IAM OIDC identity provider and an IAM role that trusts Alethia. It creates no access keys.
6. Copy the role ARN that the script prints, and paste it into **IAM Role ARN**.
 You can paste the whole output. The field keeps only the ARN.
7. Select **Connect**. Alethia assumes the role and runs read-only checks against your account.
8. When the sheet reports success, select **Done**.

The sheet also has a **Terraform / IaC** tab that creates the same role with OpenTofu or Terraform. For the details, see the [AWS connector guide](/guides/connectors/aws).

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Design a project
records.text:
1. Select **Overview** in the sidebar, then select **Create**, then **Project**.
 If the **New project** screen is already open, skip this step.
2. Under **Start from**, select **Cluster only**. It needs no Git repository.
3. Under **Cloud**, select **AWS**, then the account you connected.
4. Under **Region**, keep the suggested region or select another one.
 The hint next to the field says where the suggestion comes from.
5. Enter a name in **Project name**.
6. Select **Create project**.

Alethia creates the project as a draft with one environment, `production`, and opens its
**Architecture** canvas. Nothing is provisioned yet. The canvas shows an Amazon EKS cluster. By default it
has two worker nodes of type `t3.large`. You can change the size on the canvas before you deploy.
For what the other starting points contain, see
[Starter templates](/guides/design-project/starter-templates).

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Deploy
records.text:
1. On the bar at the bottom of the canvas, select **Review plan**.
 The **Review and deploy** panel opens.
2. Under **Plan**, select **Run plan**. Alethia saves the design and queues a plan job.
3. When the plan finishes, read the list of resources that it would create.
4. Under **Deploy**, select **Deploy**.

Alethia queues a deploy job, and a runner picks it up. If the job stays at **Waiting for a
runner**, see [The job waits for a runner](/troubleshooting/deploy#the-job-waits-for-a-runner). Before the runner changes anything in
your AWS account, it runs the [verify gate](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate). A failed gate stops
the deploy before any change is applied. To follow the job, select **View log** on the bar, or open
**Jobs** in the sidebar.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: See the cluster running
records.text:
1. When the deploy job succeeds, select **Clusters** in the sidebar.
2. Select the row for your project. A detail sheet opens.
3. Check the status. **Active** means every component is healthy.

Under **Cluster access**, the sheet shows the cluster endpoint and the command that gets a
short-lived kubeconfig:

alethia cluster kubeconfig

On a terminal, the command asks which cluster to use. The sheet shows the command with your
cluster's name already filled in. The sheet also shows the `aws eks update-kubeconfig` command, for people who can sign in to the AWS account. To install the CLI, see
[Installation](/get-started/install-the-cli). For the kubeconfig options, see
[Get a kubeconfig for your cluster](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig).

Under **ArgoCD**, the sheet shows the ArgoCD URL and the command that reads the ArgoCD admin
password.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Destroy the environment
records.text:
1. Select **Open Architecture** on the cluster sheet, or open the project's **Architecture** canvas.
2. On the canvas toolbar, select **More** (the **…** button), then **Environment settings**.
3. On the **Settings** tab, find **Danger zone**, and select **Destroy** next to
 **Destroy environment**.
4. Type the environment name, `production`, to confirm.
5. Select **Destroy environment**.

Alethia queues a destroy job. The environment's status changes to **Destroying**, then to
**Destroyed**. When the destroy job succeeds, nothing that this quickstart created is left in
your AWS account.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Clean up the rest
records.text:
The destroy step removes the cloud resources. These items stay, and cost nothing:

- **The project.** To delete it, open the project's **Settings**, then select **Delete** under
 **Danger zone**. Deleting a project destroys no cloud resources, so always destroy the environments
 first.
- **The AWS connection.** To remove it, see [Disconnect an account](/guides/connectors/managing-connections#disconnect-an-account).
- **What the setup created in your AWS account.** Alethia does not remove it for you. The
 [AWS connector guide](/guides/connectors/aws) says what it is.

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Do the same from a terminal
records.text:
The CLI declares the same project in an `alethia.yaml` file. Install the CLI first, from
[Installation](/get-started/install-the-cli).

bash

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Sign in. The browser opens to confirm the code.
records.text: alethia login

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Connect AWS.
records.text: alethia connector aws

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Write ./alethia.yaml for a project named demo.
records.text: alethia init --project demo --region eu-west-1

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Show the plan, then deploy after you confirm.
records.text: alethia apply

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: List the cluster, then get a kubeconfig for it.
records.text:
alethia cluster list
alethia cluster kubeconfig demo

records.title: Quickstart: AWS
records.heading: Destroy the environment again. You type the project name to confirm.
records.text:
alethia project destroy --project demo

The command needs the `aws` CLI, signed in to the account you connect. It creates the same IAM role with an AWS CloudFormation stack named `AlethiaConnect`. When more than one cloud account is connected, `alethia init` asks which one to
use. For every flag, see [`alethia init`](/reference/cli/init),
[Plan & Apply](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply), and [Connector commands](/reference/cli/connector).

records.heading: If something goes wrong
records.text:
- [Troubleshoot sign-in](/troubleshooting/sign-in)
- [Troubleshoot connecting a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect)
- [Troubleshoot a deploy](/troubleshooting/deploy)
- [Troubleshoot a destroy](/troubleshooting/destroy)

records.text:

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.text: Quickstart: Azure. Sign up, connect an Azure subscription, deploy a Kubernetes cluster to it, see the cluster running, and destroy it again.

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.text:
This quickstart takes you from a new Alethia account to a running Kubernetes cluster in
your Azure subscription, and then removes the cluster. It has six steps: sign up, connect, design, deploy, see the
cluster running, and destroy. Plan for about an hour. Most of that time is the cloud creating the
cluster.

 
The deploy step creates real resources in your Azure subscription, and Azure bills you for them while they
exist. The last step destroys them. Do not skip it.

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- An Azure subscription where you can create a managed identity and assign it a role. The setup script does both. It does not need directory administrator rights.
- A web browser. You do not need the Alethia CLI for this quickstart.

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Sign up
records.text:
1. Open [alethialabs.io/signup](https://alethialabs.io/signup).
2. Select **Continue with email**, or sign up with GitHub, Google, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
 The email path sends a 6-digit code to your address. Enter it on the **Enter your code** screen.
3. On **Create your organization**, keep the **Hobby** plan.
 Hobby is free and is enough for this quickstart. The **Pro** tile says whether a trial is open to you.
4. Enter a name in **Organization name**.
5. Select **Create organization**.

The console opens the **New project** screen. You come back to it in the design step.

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Connect Azure
records.text:
1. Select **Connectors** in the sidebar.
2. On the card for Azure, select **Connect**. A setup sheet opens.
3. Enter your subscription ID in **Subscription ID**.
 The setup command on the **Azure CLI** tab fills in the ID for you.
4. Under **Run the setup in Azure Cloud Shell**, copy the setup command.
5. Select **Open Cloud Shell**. Azure Cloud Shell opens in your browser.
6. Paste the command into Cloud Shell and run it.
 The script creates a managed identity with a federated credential that trusts Alethia. It creates no client secret.
7. Under **Enter the IDs it prints**, enter the **Tenant ID** and the **Client ID** that the script prints.
 To fill both from the whole output, select **Paste all**.
8. Select **Connect**. Alethia signs in as the managed identity and runs read-only checks against your subscription.
9. When the sheet reports success, select **Done**.

The sheet also has a **Terraform / IaC** tab that creates the same identity with OpenTofu or Terraform. For the details, see the [Azure connector guide](/guides/connectors/azure).

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Design a project
records.text:
1. Select **Overview** in the sidebar, then select **Create**, then **Project**.
 If the **New project** screen is already open, skip this step.
2. Under **Start from**, select **Cluster only**. It needs no Git repository.
3. Under **Cloud**, select **Azure**, then the account you connected.
4. Under **Region**, keep the suggested region or select another one.
 The hint next to the field says where the suggestion comes from.
5. Enter a name in **Project name**.
6. Select **Create project**.

Alethia creates the project as a draft with one environment, `production`, and opens its
**Architecture** canvas. Nothing is provisioned yet. The canvas shows an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster. By default it
has two worker nodes of type `Standard_D2s_v5`. You can change the size on the canvas before you deploy.
For what the other starting points contain, see
[Starter templates](/guides/design-project/starter-templates).

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Deploy
records.text:
1. On the bar at the bottom of the canvas, select **Review plan**.
 The **Review and deploy** panel opens.
2. Under **Plan**, select **Run plan**. Alethia saves the design and queues a plan job.
3. When the plan finishes, read the list of resources that it would create.
4. Under **Deploy**, select **Deploy**.

Alethia queues a deploy job, and a runner picks it up. If the job stays at **Waiting for a
runner**, see [The job waits for a runner](/troubleshooting/deploy#the-job-waits-for-a-runner). Before the runner changes anything in
your Azure subscription, it runs the [verify gate](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate). A failed gate stops
the deploy before any change is applied. To follow the job, select **View log** on the bar, or open
**Jobs** in the sidebar.

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: See the cluster running
records.text:
1. When the deploy job succeeds, select **Clusters** in the sidebar.
2. Select the row for your project. A detail sheet opens.
3. Check the status. **Active** means every component is healthy.

Under **Cluster access**, the sheet shows the cluster endpoint and the command that gets a
short-lived kubeconfig:

alethia cluster kubeconfig

On a terminal, the command asks which cluster to use. The sheet shows the command with your
cluster's name already filled in. The sheet also shows the `az aks get-credentials` command, for people who can sign in to the Azure subscription. To install the CLI, see
[Installation](/get-started/install-the-cli). For the kubeconfig options, see
[Get a kubeconfig for your cluster](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig).

Under **ArgoCD**, the sheet shows the ArgoCD URL and the command that reads the ArgoCD admin
password.

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Destroy the environment
records.text:
1. Select **Open Architecture** on the cluster sheet, or open the project's **Architecture** canvas.
2. On the canvas toolbar, select **More** (the **…** button), then **Environment settings**.
3. On the **Settings** tab, find **Danger zone**, and select **Destroy** next to
 **Destroy environment**.
4. Type the environment name, `production`, to confirm.
5. Select **Destroy environment**.

Alethia queues a destroy job. The environment's status changes to **Destroying**, then to
**Destroyed**. When the destroy job succeeds, nothing that this quickstart created is left in
your Azure subscription.

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Clean up the rest
records.text:
The destroy step removes the cloud resources. These items stay, and cost nothing:

- **The project.** To delete it, open the project's **Settings**, then select **Delete** under
 **Danger zone**. Deleting a project destroys no cloud resources, so always destroy the environments
 first.
- **The Azure connection.** To remove it, see [Disconnect an account](/guides/connectors/managing-connections#disconnect-an-account).
- **What the setup created in your Azure subscription.** Alethia does not remove it for you. The
 [Azure connector guide](/guides/connectors/azure) says what it is.

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Do the same from a terminal
records.text:
The CLI declares the same project in an `alethia.yaml` file. Install the CLI first, from
[Installation](/get-started/install-the-cli).

bash

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Sign in. The browser opens to confirm the code.
records.text: alethia login

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Connect Azure.
records.text: alethia connector azure --subscription 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Write ./alethia.yaml for a project named demo.
records.text: alethia init --project demo --region westeurope

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Show the plan, then deploy after you confirm.
records.text: alethia apply

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: List the cluster, then get a kubeconfig for it.
records.text:
alethia cluster list
alethia cluster kubeconfig demo

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: Destroy the environment again. You type the project name to confirm.
records.text:
alethia project destroy --project demo

Replace the example ID with your subscription ID. The command needs the `az` CLI, signed in to that subscription. When more than one cloud account is connected, `alethia init` asks which one to
use. For every flag, see [`alethia init`](/reference/cli/init),
[Plan & Apply](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply), and [Connector commands](/reference/cli/connector).

records.title: Quickstart: Azure
records.heading: If something goes wrong
records.text:
- [Troubleshoot sign-in](/troubleshooting/sign-in)
- [Troubleshoot connecting a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect)
- [Troubleshoot a deploy](/troubleshooting/deploy)
- [Troubleshoot a destroy](/troubleshooting/destroy)
- [Limits](/reference/limits)

records.title: alethia CLI
records.text: alethia CLI. Go command-line tool for managing multi-cloud infrastructure via the Alethia platform.

records.title: alethia CLI
records.text: alethia is the command-line interface for the platform. It provides terminal-based access to all infrastructure operations — planning and deploying Projects, monitoring jobs, and managing Runners.

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Overview
records.text:
Property Value 
 ---------- ------- 
 Language Go 
 Framework [Cobra](https://github.com/spf13/cobra) (commands) + [Charmbracelet](https://charm.sh/) (TUI) 
 Version Managed by release-please (`cli-v*` tags) 
 Distribution Homebrew · Scoop · install script (get.alethialabs.io) · .deb/.rpm/.apk · Docker · GitHub Releases (macOS/Linux/Windows, amd64/arm64)

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: How It Works
records.text:
alethia is a **thin client** that communicates with the Alethia API over HTTPS. It does not run OpenTofu directly — instead, it queues jobs that [Runners](/concepts/runner) execute. The CLI handles:

1. **Authentication** — [Device code flow](/concepts/authentication) with tokens stored locally
2. **Configuration** — Creating and inspecting Projects
3. **Job submission** — Queuing Plan / Deploy / Destroy jobs
4. **Monitoring** — Streaming logs, checking job status, waiting for completion
5. **Management** — Listing clusters, managing Runners

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Command Groups
records.text:
Connect AWS, GCP, Azure, and Hetzner accounts.
 
 
 List and inspect infrastructure configurations.
 
 
 Queue plan, deploy, and destroy jobs.
 
 
 List, stream logs, and cancel jobs.
 
 
 Register, list, and remove Runners.
 
 
 List provisioned Kubernetes clusters.
 
 
 Switch the active org and manage members and teams.
 
 
 Alerts and channels (console-managed today).
 
 
 `whoami`, `config`, output formats, and utility commands.

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Global Flags
records.text:
Every command accepts four persistent flags:

 Flag Default Description 
 ------ --------- ------------- 
 `-o, --output ` `table` Output format. `json`/`csv` print static, machine-readable output, and never open an interactive table. 
 `--no-input` off Disable interactive prompts; fail instead of prompting. Auto-enabled when stdin is not a terminal. A form is refused separately when the stream it would draw on is redirected, so `alethia … 2> log` still renders the rich table. 
 `--token ` unset Service-account token for non-interactive use. Prefer the `ALETHIA_TOKEN` environment variable in CI: a flag value lands in the process table and in shell history. 
 `--org ` the active org Organization to act in for this invocation, instead of the active one. Sent as the `X-Alethia-Org` header on every request, and used as the org in the request path of `members` and `teams`. It selects a scope rather than granting one: the control plane refuses it with `403` when you are not a member of that organization. Under a service token it must name the token's OWN organization — a different one is refused with `403`, never quietly ignored, so a pipeline cannot believe it is acting on one org while

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Quick Start
records.text:
The recommended path declares the project in an `alethia.yaml` file and applies it.

bash

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Install
records.text: brew install alethialabs-io/tap/alethia

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Sign in. The default control plane is https://alethialabs.io
records.text: alethia login

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Connect a cloud account: aws, gcp, azure, or hetzner
records.text: alethia connector gcp --project my-gcp-project

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Write ./alethia.yaml for a project named boutique
records.text: alethia init --project boutique

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Create what the file declares, show the plan, and deploy every environment
records.text:
alethia apply

On a terminal, `alethia init` shows a form for the values you do not pass as flags. It skips
the sign-in when this machine is already signed in. `alethia apply` shows the plan and asks
before it deploys. Pass `--yes` to skip the question.

`alethia up` runs the same first run in one command. It skips each step that is already done.
It cannot connect a cloud account for you, so it stops and names the `alethia connector`
command when none is connected.

See [`alethia init`](/reference/cli/init) and [Plan & Apply](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply) for every flag.

Each cloud's quickstart ends with these steps for that cloud: [AWS](/get-started/quickstart-aws#do-the-same-from-a-terminal),
[GCP](/get-started/quickstart-gcp#do-the-same-from-a-terminal), [Azure](/get-started/quickstart-azure#do-the-same-from-a-terminal), and
[Hetzner](/get-started/quickstart-hetzner#do-the-same-from-a-terminal). When a command fails, see [Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting).

records.title: Console
records.text: Console. Alethia's web control plane for multi-cloud infrastructure orchestration.

records.title: Console
records.text: The console is Alethia's web control plane. The hosted console is at [alethialabs.io](https://alethialabs.io). It provides a visual interface for configuring infrastructure, managing [cloud identities](/guides/connectors), monitoring [jobs](/guides/jobs), and viewing provisioned clusters — all from the browser. Alethia is the platform; the Console is the web app you drive it from.

records.title: Console
records.heading: Key Pages
records.text:
Project overview grid, plus project detail with services and infrastructure.
 
 
 The in-console AI — grounded in your real infrastructure, with per-project workspaces, a knowledge base, dashboards, and artifacts.
 
 
 Visual canvas for designing a project's infrastructure, with the cost from its last plan.
 
 
 Connect AWS, GCP, Azure, and Hetzner cloud accounts (each a cloud identity) plus GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket Git providers.
 
 
 Monitor infrastructure operations with real-time log streaming.
 
 
 Register, monitor, and manage your own Runners. The sidebar shows Runners only when your organization runs its own.
 
 
 View provisioned Kubernetes clusters with ArgoCD access.
 
 
 Runner, CLI, and Auth API endpoints.

records.title: Console
records.heading: Start here
records.text:
To go from a new account to a running cluster in the console, follow the quickstart for your
cloud: [AWS](/get-started/quickstart-aws), [GCP](/get-started/quickstart-gcp),
[Azure](/get-started/quickstart-azure), or [Hetzner](/get-started/quickstart-hetzner).

Every organization's data is kept apart from every other organization's. For how, see
[Security](/concepts/security).

records.title: Grant access
records.text: Grant access. Add a grant in Settings → Access, choosing who, allow or deny, a role or permission, and a scope, and revoke grants you no longer need.

records.title: Grant access
records.text:
Give a member or team access to the organization or one resource, or take it away. **Settings →
Access** lists every grant in the organization. A project's **Settings → Access** lists the grants on
that project.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The organization is on the Enterprise plan.
- Your role can manage access.
- You know the parts of a grant. See [How grants and scopes work](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes).

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Start a grant
records.text: Open **Settings → Access** and select **Add grant**.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Pick who
records.text: Pick a **Member or team**. A team grant reaches everyone on the team.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Allow or deny
records.text: Leave it as an allow, or choose **Deny** for an exception that overrides any inherited allow.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Pick what
records.text:
Choose a **Role**, built-in or [custom](/guides/access/custom-roles), or a single permission such as
`project:deploy`.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Pick the scope
records.text:
Choose **Entire organization**, or one project, runner or cloud identity. A grant on the organization
flows down to everything in it.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Save
records.text:
The grant takes effect at once.

 

To take access away, select **Revoke access** on the grant's row.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Find a grant
records.text:
Search by member, team or scope, and filter by scope, role and effect. Each row shows the principal,
the effect, the role or permission, the scope, its **Effective reach**, and when it was granted.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The grant appears in the list. Sign in as the member, or ask them, to confirm that they can do what
the grant allows and nothing it denies.

records.title: Grant access
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [How grants and scopes work](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes)
- [Create teams](/guides/access/teams)

records.title: Read the activity log
records.text: Read the activity log. See every action and every refused attempt in your organization or a project, filter it, and export it as CSV on Enterprise.

records.title: Read the activity log
records.text:
Find out who did what, and who tried something they were not allowed to do. The activity log records
every change in the organization.

records.title: Read the activity log
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your role can view activity. Every built-in role can.
- How far back you can read depends on the plan: 7 days on Hobby, 30 on Pro, 365 on Enterprise.
- Export needs the Enterprise plan.

records.title: Read the activity log
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Open **Settings → Activity** for the organization, or a project's **Settings → Activity** for one
 project.
2. Pick a time range: **Last 7 days**, **Last 30 days**, or a **Custom range**.
3. Narrow it with the search (**Search actor, action or resource…**), **Member**, **Project** and
 **Events**.
4. Select **Load more** to read further back.

Each entry is one sentence: who did what, to which resource, and when. Refused attempts are marked.
A person who left the organization shows as **Former member**.

records.title: Read the activity log
records.heading: What is recorded
records.text:
Recorded Examples 
 --- --- 
 Every action Create, edit, deploy, destroy, managing identities, members, connectors and billing, exports 
 Every refused attempt Someone tried an action their role does not allow 
 Access changes Custom roles created, changed or deleted; grants added or revoked; members joining, leaving or changing role 

Successful reads, such as opening a page or a list, are not recorded: there are too many. A refused
read is recorded.

records.title: Read the activity log
records.heading: Export the log
records.text: Select **Export CSV**, for a SIEM, a spreadsheet or an archive. On other plans, the button says that

records.title: Read the activity log
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Make a small change, such as renaming a project. Its entry appears at the top of the log, with your
name.

records.title: Read the activity log
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Access control architecture](/concepts/access-control/architecture): how decisions are made and recorded.
- [Feature matrix](/editions/feature-matrix)

records.title: Create a custom role
records.text: Create a custom role. Build a role with exactly the permissions you choose, from a matrix grouped by resource.

records.title: Create a custom role
records.text:
Make a role with exactly the permissions you need, such as "can plan and deploy projects, but never
destroy". A custom role lives in your organization next to the four built-in roles, and you grant it
the same way.

records.title: Create a custom role
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The organization is on the Enterprise plan.
- Your role can manage roles.

records.title: Create a custom role
records.heading: Open the editor
records.text: Open **Settings → Roles** and select **New role**.

records.title: Create a custom role
records.heading: Pick the permissions
records.text:
The matrix groups permissions by resource:

 Group Example permissions 
 --- --- 
 Projects `project:view`, `project:create`, `project:edit`, `project:plan`, `project:deploy`, `project:destroy` 
 Runners `runner:view`, `runner:create`, `runner:edit`, `runner:deploy`, `runner:destroy` 
 Cloud identities `cloud_identity:view`, `cloud_identity:manage_identities`, `cloud_identity:test` 
 Others Jobs, connectors, organization, members, alerts, fleet, support, activity, billing 

Each kind of job is its own permission. A role can hold `project:plan` without `project:deploy`, or
`runner:deploy` without `runner:destroy`.

records.title: Create a custom role
records.heading: Save the role
records.text:
Name the role and save it.

 

To grant it, see [Grant access](/guides/access/access-portal), or pick it when you
[invite a member](/guides/access/members-and-invitations).

When you change a role's permissions later, every grant that uses it changes at once. You do not
re-assign anything. For a one-off, grant a single permission instead of making a role.

records.title: Create a custom role
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The role is listed in **Settings → Roles**, and appears as a choice when you add a grant.

records.title: Create a custom role
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Roles and permissions](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions): every permission.
- [How grants and scopes work](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes)

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.text: How grants and scopes work. The four parts of a grant, how a grant flows down from an organization to its projects, and how an explicit deny makes an exception.

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.text:
Decide what grant to add. A grant is the unit of access, and it has four parts:

 Part Choices 
 --- --- 
 **Who** A member, or a team (everyone on it) 
 **What** A role, or a single permission such as `project:deploy` 
 **Where** The whole organization, or one resource: a project, a runner or a cloud identity 
 **Effect** Allow (the default), or an explicit deny 

You add grants in [Grant access](/guides/access/access-portal).

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The organization is on the Enterprise plan for grants and teams. On the free plan, you are the only
 owner and already hold every permission.

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.heading: Scope flows down
records.text:
Projects sit under the organization. Runners, cloud identities and connectors sit directly under the
organization too.

- A grant on the organization applies to every resource in it.
- A grant on one project applies to that project only.

So "let Dana view this one project" is one grant on that project.

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.heading: A deny always wins
records.text:
A deny makes an exception to broad access, such as "Dana can view every project except this one".

- A deny beats any allow, direct or inherited. The most specific grant does not win: any deny that
 covers the resource refuses access.
- A deny flows down like an allow. A deny on the organization excludes all its projects; a deny on one
 project excludes only that project.

The rule: access is allowed when an allow covers the resource, directly or through its organization,
and no deny covers it.

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.heading: Example: everything but one project
records.text:
1. Allow the `viewer` role to Dana on the organization. Dana can view every project.
2. Deny the `project:view` permission to Dana on project `S`.
3. Dana sees every project except `S`.

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.heading: Role or single permission
records.text:
- **A role** is a bundle of permissions. Use a built-in role, or a
 [custom role](/guides/access/custom-roles) for an exact set. Changing the role changes every grant
 that uses it.
- **A single permission** is one `resource:action`. Use it for a one-off, and for a precise deny, such
 as `project:view` on `S` and nothing more.

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The grant appears in **Settings → Access** with its principal, effect, role or permission, and scope.
Its **Effective reach** shows what it covers.

records.title: How grants and scopes work
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Roles and permissions](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions)
- [Access control architecture](/concepts/access-control/architecture): how the decision is made.

records.title: Invite members
records.text: Invite members. Invite people to an organization by email with a role, change a member's role, and remove members.

records.title: Invite members
records.text:
Bring people into your organization with the role they need. A member's role turns into their
access at once: there is no separate grant to manage.

records.title: Invite members
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The organization is on the Pro or Enterprise plan. A personal organization has one member: you.
- Your role can manage members (`owner` or `admin`).

records.title: Invite members
records.heading: Open the invite dialog
records.text: Open **Settings → Members** and select **Invite members**.

records.title: Invite members
records.heading: Enter emails and roles
records.text:
Enter each email and pick a role: one of the four built-in roles, or a
[custom role](/guides/access/custom-roles). The dialog refuses an address that is already a member,
already invited, or entered twice.

records.title: Invite members
records.heading: Send
records.text:
Alethia sends each person an email with an accept link.

 

The invitee opens the link. If they are not signed in, they sign in first and come back. Email sign-in
also creates an account, so they do not need one beforehand. Accepting makes them a member with the
role you chose.

records.title: Invite members
records.heading: Change or remove members
records.text:
- Change a member's role in the members table. Their access changes at once.
- Select **Remove member** on one row, or select several and **Remove selected**. Their access ends
 at once.

For finer access, such as one project or an explicit deny, add a grant after they join. See
[Grant access](/guides/access/access-portal).

records.title: Invite members
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The new member appears in **Settings → Members** with their role. They see the organization in their
switcher.

records.title: Invite members
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Create teams](/guides/access/teams): grant access to a group at once.
- [Create and switch organizations](/guides/access/organizations)

records.title: Create and switch organizations
records.text: Create and switch organizations. Create a shared organization to work with others, and switch between the organizations you belong to.

records.title: Create and switch organizations
records.text:
Create a shared organization so others can work on your projects, and switch between the
organizations you belong to. Every project, runner, cloud identity and job belongs to one
organization, and its members see only that organization's resources.

records.title: Create and switch organizations
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You have your **personal** organization already. It is made with your account, it is on the free
 plan, and you are its only member and its `owner`.
- To share with others, you need an organization on a paid plan. Inviting members comes with Pro and
 Enterprise.

records.title: Create and switch organizations
records.heading: Create an organization
records.text:
1. Open the organization switcher at the top of the sidebar.
2. Select **Create organization**.
3. Name it, choose a plan and pay, then invite members.

You become the new organization's `owner`. See
[Invite members](/guides/access/members-and-invitations).

records.title: Create and switch organizations
records.heading: Switch organizations
records.text:
Open the switcher and pick the organization. It lists each organization you belong to with its plan,
and marks the active one. Your personal organization shows as **Personal**.

The active organization decides what you see and what you may do. Every permission check, list and
action runs in it. From the CLI, run `alethia org switch`.

records.title: Create and switch organizations
records.heading: How roles work in an organization
records.text:
Each member has a role in the organization:

 Role Can 
 --- --- 
 `owner` Every permission, including billing 
 `admin` Every permission except billing 
 `operator` Plan, deploy and destroy projects and runners. Cannot manage cloud identities, members or billing. 
 `viewer` Look only 

A role can apply to the whole organization or to one project. The full list of permissions is in
[Roles and permissions](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions).

The database enforces the boundary too. PostgreSQL row-level security returns only the active
organization's rows, so a flaw in the application still cannot show another organization's data. See
[Security](/concepts/security).

records.title: Create and switch organizations
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The switcher shows the new organization as active, and **Overview** lists only its projects.

records.title: Create and switch organizations
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Invite members](/guides/access/members-and-invitations)
- [Access control](/concepts/access-control)
- [Feature matrix](/editions/feature-matrix): what each plan includes.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.text: Set up single sign-on. Let members sign in through your own identity provider over OIDC or SAML, by registering the provider and verifying your email domain.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.text:
Let your members sign in through your identity provider (IdP), such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID,
Google Workspace, AWS IAM Identity Center, OneLogin or Ping. Alethia is the service provider: it uses
your IdP and runs none of its own. Each organization registers its own providers, so organizations
can use different IdPs.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The organization is on the Enterprise plan. On other plans, the page offers an upgrade.
- Your role can manage SSO.
- You can create an OIDC or SAML application in your IdP, and add a DNS record for your email domain.
- A self-hosted console has the enterprise setup done. See [Enterprise setup](/self-host/enterprise-setup).

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Start the registration
records.text: Open **Settings → Single Sign-On** and select **Register provider**.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Choose the protocol
records.text:
Pick **OpenID Connect** or SAML. Protocol details are in [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc) and
[SAML and SCIM](/reference/standards/scim-saml).

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Enter the IdP's details
records.text:
OIDC SAML 
 --- --- 
 **Issuer URL** **IdP Entity ID (issuer)** 
 **Client ID** and **Client secret** from the IdP's OIDC application **IdP sign-on URL** and **Signing certificate (X.509)** from the IdP's SAML metadata

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Set the domain and mapping
records.text:
Enter a **Provider id**, a short slug such as `okta`, and the **Email domain** whose users sign in
through this provider, such as `company.com`. Change **Email claim** and **Name claim** if your IdP
uses other names.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Review and register
records.text: Check the summary and register the provider. It shows **Pending domain**.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Configure your IdP
records.text: The provider shows the **Redirect URI** (OIDC) and the **Start URL**. Add them to your IdP application.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Verify the domain
records.text:
Select **Show DNS record**, add that record to your domain's DNS, then select **Verify domain**.
When it passes, the provider shows **Verified**, and SSO sign-in is on.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Select **Test connection** on the provider. Then sign in at the **Start URL** with an account on the
email domain.

The first time someone signs in through SSO, Alethia adds them to the organization with the
least-privileged role. From then on they are an ordinary
[member](/guides/access/members-and-invitations), and you change their access with
[grants](/guides/access/access-portal). SCIM provisioning and deprovisioning from your IdP is not
available yet: users are added when they first sign in.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Edit or remove a provider
records.text:
**Edit provider** changes the details. Leave the client secret or certificate blank to keep the
stored one. **Remove provider** stops sign-in through it; the members' accounts and memberships stay.
It cannot be undone.

records.title: Set up single sign-on
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Invite members](/guides/access/members-and-invitations)
- [Enterprise setup](/self-host/enterprise-setup)

records.title: Create teams
records.text: Create teams. Group members into a team and grant access to the team once, so access follows team membership.

records.title: Create teams
records.text:
Grant access to a group of members at once. Give a team one grant, and everyone on it has that
access. Add or remove people, and their access follows. Sharing a project with five engineers is then
one grant, not five.

records.title: Create teams
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The organization is on the Enterprise plan.
- Your role can manage teams. Without it, the page says so.

records.title: Create teams
records.heading: Create the team
records.text: Open **Settings → Teams**, select **Create team**, and name it, for example `platform`.

records.title: Create teams
records.heading: Add members
records.text: Select **Manage members** on the team and add or remove organization members.

records.title: Create teams
records.heading: Grant access to the team
records.text:
In **Settings → Access**, add a grant and pick the team as the principal. See
[Grant access](/guides/access/access-portal).

 

A team grant applies to a user for as long as they are on the team. Removing someone from the team
removes that access at once. You can grant a team a [custom role](/guides/access/custom-roles), scope
the grant to one project, and still deny one member something on top.

records.title: Create teams
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The team lists its members, and **Settings → Access** shows the grant with the team as principal. A
member of the team can do what the grant allows.

records.title: Create teams
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Grant access](/guides/access/access-portal)
- [How grants and scopes work](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes)

records.title: Set up alerts
records.text: Set up alerts. Send platform events to Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Google Chat, Mattermost, Rocket.Chat, PagerDuty, a webhook or email, with policies that choose what fires.

records.title: Set up alerts
records.text:
Get notified when a deploy fails, a runner goes offline, or someone changes a role. A **channel** is
where a notification goes. A **policy** chooses which events go to which channels. Every
notification is logged as a **delivery** under **Activity**.

records.title: Set up alerts
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your organization is on the Pro or Enterprise plan. On other plans, the Alerts card on the overview
 says that alerting needs Pro. Security and access events (see [Events](#events)) need Enterprise.
- Your role can manage alerts.
- On a self-hosted console, `ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set (a stable 32-byte base64 value,
 for example from `openssl rand -base64 32`). Every channel except email stores a secret, and
 without the key those channels are disabled. A console with pluggable connectors already has it.

records.title: Set up alerts
records.heading: Channels
records.text:
Add the channels first, so that a policy has somewhere to send.

1. Open **Alerts → Channels** and select **Add channel**.
2. Pick the transport and give the channel a name.
3. Paste the destination from the table. The sheet's **Where to find this** says where the
 service shows it.
4. Select **Add channel**. Alethia sends a sample event to check the destination, and adds the channel
 only when it arrives.

 Transport You paste Where it comes from 
 --- --- --- 
 Slack Payload URL Slack: Apps → Incoming Webhooks → Add to a channel 
 Microsoft Teams Payload URL The channel's Workflows or Incoming Webhook connector 
 Discord Payload URL Channel → Edit → Integrations → Webhooks → New Webhook 
 Google Chat Payload URL The space's Apps & integrations → Webhooks 
 Mattermost Payload URL Integrations → Incoming Webhooks → Add 
 Rocket.Chat Payload URL Admin → Integrations → New → Incoming Webhook 
 Webhook Payload URL, and an optional signing secret Any HTTPS endpoint you run 
 PagerDuty Routing key The Integration Key of an Events API v2 integration 
 Email Recipients, separated by commas — 

There is no Alethia app to install in Slack or Teams, and no OAuth. A payload URL or routing key

records.title: Set up alerts
records.heading: Policies
records.text:
1. Open **Alerts → Policies** and select **New policy**.
2. Give it a **Name**, such as `Production deploy failures`, and an optional description.
3. Under **Events**, pick one or more events.
4. Set the conditions, all optional:
 - **Minimum severity**: drop events below `info`, `warning` or `critical`.
 - **Scope filters**: limit to some **Projects**, **Job types**, **Resource types** or **Actions**.
 - **Throttle & grouping**: **Notify at most once per** a time window, so repeats of the same
 event become one notification.
5. Under **Routing**, turn on the channels to notify. A policy can notify several channels, and a
 channel can serve several policies.
6. Select **Create policy**.

A disabled policy keeps its settings and sends nothing.

records.title: Set up alerts
records.heading: Events
records.text:
Events come from the platform as things happen. You do not wire them up. Every event has a severity,
which the message shows, for example as a Slack emoji, or as a field that a webhook can route on.

 Category Events that fire today Listed as soon 
 --- --- --- 
 Deploy & drift Deploy started, succeeded or failed; job cancelled; destroy requested or completed; possible orphaned resources; auto-teardown gave up; cluster missing; environment status conflict Drift detected 
 Policy (PDP) Action denied, sensitive action allowed, role permissions changed Policy overridden 
 Access & roles (RBAC) Grant added or revoked; role created, changed or deleted; SSO provider updated or removed — 
 Members Member invited, joined or removed Member suspended 
 Cloud identities Identity connected or revoked; credential expiring or failed Credentials rotated 
 Cost Budget threshold crossed Spend spike, overage started 
 Workers & runners Worker unhealthy (a runner went offline) Worker stalled, runner minutes exhausted 
 Authentication — SSO sign-in failed, new-device sign-in, sign-in blocked 
 Platform health Background loop degraded or recovered, and other platform warnings — 
 Support Case opened, r

records.title: Set up alerts
records.heading: Activity
records.text:
**Alerts → Activity** lists every notification: the event, the channel, the status, the attempts and
any error. A delivery goes from `pending` to `sent`. One that fails is `failed`, and Alethia retries
it with backoff. After the last retry it is `dead`. You do not need to schedule the retries.

records.title: Set up alerts
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Trigger an event that a policy watches, such as a plan that you cancel. A `sent` row appears under
**Activity**, and the message arrives in the channel.

records.title: Set up alerts
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Notification email setup](/self-host/email)
- [Organizations](/guides/access/organizations)

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.text: Save and share a dashboard. Save an assistant dashboard as a named artifact, open it in any chat, and share it with your organization, a team or a role.

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.text:
Keep a [dashboard](/guides/assistant/dashboards) after its chat ends, and share it. A saved dashboard
is an **artifact**. Its widgets stay tied to the tools that made them, so they refresh against live
data when you open it in a chat.

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You have a dashboard on a chat's grid.
- To share, your organization is on a paid plan and has more than one member.

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.heading: Save it
records.text:
On the grid, or on one widget, select **Save as artifact** and give it a name. The name must be unique
in your library. A new artifact is private to you.

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.heading: Find it
records.text:
Open **Artifacts** in the rail. **Yours** lists what you saved. **Shared with you** lists what others
shared with your organization, a team you are on, or a role you hold. Each card shows the kind and the
number of widgets.

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.heading: Open it
records.text: Select an artifact. It opens read-only, as it was saved, and changes no chat.

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.heading: Act on it
records.text:
On an artifact you own:

 Action What it does 
 --- --- 
 **Add to this chat** Puts its widgets on the open chat's grid. 
 **Open in new chat** Starts a chat with the artifact on its grid. 
 **Share** Shares it with the whole organization, a team or a role. 
 **Delete** Removes it from the library. 

An artifact someone shared with you is view-only.

 

To start one from nothing, select **New artifact**: a new chat opens with a few prompts to begin.
In any chat, tag an artifact with `@` to ask Elench to explain or extend it.

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The artifact is under **Yours**. A teammate you shared it with finds it under **Shared with you**.

records.title: Save and share a dashboard
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Build a dashboard with the assistant](/guides/assistant/dashboards)
- [Ask the assistant](/guides/assistant)

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.text: Build a dashboard with the assistant. Turn Elench's answers into widgets on a grid beside the chat, or ask for a whole dashboard of your live infrastructure.

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.text:
Collect Elench's answers as widgets on a grid beside the chat, and keep them up to date. Each chat
has its own grid.

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - The assistant is open. See [Ask the assistant](/guides/assistant).

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.heading: Open the grid
records.text:
Open it from the chat's top bar. It also opens when Elench builds something. The grid has five
columns and grows downward, in a pane beside the chat. Drag the divider to resize it. Drag it past a
quarter of the width and the pane closes; the chevron at the edge brings it back.

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.heading: Ask for a dashboard
records.text:
Ask, for example, "Build a dashboard of my infrastructure: clusters, jobs, cost and drift." Elench
reads the data and lays out stat cards and charts.

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.heading: Fill one cell
records.text:
Select an empty cell, type in **Describe what goes here…**, and press Enter. Elench reads one thing
and puts the result in that cell.

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.heading: Arrange the widgets
records.text:
Drag a widget's grip to move it, or press Enter on the grip to move it with the keyboard. Drag its
corner to resize it.

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.heading: Widget controls
records.text:
Control What it does 
 --- --- 
 **Live** / **Frozen** A live widget refreshes on its own. A frozen one keeps its snapshot. 
 **Refresh** Reads the latest data now. 
 **Save** Saves the widget, or the whole grid, as an [artifact](/guides/assistant/artifacts).

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The widgets show your organization's data, and **Refresh** changes the numbers when your
infrastructure changes.

records.title: Build a dashboard with the assistant
records.heading: Related
records.text: - [Save and share a dashboard](/guides/assistant/artifacts): keep a grid after the chat, or share it.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.text: Ask the assistant. Ask Elench, the assistant in the console, about your real infrastructure, tag resources, and choose how much it may change on its own.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.text:
Ask Elench, the assistant in the console, about your clusters, jobs, cost and drift. It answers from
your real state. When you ask it to change something, it proposes the change; the verification
engine and a person still decide.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- On the hosted service, the assistant is on. A self-hosted console needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Without
 it, **Ask AI** does nothing and the assistant reports that it is not configured.
- Your organization's AI plan has allowance left. The **Usage** card on the overview shows the
 current session and the week.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: Open the assistant
records.text:
Select **Ask AI** at the top right of any page. It opens as a panel beside your work. **Expand** makes
it full screen, with a list of chats, the knowledge panel and the dashboard grid. **Minimize** docks it
again. The chat carries on in both.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: Pick the workspace
records.text:
Open it from an organization page for an organization chat, or from a project's pages or canvas
for a chat about that project. See [Workspaces](/guides/assistant/workspaces).

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: Tag what you mean
records.text:
Type `@` and pick a **project**, **cluster**, **job**, **connector**, **runner**, **cloud identity** or
**artifact**. The tag becomes a pill, so Elench knows exactly which resource you mean.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: Choose how much it may change
records.text:
The pill on the composer sets the editing mode:

 Mode What Elench does with a change 
 --- --- 
 **Ask** (default) Drafts the change and waits for you to approve each one. 
 **Auto** Applies edits in this chat without asking each time. 

Neither mode skips the deploy gate: a real deploy still runs the verify checks and needs a person.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: Choose the response style
records.text:
In the composer's settings, **Fast** suits everyday questions and **Thinking** suits complex work.
On the **Max** tier, **Deep reasoning** spends more on one hard question.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: What it can and cannot do
records.text:
It can It cannot 
 --- --- 
 Read what your role can read in this organization, through the same permission checks as the console Read another organization's data 
 Answer with widgets on a [dashboard](/guides/assistant/dashboards) Invent state it cannot read 
 Propose a plan or a deploy that a person accepts Apply a change on its own: the [verification engine](/concepts/elench) runs between `tofu plan` and `tofu apply`, and a person approves the deploy 

Usage counts against your organization's AI plan.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: Ask "Which of my jobs failed this week?". The answer names real jobs from your organization.

records.title: Ask the assistant
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Knowledge base](/guides/assistant/knowledge): give every chat the same instructions and documents.
- [Connect an MCP client](/guides/assistant/mcp): read Alethia from Claude, Cursor or another agent.
- [Agent runtime](/concepts/elench/agent-runtime)

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.text: Give the assistant standing knowledge. Pin instructions and named knowledge documents to a workspace, so every chat in it starts with them.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.text:
Tell Elench once how to behave and what to know, so you do not repeat it in every chat. What you pin
goes into every chat in the current [workspace](/guides/assistant/workspaces).

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - The assistant is open in the workspace you want: the organization, or a project.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: Open the knowledge panel
records.text: Expand the assistant and open **Knowledge** in the rail.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: Write instructions
records.text:
Under **Instructions**, write how Elench should act here, for example:

> This is production. Always require approval before an apply, and never propose a destroy.

Instructions save when you leave the field.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: Add a document
records.text:
Select **Add knowledge**, give it a title such as *Runbook: production deploys*, write the body, and
select **Save document**. It appears in the list with its size and when it was last edited.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: Edit or delete a document
records.text:
Hover over a document to edit or delete it. A deleted document leaves every future chat at once.

 

Elench can tell you which document it drew on, because each one has its own title.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: Keep it short
records.text:
Instructions and documents go with every message, so their size costs on every turn. A meter shows how
much of the 50,000-character limit you use. Write what Elench cannot work out for itself: conventions,
owners, on-call, runbooks and known problems.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: What Elench already knows
records.text:
In a project workspace, the panel shows **Already known**: the live facts Elench reads on every turn.
These are the project's identity and region, its environments and their status, and its recent jobs.
Do not pin these. The organization workspace has no such section: its chats use what you pin and the
tools Elench calls.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Start a new chat in the workspace and ask Elench to restate your instructions. It quotes them, and
names any document it uses.

records.title: Give the assistant standing knowledge
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Use a workspace](/guides/assistant/workspaces)
- [Agent runtime](/concepts/elench/agent-runtime): how the prompt is put together.

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.text: Connect an MCP client. Connect an external agent such as Claude Code, Claude, Cursor or Codex to the Alethia MCP server, so it reads your infrastructure, plans, and asks you to approve an apply or a destroy.

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.text:
Let an agent outside the console, such as Claude Code, Claude, Cursor or Codex, read your
infrastructure over [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). It calls the same permission-checked tools
as Elench, so it sees only what you can see. It can start a plan, and ask you to approve an apply or a
destroy. How MCP and the [CLI](/agents/cli) fit together is in [Alethia for agents](/agents).

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your console origin: the address you sign in to. `alethia auth status` prints it as `web origin`.
 The MCP endpoint is that origin plus `/api/mcp`.
- AI is on for your organization. It is always on when self-hosted, and every hosted organization has
 at least the free AI tier, which is on. With AI off, the server answers `403`.
- A client that meets these requirements:

 Requirement Detail 
 --- --- 
 Transport Remote MCP over Streamable HTTP: `POST` requests to `/api/mcp`. No `GET`, `DELETE` or SSE transport. 
 Protocol The current generation. Requests in the 2025 format are refused. 
 Sign-in OAuth 2.1. The client finds the authorization server from the `401` answer, and you sign in in the browser. 
 Client registration A Client ID Metadata Document: the client's ID is the HTTPS URL of a document it publishes. Anonymous dynamic registration is refused. 

No test record per client is published yet. Setup for Claude Code, Claude, Cursor, VS Code and Codex
is under [Pick a client](/agents#pick-a-client).

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Connect a client
records.text: There is no key to paste.

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Add the server
records.text:
In your client, add a remote MCP server at:

https:// /api/mcp

Add `?project= ` to hold every call to one project, or `?readonly` to list no tool that
changes anything.

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Sign in to Alethia
records.text: The client opens the console's sign-in page. Sign in as usual.

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Approve access
records.text:
If the page asks, approve the scopes: `read`, `design`, `plan`, `apply`, `destroy`. Approve at least
`read`. The token acts as you, under your role, and each scope only narrows what your role allows.
The token names this endpoint as its audience, and the server refuses tokens issued for anything
else.

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Use the tools
records.text:
The client lists the tools that your scopes allow. Ask the agent about your infrastructure.

 

If it does not connect, see [Troubleshoot MCP](/troubleshooting/mcp).

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Which organization the tools read
records.text:
If your consent for the client recorded an organization, every request acts there, on the projects
the consent names. Otherwise, requests act in the organization the console picks when there is no
browser session: the first one you joined, or your personal organization if you joined none.
Switching organizations in the console does not change it.

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: What the agent can do
records.text:
It can read projects and their configuration, jobs and their results, clusters, runners, connectors,
cloud accounts and their inventory, drift, the service catalog, docs, repository scans, and usage.
Results leave secrets out: never ArgoCD passwords, tokens or credentials. The
[tool reference](/agents/tools) lists all 19 tools.

 Tool What it does 
 --- --- 
 `create_project`, `apply_design_patch` Creates a project from a design, or changes a design. Changes nothing in the cloud. 
 `scan_repo` Starts a scan that infers what a repository needs. Never runs the repository. 
 `plan` Starts a plan of one environment. Changes nothing in the cloud. 
 `request_apply`, `request_destroy` Asks you to approve an apply or a destroy, and starts it once you approve. 
 `cancel_job` Cancels a queued or running job. 

Every apply or destroy needs your approval. The agent shows a link and an 8-character digest. Open the
link, check the digest, and approve in the console. Every deploy still passes the
[verification engine](/concepts/elench).

The agent cannot approve anything, start an audit of existing infrastructure, open console pages,
build dashboards, or use [artifacts](/guides/assistant/artifact

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: Ask the agent to list your Alethia projects. It calls `list_resources` and names your projects.

records.title: Connect an MCP client
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Alethia for agents](/agents)
- [Security model for agents](/agents/security)
- [Troubleshoot MCP](/troubleshooting/mcp)

records.title: Use a workspace
records.text: Use a workspace. Chat with Elench about the whole organization or about one project, each workspace with its own chats, knowledge and memory.

records.title: Use a workspace
records.text:
Keep chats about one project apart from chats about the whole organization. Each workspace has its
own chats, knowledge and memory, and nothing moves between them.

 Workspace Scope Grounded by 
 --- --- --- 
 **Organization** The whole organization, with the organization-wide tools Organization instructions and knowledge 
 **Project** One [project](/guides/design-project) Organization instructions and knowledge, then the project's own, then live facts about the project: its identity, environments and recent jobs

records.title: Use a workspace
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - The assistant is available. See [Ask the assistant](/guides/assistant).

records.title: Use a workspace
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. To chat about the organization, select **Ask AI** on an organization page, such as **Overview**.
2. To chat about a project, select **Ask AI** on one of the project's pages or on its canvas.

The workspace follows where you open the assistant. The switcher in the panel's header moves between
chats in the current workspace, not between workspaces.

records.title: Use a workspace
records.heading: What each workspace keeps apart
records.text:
- **Chats.** You see only the current workspace's chats.
- **Knowledge.** The knowledge panel edits the current workspace's
 [instructions and documents](/guides/assistant/knowledge). Every chat in a project inherits the
 project's, and they never reach organization chats or other projects.
- **Memory.** The organization has one memory and each project has its own, kept under the
 organization's and never shared with another project. See
 [Agent runtime](/concepts/elench/agent-runtime).
- **Tools.** A project's tools are not offered in an organization chat.

Chats, knowledge and instructions belong to you. Elench reads and writes only what you own, so a
teammate cannot see them.

records.title: Use a workspace
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Open the assistant from a project page: the chat list shows only that project's chats, and the
knowledge panel shows the project's **Already known** facts.

records.title: Use a workspace
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Knowledge base](/guides/assistant/knowledge)
- [Ask the assistant](/guides/assistant)

records.title: Classify resources
records.text: Classify resources. Define dimensions and their allowed values once, then label projects, clusters, cloud identities, runners, members and more from that closed list.

records.title: Classify resources
records.text:
Label your resources from one list that an admin controls, instead of free-form tags. An admin
defines **dimensions**, such as *Environment*, and the **values** each one allows, such as `dev`,
`staging` and `prod`. People then **assign** those values to resources. So `env=prod`,
`Environment=Production` and `PROD` cannot all appear.

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- To define dimensions and values, you need the Editor role (`org:edit`). Everyone else sees a
 read-only view.
- To assign a value, you need `org:edit` and the right to edit that resource. Without both, you see
 the values but no picker.

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Open the page
records.text:
Open **Settings → Classification**. On an empty page, you can start from a template: Environment,
Data classification, Team or Cost center.

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Create a dimension
records.text:
Give it a label. The `key` fills in from the label, and cannot change after you create the
dimension, so choose it with care. Add a description if you like, and choose the mode:

 Mode A resource holds Example 
 --- --- --- 
 Single At most one value. A new value replaces the old one. *Environment*: one of dev, staging or prod 
 Multi Any number of values *Team*: platform and payments

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Add values
records.text: Type a label and press Enter. To set the slug or a color, open the value's editor.

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Put them in order
records.text:
Drag dimensions and values. Every picker shows them in this order.

 

 
Deleting a dimension deletes its values and every assignment of them. Deleting a value removes it
from every resource. Neither can be undone.

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Assign values
records.text:
Open the resource and use its classification picker:

 Resource Where 
 --- --- 
 Projects Project → **Settings → General** 
 Environments A project's **Environments** 
 Clusters **Clusters** 
 Cloud identities and connector credentials **Connectors** → the account in the detail sheet 
 Runners **Runners** 
 Members, Roles **Settings → Members**, **Settings → Roles** 
 Alert policies, alert channels **Alerts → Policies**, **Alerts → Channels** 
 Support cases The case's detail 

Alert deliveries and runner usage sessions cannot be classified: they are records, not things you
manage. From the CLI, see [Classification commands](/reference/cli/classification).

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: What classification does not do
records.text:
Classification does not enforce anything. No permission check, policy, provisioning step or
