records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.text: Plan and deploy from the console. Plan an environment, review what the plan would change, deploy exactly that plan, or destroy the environment, from the console.

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.text:
Plan an environment, review the plan, and deploy that exact plan. Nothing is provisioned until you
deploy. To do the same from a terminal, see [Plan and apply](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply).

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The project has a design on its **Architecture** canvas. See [Design a project](/guides/design-project).
- A cloud account and a Git provider are connected. See [Connectors](/guides/connectors).
- A runner is online for your organization. See [Runners](/guides/runners).
- Your role can plan and deploy the project.

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Open the review
records.text:
On the project's **Architecture** canvas, pick the environment, then open **Review and deploy** from
the changes bar at the foot of the canvas. The review lists your design changes. If it lists
**Issues to fix before planning**, fix them first.

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Run the plan
records.text:
Select **Run plan**. Alethia saves the design and queues a `PLAN` job. The runner plans the
environment, runs the [verify gate](#verify-gate) on the plan, and prices it when it can (see
[Cost estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation)).

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Review the plan
records.text:
When the plan completes, the review shows **What the plan would change**: each resource marked as a
create, change, replace or destroy, and the cost after this plan. The plan is **Current** while
the design and the environment have not changed since it ran. It is **Out of date** when the design
was saved after it, or another job ran on the environment.

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Deploy
records.text:
Select **Deploy**. When the plan
destroys or replaces resources, you type the environment's name to confirm. Alethia queues a
`DEPLOY` job that applies the saved plan. The verify gate runs again before `tofu apply`.

 

A successful plan job also has a **Deploy** button on its page, which asks which runner to use. See
[Read a job](/guides/jobs/job-detail).

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The `DEPLOY` job ends with `SUCCESS`. The runner installs ArgoCD (see
[GitOps with ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd)), and the console records the cluster, database and
cache endpoints on the environment and marks it active. The environment's cluster appears under
[Clusters](/guides/clusters).

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Verify gate
records.text:
Between `tofu plan` and `tofu apply`, the runner runs [Elench](/concepts/elench) on the plan JSON.
Each control passes, fails, or is `not_evaluable` when the plan cannot prove it. A hard failure
stops the deploy before `tofu apply`, unless an [override](/guides/jobs/verify-override) waives
that control. Plan jobs carry the same report, in `verify_result` in the job's execution metadata.
The controls are listed in the [control catalog](/reference/control-catalog).

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: How a deploy stays bound to its plan
records.text:
- The `PLAN` job must have ended with `SUCCESS`, or the `DEPLOY` job fails.
- The runner downloads the plan's saved file and applies it. If it cannot fetch the file, it logs a
 warning and plans again from the deploy job's own snapshot.
- Jobs queued through the jobs API, which the CLI uses, carry a configuration hash. When both jobs
 have one and they differ, the deploy fails with `configuration changed since plan was generated`.
 Console jobs carry no hash, so the saved plan file is what binds them.

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Destroy an environment
records.text:
A destroy has no plan step.

1. On the canvas, open the environment's settings and select **Destroy environment**.
2. Type the environment's name and confirm. If other environments are placed on its cluster, the
 dialog lists them in the order they are destroyed.

Alethia queues a `DESTROY` job, and the environment goes from destroying to destroyed.

 
A destroy removes every cloud resource of the environment and cannot be undone. The OpenTofu state
is kept, so you can deploy again, but data in databases is lost.

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Free plan limits
records.text:
The free Hobby plan has two limits on jobs:

 Limit Hobby Pro Enterprise 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Jobs running at once 2 8 No limit 
 Jobs you start in a rolling 24 hours 25 No limit No limit 

A job over the concurrency limit waits in the queue. At the daily limit, the next plan, deploy,
destroy or scan is refused with an upgrade prompt, and the limit clears as older jobs leave the
window. A self-hosted console changes the daily number with `ALETHIA_FREE_DAILY_JOB_QUOTA`.

Jobs that Alethia runs for you, such as drift detection, cluster probes, reconciliation and
ephemeral-environment cleanup, never count and are never blocked. Kubeconfig requests do not count
toward the daily limit either. They have their own limit of 20 requests in 10 minutes for each
person in an organization, and their runner time counts toward your included runner minutes.

records.title: Plan and deploy from the console
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Read a job](/guides/jobs/job-detail)
- [Troubleshoot a deploy](/troubleshooting/deploy)
- [Deploy jobs](/concepts/runner/job-execution/deploy-jobs): what the runner does inside a deploy.

records.title: Waive a verify control on one deploy
records.text: Waive a verify control on one deploy. Waive named failing controls of the verify gate on one queued deploy, for a limited time, with a recorded reason.

records.title: Waive a verify control on one deploy
records.text:
Let one deploy go ahead when the [verify gate](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) fails on a
control you have decided to accept. An override waives only the control IDs you name, on one
`DEPLOY` job, for a limited time. Every other control still blocks.

 
The console and the CLI have no control that records an override yet. It is recorded by the
`recordVerifyOverride` server action, with the rules below.

records.title: Waive a verify control on one deploy
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You have the failing control IDs, for example `LEASTPRIV-001`. They are in the plan job's
 execution metadata, under `verify_result`. The [control catalog](/reference/control-catalog) says
 what each ID checks.
- The `DEPLOY` job is still `QUEUED`. No override can be set after a runner claims the job.
- Your role can edit the job.

records.title: Waive a verify control on one deploy
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Name the failing control IDs. At least one is needed.
2. Give a reason. It cannot be empty.
3. Set how long the waiver lasts, in hours. The default is 24.

The override is refused when the list is empty, the reason is empty, the job is not found, or the
job is no longer `QUEUED`.

records.title: Waive a verify control on one deploy
records.heading: What is recorded
records.text:
Field Value 
 --- --- 
 `controls` The control IDs you named 
 `reason` Your reason 
 `by` The person who recorded it, set by the server 
 `expiry` The time of recording plus the hours you set 

When a runner claims the job, it passes the override to the gate. The gate waives only the named
controls, and the signed [evidence receipt](/concepts/elench/engine-internals) of the deploy records
the waiver as an exception.

records.title: Waive a verify control on one deploy
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The deploy passes the gate. The waiver is listed on the **Evidence** page under
**Recorded waivers**, as **Active** until it expires.

records.title: Waive a verify control on one deploy
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Plan and deploy from the console](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply)
- [Troubleshoot a deploy](/troubleshooting/deploy)

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.text: Add and manage runners. Deploy a runner into your AWS account or register one you run anywhere, then watch its status, update it, and remove it.

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.text:
Add a runner, the agent that runs your jobs, and keep it healthy. Every plan, deploy and scan runs
on a runner. How a runner works is in [Runner](/concepts/runner).

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your organization runs its own runners. The **Runners** item appears in the sidebar only then; the
 page is still at `/{org}/~/runners`.
- To deploy a runner, you have a verified AWS [connection](/guides/connectors/aws) and a runner
 that is already online to run the deploy.

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.heading: Choose the kind of runner
records.text:
Kind Where it runs How it is added Updates Billing 
 --- --- --- --- --- 
 **Managed** Alethia's Hetzner servers A [warm pool](/guides/fleet-pools) creates and removes it The pool replaces it with a new version By the hours it is provisioned 
 **Self · Deployed** One ECS Fargate task in your AWS account **Add runner → Deploy to a cloud** **Update all** rolls it in place Your AWS bill 
 **Self · Registered** Any host you run, on any cloud or on premises **Add runner → Register your own** You replace the binary or image Not billed by Alethia 

A deployed runner is AWS only, because the runner template exists only for AWS. This limits where
the runner runs, not what it provisions: a registered runner in any place provisions every cloud
Alethia supports. A deployed runner is one task that does not scale with the queue. Only managed
runners scale. See [Scaling](/concepts/runner/scaling).

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.heading: Add a runner
records.text:
### Open the dialog
 On **Runners**, select **Add runner**, then **Deploy to a cloud**.

 ### Pick the account
 Choose the AWS **Cloud account** and the region. Only verified AWS accounts are listed.

 ### Deploy
 Select **Deploy runner**. An online runner runs a `DEPLOY_RUNNER` job, which creates the ECS task
 definition, IAM roles, a CloudWatch log group and security groups. After about two minutes, the
 new runner shows **Online**.

 

 From the CLI, use `alethia runner deploy`. It refuses any cloud other than AWS, as the console does.
 
 
 

 ### Open the dialog
 On **Runners**, select **Add runner**, then **Register your own**.

 ### Name it
 Enter the **Runner name** and select **Register runner**.

 ### Save the credentials
 Copy the **Runner ID** and **Runner Token**. The token is shown once and cannot be recovered. If
 you lose it, register the runner again.

 ### Start the runner
 Set the credentials as environment variables on your host and start the runner. See
 [Self-operated runners](/guides/runners/self-operated).

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.heading: Watch your runners
records.text:
Filter the runner cards by name, **Cloud**, status (**Online**, **Offline**, **Draining**), operator
(**Managed**, **Self · Deployed**, **Self · Registered**), **Region** and **Version**. The page
updates by itself.

 Status Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Online** Ready for jobs. The runner holds a connection to the console that refreshes about every 10 seconds. 
 **Draining** Finishes its current job and takes no new ones. 
 **Offline** The connection dropped, or nothing was heard for 45 seconds. Its jobs go back in the queue. 

While a job acts on a runner, its card shows **Provisioning…**, **Updating…** or **Destroying…**.
Each card also shows the runner's operator, its clouds (or **Any**), the region for a managed runner,
its version, its active job, and its provisioned hours or when it was last seen.

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.heading: Update runners
records.text:
Each runner reports its version. Select a version on a card to read its release notes; an outdated
runner shows that an update is available. The **Versions** panel shows the **Latest release** and a
**Changelog**. When runners are behind, **Update all** queues an `UPDATE_RUNNER` job for each
deployed runner that can be updated in place. Runners it cannot update are marked as needing a new
deploy. Managed runners are replaced by their pool.

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.heading: Set a default or remove a runner
records.text:
- **Set as default** marks the runner that a job uses when you pick none. **Clear default** undoes it.
- **Destroy** tears down a deployed runner's cloud resources through a `DESTROY_RUNNER` job. You
 choose which runner runs the destroy.
- **Remove** deletes a registered runner, so it is no longer given jobs.

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The new runner's card shows **Online**. Queue a plan: its job page shows the runner that claimed it.

records.title: Add and manage runners
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Self-operated runners](/guides/runners/self-operated)
- [Run a warm pool of runners](/guides/fleet-pools)
- [Authentication](/concepts/authentication): how the runner token is checked.

records.title: Run your own runner
records.text: Run your own runner. Run a registered runner on a host you operate, on any cloud, on premises or air-gapped, with the environment variables it reads.

records.title: Run your own runner
records.text:
Run the runner binary or image on a host you control. A registered runner provisions every cloud
Alethia supports, wherever it runs. It connects out to the console over HTTPS, so it needs no
inbound port.

records.title: Run your own runner
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You registered the runner and have its **Runner ID** and **Runner Token**. See
 [Add and manage runners](/guides/runners#add-a-runner).
- The host can reach the console over HTTPS.
- If you run the binary instead of the official image, the host has these tools. The runner needs no
 cloud CLI (`aws`, `gcloud` or `az`): it gets cloud credentials itself, keylessly.

 Tool Purpose Version 
 --- --- --- 
 OpenTofu (`tofu`) Provisioning 1.9 or later 
 `kubectl` Cluster access Matches your clusters 
 Helm Installs ArgoCD and cluster components Any current 

The official image bundles all three and a cache of OpenTofu providers.

records.title: Run your own runner
records.heading: Start the runner
records.text:
./runner

The runner confirms its registration, keeps a connection to the console, and sends a heartbeat
every 30 seconds. A wake on that connection starts a job within a second. A poll every 30 seconds is
the fallback.

 

The runner holds no object-storage credentials. OpenTofu state goes through the console's state
proxy, with a token for each job. See [Cloud credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

records.title: Run your own runner
records.heading: Environment variables
records.text:
Variable Required Description 
 --- --- --- 
 `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN` Yes The console's base URL 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_ID` Yes The runner ID from registration 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_TOKEN` Yes The runner token from registration 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_OPERATOR` No `self`, the default. The older `ALETHIA_RUNNER_MODE=self-hosted` still works. 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_PROVIDERS` No The clouds this runner serves, separated by commas, such as `aws`. Unset means any. 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_SLOTS` No Jobs at once (default `1`). Above `1`, each job runs in its own worker process: run the container with an init (`docker --init`, or `init: true` in Compose) so that stray tools are cleaned up. 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_INSTANCE_ID` No A separate ID for each runner when several share a host 
 `ALETHIA_HELM_REGISTRY_ALLOW_PRIVATE` No `1` lets chart pulls reach a registry on a private network, such as Harbor on RFC 1918 addresses. Off by default. Loopback and link-local addresses, including cloud metadata, stay blocked. See [Chart repositories](/guides/connectors/chart-repositories). 
 `INFRACOST_API_KEY` No Turns on cost estimates for plans 
 `HCLOUD_TOKEN` No A Hetzner API token that this runner uses, so that Alethia does not stor

records.title: Run your own runner
records.heading: Common setups
records.text:
Setup What to do 
 --- --- 
 **On premises** Run the runner on a bastion host or a CI machine inside your network. OpenTofu then reaches resources on the internal network. 
 **Air-gapped** Download OpenTofu providers and modules in advance, set up a local provider mirror, and give the runner an approved network path to the console. 
 **Hetzner token kept by you** Set `HCLOUD_TOKEN` on this runner. Jobs for a Hetzner connection that has no stored token are marked as needing a self-operated runner, so managed runners never take them. 
 **Local development** Run the runner next to a development console, with `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN=http://localhost:3000`.

records.title: Run your own runner
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The runner's card on **Runners** shows **Online** within a few seconds of the start. Its log on
stdout shows that it registered.

records.title: Alethia documentation
records.text: Alethia documentation. Alethia designs Kubernetes clusters and the services around them, provisions them into your cloud with OpenTofu, and delivers your apps with ArgoCD. Start here.

records.title: Alethia documentation
records.text:
Alethia is a control plane for Kubernetes on AWS, GCP, Azure and Hetzner. You design a cluster and
its services in the console or in one file, and Alethia provisions them into your own cloud account
with OpenTofu, checks every plan before it applies, and delivers your apps with ArgoCD.

 
 
 Sign up, connect a cloud, and deploy your first cluster. Install the CLI.
 
 
 Do one task: connect an account, design a project, run jobs, manage access.
 
 
 How Alethia works: projects and environments, runners, verification, security.
 
 
 Every CLI command, the API, configuration, controls and limits.
 
 
 Run the whole platform on your own VM or Kubernetes cluster.
 
 
 Connect Claude, Cursor, VS Code or Codex, and let them read and plan.
 
 

New to Alethia? [Tutorials](/tutorials) build something real from start to finish. Stuck? Start at
[Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting).

records.title: Auth APIs
records.text: Auth APIs. Device code flow endpoints for CLI authentication — generate, exchange, refresh.

records.title: Auth APIs
records.text: These endpoints implement the **Device Authorization Grant** (RFC 8628) for CLI authentication. See [Authentication Flows](/concepts/authentication) for the complete flow.

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: POST /api/auth/cli/generate
records.text:
Called by the **browser** (authenticated user) to approve a CLI login attempt.

**Requires:** Active browser session (Better Auth session cookie).

**Body:**
{
 "device_code": "uuid-from-cli"
}

**Effect:**
- Upserts a `cli_logins` record keyed by the device code, storing the user's profile ID (which signifies approval) and the user's first linked git provider access token (held in the `verification_code` column for the CLI to pick up on exchange)
- Returns `{ "success": true }`

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: POST /api/auth/cli/exchange
records.text:
Called by the **CLI** to exchange the approved device code for tokens.

**No authentication required** — the browser must have already approved the device code (its `cli_logins` record must have a `profile_id` set).

**Body:**
{
 "device_code": "uuid-from-cli"
}

**Validation:**
- Looks up the `cli_logins` record by device code
- Verifies that `profile_id` is set (meaning the browser approved the login)

**Response:**
{
 "access_token": "jwt...",
 "refresh_token": "jwt...",
 "provider_token": "git-oauth-token",
 "user_email": "user@example.com"
}

**Token Details:**
- **Access token**: 1-hour TTL, HS256 signed with `CLI_JWT_SECRET`
- **Refresh token**: 90-day TTL, same signing

JWT payload:
{
 "sub": "user-uuid",
 "email": "user@example.com",
 "type": "access",
 "iss": "urn:example:issuer",
 "aud": "urn:example:audience"
}

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: POST /api/auth/cli/refresh

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: GET /api/auth/[...all]
records.text:
Better Auth's catch-all handler owns the OAuth callback at `/api/auth/[...all]` after provider authentication, along with email-OTP verify, session, account linking, and sign-out.

Better Auth persists the provider's access token to the `account` table. The CLI `generate` endpoint later reads it from there (via `auth.api.getAccessToken`) to hand the git provider token to the CLI.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.text: CLI APIs. API endpoints used by the alethia CLI for project, job, and runner management.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.text: These endpoints are called by the alethia CLI. Authentication is via `Authorization: Bearer {jwt}` header with a CLI-issued JWT. See [Authentication Flows](/concepts/authentication).

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: GET /api/cli/configurations

records.title: CLI APIs

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: POST /api/jobs
records.text:
Create a new job. Accepts:

{
 "job_type": "PLAN",
 "configuration_id": "project-uuid",
 "assigned_runner_id": "runner-uuid",
 "plan_job_id": "plan-job-uuid"
}

Valid job types: PLAN, DEPLOY, DESTROY, DESTROY_RUNNER.

If `configuration_id` is provided, the server auto-resolves `cloud_identity_id`, computes config hash, and creates a config snapshot.

records.title: API Overview
records.text: API Overview. Alethia API endpoints — authentication methods, base URLs, and route categories.

records.title: API Overview
records.text: Alethia exposes three categories of API routes, each with its own authentication mechanism.

records.title: API Overview
records.heading: Authentication Methods
records.text:
Category Auth Header Token Type Used By 
 ---------- ----------- ------------ --------- 
 **Runner APIs** `X-Runner-ID` + `X-Runner-Token` SHA-256 hashed token Runner agents 
 **CLI APIs** `Authorization: Bearer {jwt}` HS256 JWT (1h access, 90d refresh) alethia CLI 
 **Release APIs** `Authorization: Bearer {secret}` Static secret (`RELEASE_API_SECRET`) CI/CD pipeline 

See [Authentication Flows](/concepts/authentication) for details on each mechanism.

records.title: API Overview
records.heading: API Categories
records.text:
Job claiming, heartbeat, status updates, log streaming, plan artifacts.
 
 
 Configurations, jobs, runners, repositories.
 
 
 Device code flow: generate, exchange, refresh.

records.title: API Overview
records.heading: Request Format
records.text:
All APIs accept and return JSON. Errors return a consistent format:

{
 "error": "Human-readable error message"
}

HTTP status codes:
- `200` — success
- `201` — created
- `400` — validation error
- `401` — authentication failure
- `404` — not found
- `409` — conflict (e.g., duplicate release version)
- `500` — internal error

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.text: OIDC APIs. The public, unauthenticated discovery and JWKS endpoints of the Alethia workload-identity OIDC issuer.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.text:
Alethia is its own OpenID Connect identity provider for cloud workload-identity federation. It mints a short-lived, signed JWT so managed cloud connectors can federate **keylessly** — the private signing key never leaves the vault, and a customer's cloud verifies the token against Alethia's published public keys.

This surface is deliberately minimal. It has no interactive or user-facing endpoints — it is not a general OAuth server. Only two routes are public: the discovery document and the JWKS. Both serve static signed material.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Base URL
records.text:
The issuer is served under `/api/oidc` on the app origin. The full issuer URL is:

${APP_URL}/api/oidc

This value is the token `iss` claim and the URL a customer's cloud is configured to trust.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Authentication
records.text:
Both endpoints are **public, unauthenticated, and `GET`-only**. Anyone can fetch them. Only public key material is served — no private key fields are ever exposed.

Responses are cacheable:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=300

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Availability

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: GET /api/oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration
records.text:
Returns the OIDC discovery document. A customer's cloud fetches this to locate the JWKS before verifying a minted token.

**Response:**

{
 "issuer": "https://app.example.com/api/oidc",
 "jwks_uri": "https://app.example.com/api/oidc/jwks",
 "response_types_supported": ["id_token"],
 "subject_types_supported": ["public"],
 "id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": ["RS256"],
 "scopes_supported": ["openid"],
 "claims_supported": ["iss", "sub", "aud", "iat", "exp"]
}

Only `issuer` and `jwks_uri` are load-bearing for federation. The remaining fields satisfy the validators that fetch discovery.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: GET /api/oidc/jwks

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Minted Token
records.text:
The issuer mints tokens server-side for a cloud's token exchange; there is no public token endpoint. The token is an RS256-signed JWT with these characteristics:

 Field Value 
 ------- ------- 
 `alg` (header) `RS256` 
 `kid` (header) Thumbprint of the signing key 
 `typ` (header) `JWT` 
 `iss` The issuer URL (`${APP_URL}/api/oidc`) 
 `sub` `alethia-connector` — a single stable, non-secret workload subject, never per-customer 
 `aud` The cloud's expected audience (for example `api://AzureADTokenExchange`) 
 `iat` Issued-at timestamp 
 `exp` Expiry — a maximum lifetime of 600 seconds 

The `sub` claim must match the Azure federated-credential subject. The `aud` claim scopes the token to one cloud so it cannot be replayed at a different cloud.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Auth APIs](/reference/api/auth-apis) — device code flow for CLI authentication.
- [Runner APIs](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/runner-apis.md) — endpoints used by Runner agents.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.text: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO). Manage RBAC roles and access grants, and inspect SSO providers, from the alethia CLI.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.text:
Alethia's authorization model has three CLI-manageable parts:

- **Roles** are permission bundles. Four **built-in** templates ship with every org
 (`owner`, `admin`, `operator`, `viewer`) and are read-only; **custom** roles are org-scoped
 and editable.
- **Grants** bind a **principal** (a user or a team) to a role **or** a single permission, at a
 resource scope, as an **allow** or an explicit **deny** (deny wins).
- **SSO providers** are the configured OIDC/SAML identity providers (read-only from the CLI).

All commands operate on the **active organization**, set with
[`alethia org switch`](/reference/cli/organizations), or on the organization named by the global
`--org ` for a single invocation. `--org` selects a scope rather than granting one: naming an
organization you are not a member of is refused with `403`. Every command accepts it, along with the
global [`-o, --output `](/reference/cli/identity#output-formats) and `--no-input` flags.

 
Authoring **custom roles** and **access grants** requires an **Enterprise** license. Listing roles
(the built-in templates) and reading SSO providers work on any plan. SSO provider secrets and
config JSON are never returned by the API.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia roles list
records.text:
Lists the active organization's roles — the four built-in templates (flagged) followed by any
custom roles, with a permission count.

alethia roles list
alethia roles list -o json

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia roles create
records.text:
Creates a custom role. Repeat `--permission` for each `resource:action` key the role should carry;
with no `--permission` on a terminal, the keys are offered as a checklist read from the control
plane's own catalog, so a permission added to the product appears here without a CLI release.

alethia roles create deployers --permission project:plan --permission project:deploy
alethia roles create

{/* fieldspec: alethia roles create */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Name What the custom role is called `[name]` — 
 Permissions The resource:action keys the role carries, offered from the server's own catalog `--permission` — 

A role with no permissions is accepted, so `--no-input` without `--permission` is not an error — it
creates a role that grants nothing yet. `--dry-run` prints the role that would be created and
creates nothing.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia roles delete
records.text:
Deletes a custom role. Name it with `--name`, or pick from the org's custom roles; grants
referencing the role are removed with it.

alethia roles delete --name deployers --yes
alethia roles delete

{/* fieldspec: alethia roles delete */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Role Which custom role to delete; built-in templates cannot be deleted `[role_id]` `--name` 

The four built-in templates cannot be deleted. They are not offered in the picker, and naming one
is refused whether you name it with `--name` or by its id: the control plane's delete skips a
built-in role and still answers `ok`, so sending it would report a deletion that did not happen.

Destructive, so it confirms: you type the role's name. `--yes` skips the prompt and is required
with `--no-input`; without it the command exits `9` and deletes nothing. `--dry-run` names the role
that would be deleted and deletes nothing.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia grants list
records.text:
Lists the active organization's access grants.

alethia grants list
alethia grants list -o json

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia grants add
records.text:
Assigns a grant. A grant binds a principal to **exactly one** of a role (`--role`) or a single
permission (`--permission`), at a resource scope. Omit `--resource` for an **org-wide** grant.

`--principal` takes an **email** (or a team name) as readily as an id, and `--role` takes a **role
name**; anything that is not already a uuid is looked up against the active org. With no
`--principal` on a terminal, the whole grant is asked for, one question at a time. `--dry-run`
resolves every name to its id, prints the grant that would be written, and writes nothing.

alethia grants add --principal ada@example.com --role deployers
alethia grants add --principal platform --principal-type team --permission project:deploy --resource-type project
alethia grants add

With no `--principal` on a terminal you are asked for all seven, in order, and every one of them
that has a list behind it is a **picker over live values** — the members and teams of the org, its
roles or the server's permission catalog, and the projects, runners or cloud accounts of the kind
you scope to.

{/* fieldspec: alethia grants add */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ------

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: A grant stays inside its organization
records.text:
Everything a grant names must belong to the organization you write it in. The control plane
refuses the grant with a `400` and a `reason` when:

- the role is a custom role of another organization (`foreign_role`). Built-in roles are valid
 in every organization.
- the team is a team of another organization (`foreign_team`).
- the resource is not a project, runner or cloud account of this organization
 (`foreign_resource`). An id that names nothing is refused the same way.

A connector cannot be a grant's scope. The connector catalog is shared by every organization, so no
organization owns a connector.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: The resource is picked, not typed
records.text:
Once you have chosen a **kind**, the form lists that kind's live resources and you choose one:
projects from `alethia project list`, runners from `alethia runner list`, cloud accounts from
`alethia connector list`. Nothing has to be copied out of another command's output.

Every one of those lists opens with **Every _kind_ in this organization** — the id-less scope, which
is what `--resource-type project` with no `--resource` has always meant and what `grants list`
renders as a bare `project`. Choosing it is how you grant over a whole kind.

The `org` kind asks nothing at all. `org` *is* org-wide: the control plane treats a grant as
org-wide when the kind is `org` **or** the id is absent, so an id given alongside `--resource-type
org` would be stored on the grant and then ignored by everything that reads it. `--resource` with
the `org` kind is therefore **refused** rather than sent — and since `org` is the default kind, that
refusal is what you get from `--resource ` with no `--resource-type`, which would otherwise have
granted over the whole organization while the command line read as one project.

A kind this CLI has no list for is still askable — you are asked for the id, and th

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia grants remove
records.text:
Revokes a grant. A grant has no name — it *is* the binding — so pass the id you have, or pick one
from the org's grants.

alethia grants remove --yes
alethia grants remove

{/* fieldspec: alethia grants remove */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Grant Which grant to revoke; pick it from the org's grants rather than copying an id `[grant_id]` — 

Destructive, so it confirms; `--yes` skips the prompt and is required with `--no-input` — without
it the command exits `9` and revokes nothing. When the CLI picks the grant for you, it prints which
one on stderr before it asks. `--dry-run` names the grant that would be revoked and revokes
nothing.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia sso list
records.text:
Lists the active organization's configured SSO identity providers (OIDC and SAML). Read-only —
registering a provider is done in the console. Secrets and config JSON are never shown; `Enabled`
reflects whether the provider's domain is verified.

alethia sso list
alethia sso list -o json

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia sso get
records.text:
Shows a single provider as a detail card. Name it by the email domain it serves, or pick from the
org's providers.

alethia sso get --domain example.com
alethia sso get

{/* fieldspec: alethia sso get */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Provider Which configured provider to show; name it by its email domain `[id]` `--domain`

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.text: Add-on Commands. Enable, reconfigure, disable and inspect the marketplace add-ons in a project environment.

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.text:
The `addon` group (alias `addons`) manages the **marketplace add-ons** (observability, databases,
caches, … — OSS Helm charts deployed via ArgoCD) in an environment: enable one, reconfigure it,
disable it, or list what is installed.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These subcommands call `/cli/projects/ /addons`
with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on the **active organization**
(`alethia org switch`). Pass `--org ` to scope a single invocation to a different organization —
it is refused with `403` if you are not a member of it.

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: No id is copied between commands
records.text:
`enable`, `disable` and `bump` take the add-on id as an **optional** first argument. Omit it on a terminal
and the add-ons installed in the environment are offered to choose from, so nothing has to be read
out of one command's output and pasted into the next. The add-on the CLI resolved is printed on
**stderr**, so `-o json` still emits a document that parses.

Pass `--project` and the id is the only thing missing; omit `--project` too and you are asked for
that as well. With `--no-input` (or a non-terminal stdin/stdout) nothing is asked: the command
exits `9` naming the argument to pass, so a script never blocks on a prompt it cannot answer.

 
One handoff remains, and it is the CLI's only one here: installing an add-on that is **not yet
enabled** needs its catalog id, and the CLI has no endpoint that enumerates the marketplace
catalog — browse it in the console. The picker offers what is installed, which covers every
reconfigure and every disable.

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Output and exit codes
records.text:
**The result is on stdout, and everything else is on stderr.** With `--output json`, `enable`,
`disable` and `bump` print one object:

{
 "id": "loki",
 "kind": "addon",
 "action": "updated",
 "job": null,
 "dry_run": false,
 "object": { "project": "shop", "env": "staging", "enabled": true, "mode": "", "version": null }
}

`enable` and `disable` both report `updated`: an enable is an upsert, and a disabled add-on keeps
its record with `enabled` set to `false`. In the object, an empty `mode` and a `null` `version` mean
that the stored value was kept. `bump` reports `created` when it opened a pull request and
`unchanged` otherwise, and its object is described under [`alethia addon bump`](#alethia-addon-bump).
When the next step needs saying — "it reaches the cluster on the next apply" — it is a line on
stderr.

**A refusal exits with the code of its kind.** stdout stays empty, and stderr says what happened
and the command to run next.

 Exit Meaning on this page 
 ------ ---------------------- 
 `6` The add-on, project or environment that you named does not exist, or the picker had nothing installed to offer 
 `8` A flag value is not valid: a `--mode` outside the enum, a `--set` with

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: alethia addon list
records.text:
List the add-ons installed in a project environment.

alethia addon list --project my-project
alethia addon list -p my-project -e staging
alethia addon list -p my-project -o json

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `--project`, `-p` No Project name or id. Omit it on a terminal and you are asked. 
 `--env`, `-e` No Environment id, name or stage; an exact name wins over a stage. Omit to use the project's default environment. 

Columns: **Add-on** (the catalog id), **Enabled** (✓ / —), **Mode** (`managed` `gitops`),
**Version**, **Update**, **Status**, **Sync**, **Health**, **Last synced**.

**Version** is the chart version the add-on deploys with: your pin if you set one with
`addon enable --version`, otherwise the catalog default. In `-o json`, `version_pinned` is `true`
for a pin and `false` for the catalog default.

**Update** is what the catalog offers this add-on. A catalog chart update reaches an unpinned
`managed` add-on on the environment's next deploy, and nothing else, so the column is about the
other two cases:

- A pin older than the catalog's version shows `4.15.1 available`.
- A `gitops` add-on shows `repo decides (catalog 4.15.1)`. The file

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: alethia addon enable
records.text:
Enable an add-on in an environment, or reconfigure one already enabled.

bash

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Reconfigure: pick from what is installed
records.text: alethia addon enable -p my-project

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Enable with the catalog defaults
records.text: alethia addon enable kube-prometheus-stack -p my-project

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: With settings, in one environment
records.text: alethia addon enable loki -p my-project -e staging --set retention_days=7

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: GitOps delivery: the manifest is written to your apps repo, and you own it
records.text: alethia addon enable falco -p my-project --mode gitops

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Advanced: a raw Helm values override
records.text: alethia addon enable loki -p my-project --values-file ./loki-values.yaml

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Remove the Advanced override
records.text: alethia addon enable loki -p my-project --values-file ""

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Reset one setting to the add-on's default
records.text: alethia addon enable loki -p my-project --set retention_days=null

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Pin the chart version in one environment
records.text: alethia addon enable kube-prometheus-stack -p my-project -e staging --version 58.2.1

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Remove the pin: the catalog default version applies again
records.text:
alethia addon enable kube-prometheus-stack -p my-project -e staging --version ""

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[addon-id]` No Catalog id (positional). Omit it on a terminal to pick from the installed add-ons. 
 `--project`, `-p` No Project name or id. Omit it on a terminal and you are asked. 
 `--env`, `-e` No Environment id, name or stage; an exact name wins over a stage. Omit for the project's default. 
 `--mode` No Delivery mode: `managed` (Alethia applies it) or `gitops` (written to your apps repo). `gitops` needs an apps repo on GitHub for now; on GitLab or Bitbucket it is refused. See [Which Git providers support GitOps mode](/concepts/apps-repository#which-git-providers-support-gitops-mode). 
 `--set` `key=value` No An add-on setting. Repeatable; values are JSON-typed when they parse. `key=null` resets that setting to its default. Settings you do not pass keep their stored values. 
 `--values-file` No Path to a raw Helm values YAML override (Advanced). `--values-file ""` removes the override. Omit it to keep the current override. 
 `--version` No Pin the chart version, for example `58.2.1`. `--version ""` removes the pin. Omit it

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Reconfigure an installed add-on
records.text:
Re-running `enable` on an installed add-on **updates** it. A flag you leave out keeps what is
stored, so you can change one value without restating the rest:

bash

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Change one setting. The other settings, the Advanced override, the mode and the version pin stay.
records.text:
alethia addon enable loki -p my-project -e staging --set retention_days=14

 What you pass `--set` settings `--values-file` override `--version` pin `--mode` 
 ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ 
 Nothing Each stored setting is kept Kept Kept Kept 
 A value Merged key by key over the stored settings The file replaces the stored override whole Replaced Replaced 
 An empty value `--set key=null` resets that setting to its default `--values-file ""` removes the override `--version ""` removes the pin Not available 

- The Advanced override is one YAML document. A new `--values-file` replaces the stored one; it is
 not merged with it. A file that is empty or only whitespace also removes the override.
- A secret setting you do not resend is kept. `key=null` does not remove a stored secret.
- The merged settings are validated together, so a setting you did not pass can still make the
 request fail if the add-on's schema has changed.
- The console's configure card shows every stored value and sends all of them back when you save.
 There, an emptied **Advanced** box removes the override and an emptied **Chart version** field
 removes the pin.

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Pin the chart version
records.text:
By default an add-on deploys the chart version the catalog pins. To deploy a different version in
one environment, pass `--version` with an exact chart version:

alethia addon enable kube-prometheus-stack -p my-project -e staging --version 58.2.1

- The version must be one exact version, such as `58.2.1`. Ranges (`^58`, `~58.2`, `>=58`, `*`)
 are refused with a 400, because a range lets the deployed chart change without you.
- The value must match the version string the chart repository publishes, character for
 character. A leading `v` is accepted, but most charts publish `58.2.1`, not `v58.2.1`, and
 a version the repository does not publish fails at sync time.
- A later `enable` without `--version` keeps the pin.
- `--version ""` removes the pin, and the catalog default applies again on the next apply.
- The console sets the same pin: the **Chart version** field on the add-on's configure card.

 
A pinned chart is not checked against the catalog's default values. The catalog's settings and
defaults are written for the catalog's version, so a major-version jump can rename or remove the
chart values they set and break the add-on. Read the chart's upgrade notes before you pin a new

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: alethia addon disable
records.text:
Disable an add-on in an environment.

alethia addon disable falco -p my-project -e staging
alethia addon disable falco -p my-project --yes
alethia addon disable -p my-project

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[addon-id]` No Catalog id (positional). Omit it on a terminal to pick from the installed add-ons. 
 `--project`, `-p` No Project name or id. Omit it on a terminal and you are asked. 
 `--env`, `-e` No Environment id, name or stage; an exact name wins over a stage. 
 `--yes`, `-y` No Skip the confirmation prompt. Required with `--no-input`. 

 
 Disabling removes the add-on's workloads from the cluster on the next sync. Data held in its
 volumes may not survive — take a backup first if it matters. The add-on the CLI resolved is
 named on stderr **before** the confirmation, so what you are confirming is always something you
 can read. The command requires `--yes` when it cannot prompt, and exits `9` rather than exiting 0
 having done nothing.

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: alethia addon bump
records.text:
Open a pull request that moves a GitOps add-on to the chart version that a deploy would seed.

alethia addon bump ingress-nginx -p my-project -e production
alethia addon bump -p my-project
alethia addon bump ingress-nginx -p my-project --again

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[addon-id]` No Catalog id (positional). Omit it on a terminal to pick from the installed add-ons. 
 `--project`, `-p` No Project name or id. Omit it on a terminal and you are asked. 
 `--env`, `-e` No Environment id, name or stage; an exact name wins over a stage. 
 `--again` No Open the pull request again after you closed the last one without merging it. 

Alethia seeds a GitOps add-on's `addons/ .yaml` once and does not rewrite it. A newer
catalog version therefore does not reach the add-on until the file changes. The Deploy tab names
each add-on whose file is behind.

This command opens a pull request in the environment's apps repo. The pull request sets
`spec.source.targetRevision` in that file to the version a deploy would seed: the catalog's
version, or your pin. It changes only that field. Every other byte of the file stays the same. It
does not migrate values

records.title: Agent Commands
records.text: Agent Commands. Inspect agent identities, and connect coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and VS Code to Alethia.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.text:
The `agent` group (alias `agents`) reads **agent identities** — machine/agent personas, each with a
persona, a mission, an allowed tool scope, and a memory namespace, scoped to your account or org.
`agent setup` connects the coding agents on your machine to the Alethia MCP server.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These subcommands call `/cli/agents[/…]` with your
[CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and resolve within your tenancy — an agent id from another org
returns not-found, never its persona/mission.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: No id is copied between commands
records.text:
`get` takes the agent id as an **optional** first argument. Omit it on a terminal and the
identities you can see are offered to choose from, so the id never has to be read out of
`agent list` and pasted back in. The identity the CLI resolved is printed on **stderr**, so
`-o json` still emits a document that parses.

Only an **id** is accepted as the argument, and it is passed through byte for byte. A persona is
not resolved to an id on purpose: personas are not unique, so "the one whose persona matches"
would silently read a different identity the day a second agent takes the same persona. With
`--no-input` (or a non-terminal stdin/stdout) nothing is asked and the command fails naming the
argument to pass.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: alethia agent list
records.text:
List the agent identities you can see.

alethia agent list
alethia agent list -o json

Columns: **ID**, **Persona**, **Tools** (count of allowed tools), **Namespace** (memory
namespace), **Version**. Add `-o json` for the raw objects. Backing call: `GET /cli/agents`.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: alethia agent get
records.text:
Show one agent identity's persona, mission, and tool scope.

alethia agent get
alethia agent get ag_01J8Z9QK3F
alethia agent get ag_01J8Z9QK3F -o json

 Argument Required Description 
 ---------- ---------- ------------- 
 `[agent-id]` No The agent identity's id. Omit it on a terminal to pick from a list. 

Renders a field/value card: **id**, **persona**, **mission**, **tool scope** (the allowed tools),
**namespace**, **project** (the project it is scoped to, or `—` for an org-wide identity),
**created**, **version**. Add `-o json` for the full object. Backing call:
`GET /cli/agents/ `.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: alethia agent setup
records.text:
Connect coding agents to Alethia. For each agent, `setup` writes an MCP configuration into the
project directory that points at the Alethia MCP server, and it adds an Alethia section to
`AGENTS.md`.

alethia agent setup
alethia agent setup --client claude-code --client codex --project boutique
alethia agent setup --client cursor --read-only --dry-run

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `--client` No The agents to configure: `claude-code`, `cursor`, `codex`, `vscode`. Repeatable. Default: the agents found on this machine; on a terminal you choose from the list. 
 `--project` No Pin the MCP server to one project, by **name** or id. On a terminal you are offered the choice. Default: every project you can see. 
 `--read-only` No List only the tools that change nothing. 
 `--dir` No The project directory to write into. Default: the current directory. 
 `--no-agents-md` No Do not add the Alethia section to `AGENTS.md`. 
 `--dry-run` No Say what would be written, and write nothing. 

Each agent reads its own file:

 Agent File 
 ------- ------ 
 Claude Code `.mcp.json` 
 Cursor `.cursor/mcp.json` 
 Codex `.codex/config.toml` 
 VS Code `.vscode/mcp.json` 

The s
