records.title: Authentication
records.text: Authentication. Device Authorization Grant flow for people, service-account tokens for pipelines, credential storage in the system keychain, and automatic refresh.

records.title: Authentication
records.text:
alethia authenticates two ways, for two different callers:

- **You, at a terminal** — the **Device Authorization Grant** (RFC 8628). You never type a password.
- **A pipeline** — a **service-account token**, supplied through `$ALETHIA_TOKEN`. No browser, no prompt.

For why the CLI authenticates this way, see [Authentication flows](/concepts/authentication); for
the protocol, its endpoints and its deviations from RFC 8628, see
[Device Authorization Grant](/reference/standards/device-code).

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Login
records.text:
alethia login

1. The CLI prints a short `user_code` and opens your browser at the Console's `/cli/login` page.
2. Sign in there with any OAuth provider (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Google) or email OTP, if you are
 not already. The page names the account that is about to be bound, what approval hands over, who
 is asking and how long is left.
3. Check that the code on screen is the one your terminal printed, then approve. Nothing is typed
 back into the terminal.
4. The CLI, which has been waiting with a spinner, receives an access and refresh token pair and
 stores it in the system keychain. It then prints one line that says where the credential was
 stored. See [Credential storage](#credential-storage).

The URL, the code and every notice go to stderr. The result goes to stdout: one sentence, or one JSON
object with `--output json`.

alethia login --output json

{
 "id": "alethialabs.io",
 "kind": "session",
 "action": "created",
 "job": null,
 "dry_run": false,
 "object": { "user": "you@example.com", "origin": "https://alethialabs.io", "stored_in": "keychain" }
}

 Flag What it does 
 --- --- 
 `--force`, `-f` Sign in again even when a session is already stored 
 `--web-origin`

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Refusing a login you did not start
records.text:
If the code on screen is not the one your terminal printed, or you did not run `alethia login` at all,
press **This isn't me**.

That records the refusal in Console rather than only in the browser. Three things follow:

- The device that is polling is told at once, with the standard `access_denied` error, instead of waiting
 out its own timeout.
- Nothing is handed over — no access token, no refresh token, and none of your linked git provider's
 OAuth token.
- The refusal is final for that link. Opening it again cannot approve it; a genuine sign-in needs a fresh
 `alethia login`.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Force Re-authentication
records.text:
alethia login --force

Re-authenticates even if a valid token already exists. Useful when switching accounts.

On a terminal you do not need the flag. If you are already signed in, `alethia login` names the account
and asks whether to keep that session or sign in again. **Keep this session** is the first option, so
pressing Enter changes nothing. With `--no-input`, with no terminal, or when an agent runs the command,
it asks nothing: it names the account, keeps the session, reports `"action": "unchanged"` and exits 0.
Pass `--force` to sign in again from a script.

A first sign-in asks no question. The control-plane URL is not asked for here: pass `--web-origin`, or
use `alethia init` for the guided first-run setup.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Logout
records.text:
alethia logout

Removes the stored credential for the current control plane from both places it can be: the system
keychain and the credentials file. It also deletes the kubeconfig credential cache, for every
organization. After that, an exec kubeconfig from `alethia cluster kubeconfig` fails until you run
`alethia login` again. See [Revoke access](/concepts/cluster-access#revoke-access).

`alethia logout` tries every removal before it reports a failure. If it cannot delete the keychain
entry, the file or the cache, it prints the reason on stderr and exits with a non-zero status. If you
are not signed in, it changes nothing and exits 0.

`alethia logout` does not unset `ALETHIA_TOKEN`. A token from the environment is never stored, so
there is nothing to remove. The command warns you that the variable is still set.

alethia logout --output json

{
 "id": "alethialabs.io",
 "kind": "session",
 "action": "deleted",
 "job": null,
 "dry_run": false,
 "object": { "origin": "https://alethialabs.io", "keychain": true, "file": false, "kubeconfig_cache": true }
}

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Check the credential in use
records.text:
alethia auth status

Shows the credential that the next command would send: the account, the control plane, where the
credential is stored and when the access token expires. The credential itself is never printed.

`alethia auth status` reads the stored credential and sends no request. Use `alethia whoami` when
you want the control plane to confirm the identity. `alethia whoami` shows the same storage and
expiry lines.

alethia auth status --output json

{
 "user": "you@example.com",
 "origin": "https://alethialabs.io",
 "source": "keychain",
 "stored_in": "the system keychain",
 "expires_at": "2027-01-31T10:15:00Z",
 "renews_automatically": true
}

`source` is one of four values:

 `source` Where the credential comes from 
 --- --- 
 `flag` The `--token` flag. Not stored. 
 `env` The `ALETHIA_TOKEN` environment variable. Not stored. 
 `keychain` The system keychain 
 `file` The owner-only credentials file. `path` gives its location. 

For `flag` and `env`, `user` is absent, because a supplied token does not name an account that the
CLI can read. `expires_at` is `null` when the token does not state its own expiry, as a
service-account token does not. With no credential, the command

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Token Lifecycle
records.text:
Token TTL Purpose 
 ------- ----- --------- 
 Access token 1 hour `Authorization: Bearer` header on API calls 
 Refresh token 90 days Obtain new access tokens transparently 

Before each API call, alethia checks the access token's expiry and refreshes it automatically when it
is within a minute of expiring — see [Refresh](/reference/standards/device-code#refresh). You never
notice it.

If the control plane refuses a stored access token during a command, the CLI renews the credential
once and sends the request again. A token from `ALETHIA_TOKEN` or `--token` is never renewed.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Identity & Active Org
records.text:
After logging in, confirm who you are signed in as and which organization the CLI is scoped to:

alethia whoami # user, active org, role, plan, default runner
alethia config # control-plane URL, active org, on-disk file paths

The active organization is sent as the `X-Alethia-Org` header on every request. Set or change it
with `alethia org switch`. See [Identity & Global Options](/reference/cli/identity) and
[Organizations, Members & Teams](/reference/cli/organizations).

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Running in CI
records.text:
The device flow needs a browser and a person, so a pipeline cannot use it. Mint a **service-account
token** instead:

alethia token create --name "github-actions"

The token is printed **once**, on stdout, with everything else on stderr — so you can pipe it
straight into a secret store without selecting it by eye:

alethia token create --name "github-actions" gh secret set ALETHIA_TOKEN

Then set `ALETHIA_TOKEN` in your job and use the CLI normally. Nothing is written to disk, and no
`alethia login` is needed:

- name: Deploy staging
 env:
 ALETHIA_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.ALETHIA_TOKEN }}
 run: 
 alethia project apply --env staging --wait --no-input

Pair it with `--no-input`, which makes the CLI fail rather than prompt — together they mean a job
never hangs waiting for an answer nobody is there to give.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: What a service token can do
records.text:
A token **acts as the person who created it**, inside the **one organization** it was minted for.
That org is fixed when the token is created: an `X-Alethia-Org` header that disagrees with it is
refused, not ignored, so a token issued for one organization can never act on another.

It also stops working the moment its creator leaves that organization — membership is re-checked on
every request, not trusted from when the token was minted.

A service token cannot run [break-glass](/reference/cli/ops). The `alethia ops` verbs need an
interactive session from `alethia login`, and the server refuses a service token there with a
`403` — even when the person who created it is a break-glass operator. A token pinned to one
organization must not carry an identity that acts across every tenant. The server refuses the
service token itself, not a delivery path: an operator's session token is still accepted from
`ALETHIA_TOKEN` or `--token`, so never place one in CI.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Minting a token
records.text:
Run `alethia token create` on a terminal with no flags and it asks for the two things it needs:

{/* fieldspec: alethia token create */}

 Field What it is Set without the form 
 --- --- --- 
 Name What this token is for, so a list of tokens is a list of purposes `--name` 
 Expires A token that never expires is a credential nobody remembers to rotate `--expires-in-days` 

The flags are the complete contract: anything the form can ask, a flag can set, so
`--no-input` never needs a prompt.

alethia token create # asks for the name and the lifetime
alethia token create --name ci --expires-in-days 90 # the same, unattended

`--expires-in-days 0` — the default — never expires. That is a deliberate choice rather than an
oversight, and it is why the form asks: a credential with no end date is one nobody remembers to
rotate.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Managing tokens
records.text:
alethia token list # id, name, prefix, created, expires, last used, status
alethia token revoke # pick from the live tokens, or pass an id

`alethia token list` shows `last used: never` for a token nothing has ever presented. That is usually
the most interesting row on the list — a credential that was minted, put somewhere, and forgotten.

`alethia token revoke` with no argument shows the tokens that are still live and revokes the one you
pick, so you never have to copy an opaque id out of `token list` by eye. Already-revoked tokens are
left out of the picker; revoking one again does nothing.

{/* fieldspec: alethia token revoke */}

 Field What it is Set without the form 
 --- --- --- 
 Token The token to revoke; it stops working on its very next request `[id]` 

alethia token revoke # pick from a list
alethia token revoke 3f2b9c14-7a1e-4d68-9c05-2b8e6a1d40f7 # revoke a known id, no prompt

 
Revoke carries **no `--yes`**, unlike every other destructive command. Its asymmetry runs the other
way: revoking a token you did not mean to costs one `alethia token create`, while failing to revoke a
leaked one costs the organization. A confirmation here would fail an incident-response pipe

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Environment Variables
records.text:
Variable Default Purpose 
 ---------- --------- --------- 
 `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN` Production URL (baked at build) Override the Alethia API URL 
 `ALETHIA_TOKEN` unset A service-account token for non-interactive use. When set, the CLI uses it before any stored credential, and never writes it to the system keychain or to a file. 

alethia login # authenticates against local dev server

The `--token` flag does the same thing as `$ALETHIA_TOKEN` and takes precedence over it. Prefer the
environment variable in CI: a flag value lands in the process table and in shell history, where an
environment variable does not.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Credential storage
records.text:
`alethia login` stores the credential in the credential store of the operating system:

 System Store 
 --- --- 
 macOS Keychain 
 Linux The Secret Service, for example GNOME Keyring or KWallet 
 Windows Credential Manager 

The entry is filed under the service `alethia`, with the host of the control plane as the account.

Some hosts have no credential store: a container, a CI runner, or a Linux host with no desktop
session. On those hosts the CLI stores the credential in a file that only your user can read:

~/.config/alethia/credentials.json

The CLI also uses the file when the credential store does not answer within 3 seconds, and when you
pass `--insecure-storage`. In each case `alethia login` prints one line on stderr that says which of
the two it used. The file has mode `0600` and its directory has mode `0700`.

{
 "access_token": "eyJ...",
 "refresh_token": "eyJ...",
 "user_email": "you@example.com",
 "origin": "https://alethialabs.io"
}

The access-token expiry is read from the JWT itself (the `exp` claim), so no separate timestamp is
stored. The active-org context is kept separately in `~/.config/alethia/config.json` (see
[Configuration](/reference/cli/configuration)).

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: The order the CLI looks for a credential
records.text:
1. The `--token` flag
2. The `ALETHIA_TOKEN` environment variable
3. The system keychain
4. The credentials file

The first one found is used. A supplied token always wins over a stored sign-in.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: One credential for each control plane
records.text:
A stored credential records the control plane that issued it, and the CLI uses it for that control
plane only. If you change `web-origin`, the CLI does not send the old credential to the new URL. It
reports that you are not signed in, and you run `alethia login` again. The system keychain holds one
entry for each control plane. The credentials file holds one credential.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Moving from the file to the keychain
records.text:
An earlier version of the CLI stored every credential in the file. This version reads that file
without changing it. The next time you sign in, or the next time the CLI renews the access token, it
writes the credential to the system keychain, reads the entry back, and compares it with what it
wrote. Only then does it remove the file, and it prints one line that says the credential moved. If
the keychain entry does not read back, the file stays.

A credential stored with `--insecure-storage` stays in the file.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.text: Billing, Usage & Fleet. Inspect the active organization's billing and usage, and configure managed-fleet warm pools, from the alethia CLI.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.text:
Three related views into an organization's plan and the platform's provisioning capacity:

- **`billing`** — the active organization's plan, subscription status, seats, and period boundaries.
- **`usage`** — current consumption: seats, runner-minutes, projects, and AI credits.
- **`fleet`** — the managed pool of warm provisioning runners (platform-operator config).

`billing` and `usage` operate on the **active organization** (set via `alethia org switch`), or on
the organization named by the global `--org ` for a single invocation — which is refused with
`403` if you are not a member of it. Every command accepts the global
[`-o, --output `](/reference/cli/identity#output-formats) flag.

 
`billing` and `usage` are **read-only** — manage the subscription, cards, and invoices in the
console. No Stripe customer ids or charge amounts are ever returned by the CLI.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia billing
records.text:
Shows the active organization's billing state as a detail card: its plan, subscription status, the
purchased seat count, the Stripe subscription id, and the trial / current-period boundaries. An
organization with no subscription reads as the free `community` plan.

alethia billing
alethia billing -o json

 Field Meaning 
 -------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------- 
 `Plan` `community`, `team`, or `enterprise` 
 `Status` Subscription status (`active`, `trialing`, `none`, …) 
 `Seats` Purchased seats (per-seat plans); a dash on flat/no subscription 
 `Subscription` Stripe subscription id, if any 
 `Trial ends` When a `trialing` subscription's trial ends 
 `Period ends` End of the current paid period

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia usage
records.text:
Shows the active organization's current usage as a detail card: billable seats used vs the purchased
cap, managed-runner minutes consumed this period, the project count, and AI credits used in the
trailing week vs the plan's weekly grant.

alethia usage
alethia usage -o json

 Field Meaning 
 ---------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 
 `Seats` Billable seats used **/** purchased cap 
 `Runner minutes` Managed-runner minutes consumed this billing period, written for a person: `0 min`, `47 min`, `2h 15m` 
 `Projects` Projects in the organization 
 `AI credits` Included AI credits used this week **/** the weekly grant 

 
`Runner minutes` has no **/ cap** beside it, unlike `Seats` and `AI credits`. The usage API returns
a consumed figure and no runner-minute allowance, so the CLI shows what you have used and does not
state an allowance nobody sent. The console's usage page reads the allowance from the plan
catalogue; see **Settings → Usage** there for minutes used against minutes included.
 

Use `-o json` or `-o csv` when a script needs the raw counters. Only the card is written for a
person: `runner_minutes` is a plain integer of

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Output and exit codes
records.text:
The card is the only thing `billing` and `usage` write on stdout, and they write nothing there when
they fail. A failure exits with the code of its kind and says on stderr what happened: `4` when you
are not signed in, `5` when you are not permitted to read the organization's billing, and `11` when
the control plane cannot be reached.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia fleet
records.text:
The **managed fleet** is the platform's pool of warm provisioning runners — one pool per cloud — that
the Fleet Controller reconciles toward a declarative target (warm floor, ceiling, locations, version).

 
Fleet configuration is **platform-operator infrastructure** (the pools are global, not per-org). It
is only available on **self-managed deployments**, to organization **owners/admins**. On the hosted
service `fleet list` returns an empty list, and `fleet set` is refused.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia fleet list
records.text:
Lists the configured warm pools. On a TTY this opens the interactive table; with `--output json csv`
(or `--no-input`) it prints a static table.

alethia fleet list
alethia fleet list -o json

Columns: `Provider`, `Enabled`, `Warm` (floor), `Max` (ceiling), `Slots` (concurrent jobs per
runner), `Locations`, and `Version` (a pinned version, or the tracked channel). The command takes
no input of its own.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia fleet set
records.text:
Creates or updates the warm pool for one cloud. For an existing pool, only the flags you pass are
changed; the rest keep their stored value. For a cloud with no pool yet, the command creates one: the
flags you pass are applied, and every other setting takes its default — warm-min `1`, max `10`, slots
`1`, enabled. A pinned `--version` and a release `--channel` are **mutually exclusive** — a version
pin clears the channel.

The provider is optional at a terminal: omit it and you choose from the clouds this release
offers — `aws`, `gcp`, `azure`, `hetzner`. That is the same list `alethia connector` offers, and
**nothing is refused on it**: a provider you pass as the argument is sent as written, and which
clouds a given deployment's fleet controller actually serves is the server's answer, not the CLI's.

bash

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Choose the cloud at a terminal
records.text: alethia fleet set --warm-min 2

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Raise the AWS pool's warm floor and ceiling
records.text: alethia fleet set aws --warm-min 2 --max 20

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Pin a runner version (clears any tracked channel)
records.text: alethia fleet set gcp --version v1.4.0

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Pause a pool (drains its runners — prompts for confirmation)
records.text: alethia fleet set azure --enabled=false

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Show the request a change would send, and send nothing
records.text:
alethia fleet set aws --max 3 --dry-run

`--dry-run` prints the request that `fleet set` would send and sends nothing: the provider, plus
only the fields you passed. A person reads it as one sentence, for example
`Would set the aws pool to max 3`, and `-o json` prints the request itself. A dry run asks for no
confirmation, not even for `--enabled=false`, because nothing changes.

{/* fieldspec: alethia fleet set */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Provider Which cloud's warm pool to configure; omit it to choose from the clouds Alethia supports `[provider]` 
 Warm floor How many runners stay provisioned with no work to do `--warm-min` 
 Ceiling The most instances the controller may ever run for this cloud `--max` 
 Slots per runner How many provisioning jobs one runner takes at once `--slots` 
 Enabled Whether the controller provisions for this cloud at all; disabling drains it `--enabled` 
 Release channel A runner channel to track, e.g. stable; mutually exclusive with a pinned version `--channel` 
 Pinned version An exact runner version to hold this pool at; setting it clears the channel `--version` 

 
Disabling a pool drains its runners (a capacit

records.title: Chart Commands
records.text: Chart Commands. Attach, scan, list and detach the BYO Helm charts on a project environment.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.text:
The `chart` group (alias `charts`) manages your **BYO Helm charts** — your own charts, pulled from a
connected git repo or an OCI registry and deployed into an environment through ArgoCD alongside the
marketplace add-ons.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These commands call `/cli/projects/PROJECT/byo-charts`
with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on the **active organization**.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: Common flags
records.text:
Every command in the group takes the same two selectors. They are registered on the group, so they
work in any position.

{/* fieldspec: alethia chart */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Project The project, by name or id; omit it on a terminal and you are asked `--project` 
 Environment The environment, by id, name or stage (an exact name wins over a stage); empty means the project's default `--env` 

`--project` has the short form `-p` and `--env` has `-e`. On a terminal, omitting `--project` opens
the project picker; with `--no-input`, with `-o json`, or with the output redirected to a file, it
is required — a form drawn into a redirected stream would corrupt the document you are piping.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: Output and exit codes
records.text:
**The result is on stdout, and everything else is on stderr.** With `--output json`, `attach`,
`scan` and `detach` print one object:

{
 "id": "api",
 "kind": "byo_chart",
 "action": "queued",
 "job": { "id": "0b7e6c55-2f0a-4d0e-9a3b-6c1d2e3f4a5b", "type": "CHART_SCAN" },
 "dry_run": false,
 "object": { "project": "shop", "env": "dev", "job_status": "QUEUED", "warnings": [] }
}

`action` is `updated` for `attach` (an attach is an upsert, and the control plane does not say
whether the id was new), `queued` for `scan` and `deleted` for `detach`. `job` is `null` unless the
command queued a scan. The next step — the scan to run, the command that follows a queued job, the
flags that reproduce an interactive run — is a line on stderr.

**A refusal exits with the code of its kind.** stdout stays empty, and stderr says what happened
and the command to run next.

 Exit Meaning on this page 
 ------ ---------------------- 
 `6` The project, environment or chart that you named does not exist 
 `8` A flag value is not valid, for example a `--set` without `=` or a values file that cannot be read 
 `9` A value or a confirmation is needed and nothing can ask for it: pass the flag the message name

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: alethia chart list
records.text:
List the BYO Helm charts attached to a project environment.

alethia chart list --project my-project
alethia chart list -p my-project -e staging
alethia chart list -p my-project -o json

Columns: **Chart** (its per-env id and release name), **Repo** (the git or OCI URL), **Path** (the
chart directory, a dash for an OCI chart), **Ref** (the git ref, a dash when it tracks the default
branch), **Status**, **Scan** (chart-safety scan lifecycle: `unscanned`, `scanning`, `done`,
`failed`). Add `-o json` for the full view — the Elench scan report itself is console-only — or
`-o csv` for the rows. The dashes in **Path** and **Ref** are for a person reading a column; under
`-o csv` a chart that has neither gets an empty cell, the same split `alethia config get` makes.
Backing call: `GET /cli/projects/PROJECT/byo-charts`.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: alethia chart attach
records.text:
Attach a chart from your own repository — git or OCI — to one environment.

alethia chart attach api -p shop -e dev --repo https://github.com/acme/charts --chart-path charts/api --ref v1.2.3
alethia chart attach api -p shop --repo oci://registry.example.com/acme/api
alethia chart attach api -p shop --repo https://github.com/acme/charts --chart-path charts/api --set replicas=2 --values-file ./api-values.yaml

{/* fieldspec: alethia chart attach */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Chart id Your name for this chart; the server slugifies it and the result is the id every later command uses `[id]` 
 Repository Where the chart lives — a git URL, or an oci:// reference to a chart registry `--repo` 
 Chart path Where the chart sits inside a git repository; an OCI chart is named by its URL and needs none `--chart-path` 
 Git ref The branch, tag or commit to deploy; empty tracks the repository's default branch `--ref` 
 Namespace The destination namespace; empty gives the chart a namespace of its own (byo- followed by the chart id) `--namespace` 
 Values file A path on this machine to a raw Helm values YAML override, sent as the file's content `--values-file` 
 Chart value O

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: The interactive path
records.text:
Run `alethia chart attach` on a terminal with nothing else and it asks for each field it was not
given. A flag you did pass is never questioned again, so a half-written command finishes itself.

The **repository is chosen, not typed**: the form asks which connected provider to look in, then
offers the repositories Alethia can already see, with `Type a URL instead…` at the bottom of the
list for anything else. That is the whole reason this form exists — the URL used to be something you
read off `alethia repo list` and typed back in. If no provider is connected, or the listing fails,
the question falls back to a plain typed line rather than refusing the attach.

`--chart-path` is asked for git repositories only: an OCI chart is named by its URL's last segment.

The run finishes by printing the flags that would have produced the same result, so the command you
answered once is the command you can commit to a repository.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: With --no-input
records.text:
Nothing is asked, and the chart id and `--repo` are required. Leaving one out exits `9`, names it,
and sends nothing.
Every field above has a flag, so any attach the form can perform, a script can perform.

 
 **A private repository needs no credential flag.** The runner fetches a short-lived token at job
 time from your linked GitHub or GitLab account, scoped to the repositories this project declares,
 and refreshed per job — so nothing is stored against the chart. Link that account once in the
 console and private repositories work.
 

Re-attaching the same id **updates** it, so this is also how you move a chart to a new ref. The
result's `id` is the one the server stored, because it slugifies what you send.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: alethia chart scan
records.text:
alethia chart scan api -p shop -e dev
alethia chart scan -p shop -e dev

{/* fieldspec: alethia chart scan */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Chart Which attached chart to scan; an unscanned chart is refused at deploy `[id]` 

An attached chart is **not deployable until it has been scanned**: the scan renders it and records
the verdict the plan-time gate reads. Re-scan whenever the chart's repository moves.

The id is optional. Omit it on a terminal and the environment's attached charts are offered, so
nothing is copied out of `alethia chart list`. With nobody to ask, the id is required (exit `9`).

The scan is a job. Without `--wait` the command returns once it is queued: the job id is in the
result, and `alethia jobs logs --latest --follow` tails it without repeating that id back. With
`--wait` the command follows the job to its end and reports its final status.

 Flag What it does 
 --- --- 
 `--wait` Wait for the scan to finish. The command exits `13` when the scan fails 
 `--timeout` With `--wait`, stop waiting after this long, for example `10m`. The scan keeps running and the command exits `12` 

alethia chart scan api -p shop -e dev --wait --timeout 10m

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: alethia chart detach
records.text:
alethia chart detach api -p shop -e dev
alethia chart detach api -p shop --yes

{/* fieldspec: alethia chart detach */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Chart Which attached chart to detach; its workloads leave the cluster on the next sync `[id]` 

Like `chart scan`, the id is optional on a terminal and the attached charts are offered instead.

 
 Detaching removes the chart's workloads from the cluster on the next sync. The command confirms
 first, and the confirmation **names the chart it resolved to** — including the one you picked from
 the list. With `--no-input`, or when stdin is not a terminal, `--yes` is required: without it the
 command exits `9` and detaches nothing, rather than cancelling quietly.
 

 
 These commands need `ALETHIA_BYO_HELM_ENABLED=true` on the instance. Without it they return **501**
 with the variable named, rather than a permissions error you would go looking for in vain.

records.title: Classification Commands
records.text: Classification Commands. Read and edit the org's governed taxonomy — dimensions, values, and per-resource assignments — from the terminal.

records.title: Classification Commands
records.text:
The `classification` group (alias `class`) drives the same **governed taxonomy** as the console's
[Classification](/guides/classification) page — from the terminal. Instead of free-form tags, an
admin defines a fixed set of **dimensions** (axes) and their **allowed values** once; every resource
is then labeled from that closed vocabulary. The CLI lets you list that taxonomy, read a resource's
labels, and set or clear them.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API — it authors nothing locally. Every subcommand calls
`/cli/classification/*` with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operates on the **active
organization**, which you change with `alethia org switch`. Pass `--org ` to scope a single invocation to a different
organization — it is refused with `403` if you are not a member of it.

records.title: Classification Commands
records.heading: The model
records.text:
Three concepts, in a strict hierarchy — the CLI vocabulary matches the console's exactly:

- **Dimension** — a named axis (one question you can ask about every resource: *Environment*,
 *Team*, *Data classification*). It has a `key` slug (immutable, wire-stable), a `label`, an
 optional description, a **single/multi** mode (`Multi bool`), and an `applies_to` list of resource
 kinds it targets (empty = all resource kinds).
- **Value** — an allowed answer on that axis (`dev` / `staging` / `prod`). Each has an immutable
 `value` slug and a `label`. `assign` takes the **value slug**, so slugs must be discoverable —
 which is why `dimensions` prints them, not just a count.
- **Assignment** — a value pinned to one concrete resource, addressed by its **kind** and **id**.

 
Classification is **organizational metadata** — it does not enforce anything today. No policy,
permission check, provisioning step, or the [verify](/reference/glossary) gate reads these labels to
allow, deny, or route. See [Classification](/guides/classification#what-classification-does-not-do).

records.title: Classification Commands
records.heading: Addressing a resource: <kind> <id>
records.text:
`show`, `assign`, and `unassign` all target a resource by its **kind** (a snake-case record type) and
its **id** (a UUID). Those two are always yours to supply; the **dimension key** and the **value
slug** are not — omit them at a terminal and you are asked, from the org's own taxonomy. For example a project's default environment is `project_environment `.
The classifiable kinds mirror the console — projects, environments, clusters, cloud identities
(connectors), runners, members, roles, alert policies, alert channels, support cases. Audit-trail
records (alert *deliveries*, runner *usage sessions*) are intentionally not classifiable.

records.title: Classification Commands
records.heading: alethia classification dimensions
records.text:
List the org's dimensions and, for each, its allowed value slugs.

alethia classification dimensions

records.title: Classification Commands
records.heading: alias:
records.text:
alethia class dimensions

Columns: **Key**, **Label**, **Mode** (`single` `multi`), **Applies to** (the resource kinds, or
`all resources`), **Values** (the value slugs, comma-separated). In an interactive TTY this renders
as a navigable [TUI table](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/cli-tui.md); otherwise it prints a plain table. Add `-o json` for the raw
`ClassificationDimension` objects (including value `id`/`label` and per-dimension `description`).

KEY LABEL MODE APPLIES TO VALUES
environment Environment single project, project_environment dev, staging, prod
team Team multi all resources platform, payments, data
data-class Data classification single project_environment, cluster public, internal, restricted

Backing call: `GET /cli/classification/dimensions`.

records.title: Classification Commands
records.heading: alethia classification show
records.text:
Show the values currently assigned to one resource.

alethia classification show
alethia classification show project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000

Both tokens are optional at a terminal. Given neither, you are asked which **kind** — offered from
the kinds the org's own dimensions target, so it is not a string you have to have read out of
`dimensions` first — and then for the resource id. Scripted, pass both; `--no-input` with either
missing is refused, and the refusal names the two tokens rather than the prompt it could not open.

{/* fieldspec: alethia classification show */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Resource kind The record type being labelled, e.g. project_environment `[kind]` 
 Resource id The UUID of the resource whose labels to read `[id]` 

Columns: **Dimension**, **Value** (both rendered as their human labels). When the resource carries
no values it says so on stderr, and prints `[]` under `-o json`. Backing call:
`GET /cli/classification/assignments?kind= &id= `.

alethia classification show project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000 -o json

records.title: Classification Commands
records.heading: alethia classification assign
records.text:
Pin a value to a resource.

alethia classification assign project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000
alethia classification assign project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000 environment prod

Given only the kind and the id at a terminal, you are asked which dimension — from the ones that
target that kind — and then which of **that dimension's** allowed values. Neither is a slug you
have to have read out of `dimensions` first.

Given all four, both slugs are checked against the org's taxonomy before anything is sent, and a
miss names the real keys or the real values rather than surfacing a 4xx: an unknown dimension
exits `6`, a value the dimension does not have exits `8`. With a slug missing and nothing to ask,
the command exits `9`.

`--dry-run` makes the same checks and assigns nothing. Under `-o json` the command prints one
result whose `object` names the resource, the dimension and the value; the shape is described under
[What a command prints and how it fails](/reference/cli/organizations#what-a-command-prints-and-how-it-fails).

{/* fieldspec: alethia classification assign */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Resource

records.title: Classification Commands
records.heading: Label a project's default environment as prod, and tag two owning teams (multi dimension)
records.text:
alethia classification assign project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000 environment prod
alethia classification assign project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000 team platform
alethia classification assign project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000 team payments

records.title: Classification Commands
records.heading: alethia classification unassign
records.text:
Clear a value from a resource (addressed by its **slug**, not the dimension key).

alethia classification unassign project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000
alethia classification unassign project_environment 8f3c1a2b-0000-4000-8000-000000000000 payments --yes

Clearing a value is destructive — policy that selects on it stops matching the resource — so it
asks before acting. In a pipeline `--yes` is **required**: without it the command exits `9` and
clears nothing. `--dry-run` names the value that would be cleared and clears nothing.

Omit the slug at a terminal and you choose from the values **the resource actually carries** — a
different source from `assign`'s, deliberately. `assign` chooses from everything that could be true
of the resource; `unassign` from what currently is, so you cannot clear a value it never had.

{/* fieldspec: alethia classification unassign */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Resource kind The record type being labelled, e.g. project_environment ` ` 
 Resource id The UUID of the resource to clear a value from ` ` 
 Value The value slug to clear; omit it to choose from what the resource actually carries `[valu

records.title: Cloud Commands
records.text: Cloud Commands. Inspect the networking and regions Alethia discovered in a connected cloud account.

records.title: Cloud Commands
records.text:
The `cloud` group reads the **inventory** Alethia discovered in a connected cloud account — the
networks (VPCs/VNets), subnets, and regions it swept.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. `cloud inventory` calls
`/cli/cloud-identities/ /inventory` with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operates on
the **active organization** — the cloud identity must belong to it.

records.title: Cloud Commands
records.heading: alethia cloud inventory
records.text:
Show the discovered networking + regions for a connected cloud account.

bash

records.title: Cloud Commands
records.heading: Name the account by its provider
records.text:
alethia cloud inventory aws
alethia cloud inventory gcp -o json

records.title: Cloud Commands
records.heading: Or omit the argument for a picker over your connections
records.text:
alethia cloud inventory

 Argument Required Description 
 ---------- ---------- ------------- 
 `[provider\ cloud-identity-id]` No `aws`, `gcp`, `azure`, or `hetzner`, or the id of one connection. Omit for a picker. 

 
**No id to copy.** This command used to take a bare ` ` — an opaque token
you had to copy out of another command's output before you could run it. Naming the provider
does the lookup for you, and omitting the argument shows a picker. An id a script already
holds keeps working, byte for byte: an id is a lookup key, so nothing here rewrites one.

Under `--no-input` there is no picker to show, so the argument is required and the refusal
says which providers are valid, with exit `9`. If two accounts are connected for the same
provider, the command reports the ambiguity with exit `8` and lists their ids rather than
guessing. A provider with no connected account exits `6` and names the command that connects one.
 

Renders a **Networks** table (network id, name, region, CIDR, default), a **Subnets** table
(subnet id, name, region, AZ, CIDR, public), and a **Regions** line. Add `-o json` for the full
inventory object; `-o csv` emits the networks rows. When the account hasn

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.text: Cluster Commands. List the Kubernetes clusters your projects run on, and inspect one — status, sizing, cost, the kubeconfig command and ArgoCD access.

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.text:
A cluster is what a project environment runs on. You do not create one here: provisioning an
environment creates it, and this group reads it back. The command is `alethia cluster` (singular)
with a `clusters` alias, so both forms work interchangeably.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These commands call `/cli/clusters` with your
[CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on the **active organization**, which you change with
`alethia org switch`. For one invocation, `alethia cluster list --org ` scopes the call to a
different organization instead — `--org` is a global flag, accepted on every command, and refused
with `403` if you are not a member of the organization you name.

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: alethia cluster list
records.text:
List every cluster across your projects — one row per project environment.

alethia cluster list
alethia clusters list
alethia cluster list -o json

The command takes no input of its own; only the [global flags](/reference/cli) apply.

 Column Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 Project The project and its environment — the same label `cluster get` titles its card with. 
 Cluster The cloud's name for the cluster, or `—` before it is provisioned. 
 Version The Kubernetes version. 
 Status A glyph and the status, with the status message appended when a cluster is degraded or failed. 
 ArgoCD `exposed` when a managed-ingress URL exists, `port-fwd` when access is by port-forward, `—` when the cluster is not provisioned yet. 
 Nodes Min / desired / max node count. 
 Region The cloud region. 
 Cost The estimated monthly cost, rendered exactly as the console's billing pages render it. 

Project Cluster Version Status ArgoCD Nodes Region Cost
api-backend (production) api-backend-production 1.30 ● active exposed 1/3/5 eu-west-1 $210.00/mo
data-pipeline (staging) data-pipeline-staging 1.29 ● active port-fwd 1/2/3 us-east4 $95.00/mo

At a terminal this is a navigable table; in a pipe, with `--no-i

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: alethia cluster get
records.text:
Show one cluster in full, including the command that gets you a kubeconfig and how to reach its ArgoCD.

alethia cluster get
alethia cluster get api-backend
alethia cluster get api-backend-production -o json

 Input Required Description 
 ------- ---------- ------------- 
 `[selector]` No — at a terminal Matches a project name, a cluster name, or a cluster id, case-insensitively. Falls back to a project-name substring. 

**Run it with no selector and the CLI asks which cluster**, listing every one you have with its
status. That is the whole reason the selector is optional: you never have to run `cluster list`
first and copy a name out of it.

The selector is required when a prompt could not work: with `--no-input`, with a piped stdin that
could never answer one, and with a redirected stdout that has no screen to draw one on. In each
case the command exits `9` explaining what to pass. The last is the easy one to hit —
`alethia cluster get -o json > clusters.json` refuses rather than writing a form into your file.
A selector that matches **nothing** is an error too, not an empty screen: the command exits `6`,
lists the clusters you have, and `alethia cluster get typo echo missing` pr

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: ArgoCD access
records.text:
ArgoCD is installed on every provisioned cluster. The **ArgoCD** row is its URL where a managed
ingress exists, and a note to port-forward where the cloud does not have one yet.

The admin password is **never stored by Alethia** — it would be plaintext in the control-plane
database — so the card prints the command that reads it from the cluster's own initial-admin
secret. It is a `kubectl` command, so get a kubeconfig first (the **Kubeconfig** row, above it),
then run:

kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' base64 -d

Where there is no managed ingress, reach the UI through a port-forward first:

kubectl -n argocd port-forward svc/argocd-server 8080:443

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: GitOps posture
records.text:
The **GitOps** row summarises the cluster's ArgoCD applications: how many are synced, how many are
healthy, and the short revision they are deployed at. It reads `failed at ` when the last
deploy failed, and `unknown (no snapshot yet)` when there is no trustworthy reading — which is a
different statement from "nothing is deployed", and deliberately not rendered as one.

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: alethia cluster kubeconfig
records.text:
Get a short-lived kubeconfig for a cluster without a cloud login of your own. A runner in the
cluster's network mints the credential and seals it to a one-time key that this command makes.
Only this machine can open the result. For the task, with the tiers, lifetimes and revocation, see
[Get a kubeconfig for your cluster](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig).

alethia cluster kubeconfig
alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend
alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend --admin --ttl 4h
alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend --out api-backend.kubeconfig
alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend --static --out -
alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend-production --no-input

 Input Required Default Description 
 ------- ---------- --------- ------------- 
 `[selector]` No — at a terminal The picker The same selector as `cluster get`: a project name, a cluster name or a cluster id. Omit it at a terminal and the CLI asks which cluster. 
 `--admin` No Off (read-only) Get the admin tier. Needs the `cluster:access_admin` permission, which owners and admins hold. Without it, the tier is read-only, which needs `cluster:access_readonly` (owners, admins and operators). 
 `--ttl` No `1h` The credential's lifetime,

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: Where the kubeconfig goes
records.text:
Flags Result 
 ------- -------- 
 None, or `--merge` The CLI merges the context `alethia- - ` into the first file in `$KUBECONFIG`, or into `~/.kube/config`, and makes it the current context. It replaces the cluster, user and context entries with that name, and keeps every other entry, unknown key and comment. It takes kubectl's ` .lock` lock while it writes, and follows a symlinked kubeconfig. 
 `--out FILE` The CLI writes a standalone kubeconfig to that file. 
 `--out -` The CLI writes the kubeconfig to stdout. This is the only way the credential goes to stdout. 

Every file the command writes gets mode `0600`, including a kubeconfig that was readable by others
before the merge, and the write is atomic. The command says on stderr which file it wrote. All
other messages go to stderr too, so stdout is empty unless you pass `--out -`. No message, error or
`--debug` line contains the credential.

**The `--out` and `--output` rules.** `--out` is the flag [`alethia export`](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply)
uses for the same thing. `--output FILE` is its older spelling on this command. It still works for
now and prints one line on stderr naming `--out`; in a later release `--output` becom

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: Exec and static
records.text:
Shape Clouds What the kubeconfig holds 
 ------- -------- --------------------------- 
 Exec (the default) AWS, GCP, Azure No credential. It runs `alethia cluster token` with the cluster id, so `kubectl` gets a new token whenever one expires. The command also caches the token it just minted, so the first `kubectl` call does not wait for a runner. 
 Static (`--static`) All four, and always on Hetzner The credential itself: a bearer token, or a client certificate and key. It stops working at its expiry. 

The cluster list does not tell the CLI which cloud a cluster is on. So without `--static`, the CLI
asks for exec. If the cloud refuses (`422`), it asks again for static. A second `422` means the cloud
cannot mint either shape.

The exec kubeconfig pins the cluster's API server and certificate authority, and it never turns off
TLS verification. It needs the `alethia` command on the `PATH` of every machine that runs `kubectl`
with it.

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: What the command prints

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: Exit codes and refusals
records.text:
The command exits `0` when it wrote the kubeconfig. Every error is one line on stderr, with a hint
when there is a next command to run, and an exit code that says what kind of failure it was. A flag
that is wrong exits `8` before anything is sent. A missing selector, or one that matches several
clusters, exits `9` when there is no terminal to ask on. A selector that matches nothing exits `6`. These are the refusals
from the control plane, and what the CLI prints:

 Status Exit Cause The CLI prints 
 -------- ------ ------- ---------------- 
 `401` `4` The session is not valid. Run `alethia login`. 
 `402` `10` A usage limit of the organization's plan. The mint runs on a runner and uses runner minutes. The server's reason, and a pointer to `alethia usage`. 
 `403` `5` Your role does not hold the tier's permission. Which roles can mint that tier. For `--admin`, a hint to drop it. 
 `404` `6` No such cluster in the active organization. A pointer to `alethia org switch` and `--org`. 
 `409` `7` The environment is a draft, is being destroyed, or has no successful deploy. The server's reason, and a pointer to `alethia project apply`. 
 `422` `8` The cluster's cloud cannot mint a kubeconf

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: alethia cluster token
records.text:
Print a credential for `kubectl`. This is the exec plugin that the kubeconfig from
`alethia cluster kubeconfig` runs. You do not usually run it yourself.

alethia cluster token

 Input Required Default Description 
 ------- ---------- --------- ------------- 
 `[cluster-id]` No — at a terminal The picker The cluster id, a lowercase UUID as `cluster get` shows it. `kubectl` always passes it. Omit it at a terminal and the CLI asks which cluster, which is a way to check that your session can still mint. Without a terminal, it is required. 

The command takes no flags of its own. The global `--org` and `--token` flags apply.

**Stdout** carries one `client.authentication.k8s.io/v1` `ExecCredential` document and nothing
else: the token and its expiry. **Stderr** carries every error, as one line that names
`alethia cluster token:`, and `kubectl` shows that line. No error, note or `--debug` line contains
the token. The command exits `0` when it printed a credential. Otherwise it exits with the code of
the failure, the same codes as [`alethia cluster kubeconfig`](#exit-codes-and-refusals): `4` for a
session that is not valid, `5` when your role no longer allows the mint, `8` for an argumen

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: The cache
records.text:
The command keeps each credential in a cache until 60 seconds before the credential expires. So
only the first `kubectl` call in each credential's lifetime waits for a new mint.

 Property Value 
 ---------- ------- 
 Directory `alethia/kubecache` in the user configuration directory: `~/.config` on Linux (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`), `~/Library/Application Support` on macOS, `%AppData%` on Windows 
 Modes Directory `0700`, files `0600`. A directory that others can read is tightened. A cache file that is a symlink, is owned by another user, or that others can read is refused, not replaced. On Windows the user profile's access control applies instead. 
 Files per cluster The token and its expiry for each tier, the re-mint profile, and a lock file 
 Locking One lock per cluster. If several `kubectl` calls start on an empty cache, the first one mints and the others wait for it, so there is one mint.

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: Re-minting
records.text:
When the cache has no fresh credential, the command mints a new one, in the exec shape, with the
profile that `alethia cluster kubeconfig` recorded: the tier, the TTL and the organization. It
uses that organization even if your active organization changed since, unless you pass `--org`.
A cluster with no profile, for example a kubeconfig copied from another machine, gets the
read-only tier with a 1-hour TTL in the active organization, never the admin tier.

Each mint checks your permission again. So a person whose role changes, or who leaves the
organization, stops getting tokens when the current one expires.

records.title: Cluster Commands
records.heading: Accessing a cluster with kubectl
records.text:
The **Kubeconfig** row is the command that writes a kubeconfig with **your own cloud CLI**, under
your own cloud login. Alethia does not issue a credential through this row: whether the command
works is your cloud account's decision. To get a kubeconfig through Alethia instead, use
[`alethia cluster kubeconfig`](#alethia-cluster-kubeconfig). In `-o json` output the same answer is the
`kubeconfig` object, with `command` and `note` fields.

Alethia builds the command from values the cluster's last successful deploy recorded, so it is
the same command the console's cluster card shows. Run it, then use `kubectl`:

 
 
 aws eks update-kubeconfig --name api-backend-production --region eu-west-1
 kubectl get nodes
 
 
 gcloud container clusters get-credentials data-pipeline-staging --region us-east4 --project acme-data-prod
 kubectl get nodes
 
 For a zonal cluster, one deployed to a zone such as `us-east4-a`, the command names the zone
 instead of the region.
 
 
 az aks get-credentials --resource-group rg-api-backend-production --name api-backend-production
 kubectl get nodes
 
 
 Hetzner has no cloud CLI command for a kubeconfig, so the **Kubeconfig** row has none. The
 cluster's Talos
