records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.text: Organizations, Members & Teams. Switch the active organization and manage its members and teams from the CLI.

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.text:
alethia scopes everything you do — projects, runners, jobs, connectors — to an **active
organization**. The active org is persisted locally (in `~/.config/alethia/config.json`) and sent as
the `X-Alethia-Org` header on every request.

`--org ` targets a different organization for a single invocation, on every command in the CLI
and not only the ones on this page. It sets the `X-Alethia-Org` header, and for `members` and
`teams` — the two commands that address the org in their request path — it sets the org in the path
as well, from the same value. Naming an organization you are not a member of is refused with `403`.
Under a service token the flag must name the token's own organization: a different one is refused
with `403` rather than quietly ignored, so a pipeline cannot believe it is acting on one org while
every write lands in another.

Every command here also accepts the global `--org `,
[`-o, --output `](/reference/cli/identity#output-formats) and `--no-input` flags.

 
Nothing on this page asks you to copy an id out of a previous command. `members remove` takes
`--email`, `teams delete` takes `--name`, and both offer a picker when you name nothing — so
`--no-input` always has

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: What a command prints and how it fails
records.text:
A command that lists prints one table, or one array under `-o json`. An empty list prints `[]`
under `-o json` and says so on stderr otherwise.

A command that changes something prints one sentence, or one result under `-o json`:

{
 "id": "t2",
 "kind": "team",
 "action": "created",
 "job": null,
 "dry_run": false,
 "object": { "id": "t2", "name": "platform", "member_count": 0 }
}

`action` is `created`, `updated`, `deleted` or `unchanged`. `--dry-run` checks the input, sends
nothing, and prints the same result with `dry_run: true` and the request under `object.request`.

Stdout carries the result and nothing else. Notes, the resolved target and every error go to
stderr. A failure exits with the code of its class: `5` when you are not permitted, `6` when the thing named does
not exist, `8` for input that cannot be right, `9` when a value or a confirmation is needed and
nothing can ask for it, `10` when the plan does not include the feature. The message is the
control plane's own sentence.

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia org list
records.text:
List the organizations you belong to. The active org is marked in the `Active` column.

alethia org list

Output:

NAME SLUG ROLE PLAN ACTIVE
Acme acme owner pro ◆
Personal you owner free

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia org switch
records.text:
Set the active organization. Pass an org **id, slug, or name**; with no argument, pick one
interactively.

alethia org switch acme
alethia org switch

{/* fieldspec: alethia org switch */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Organization The organization to make active; its id, slug, or name `[org]` — 

The selection is persisted locally and sent as `X-Alethia-Org` on subsequent commands. Clear it with
[`alethia config clear-context`](/reference/cli/configuration#alethia-config). Nothing changes on
the control plane. Switching to the organization that is already active reports `unchanged`. With
no argument and nothing to ask, the command exits `9`; an organization that matches nothing exits
`6`.

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia org settings
records.text:
Show the active organization's general settings.

alethia org settings
alethia org settings -o json

Renders a field/value card: **name**, **slug**, and **description**. The command is read-only; you
change these settings in the console. Under `-o json` it prints the whole record, which still
carries the `region`, `default_env`, and `terraform_version` keys so existing scripts keep working.
These three keys are deprecated: nothing reads them, the console no longer sets them, and the table
and `-o csv` don't show them. Stop relying on them in scripts. When the caller has no real org (personal scope) it prints `null` under `-o json`, and otherwise says
`Not in an organization (community mode).` on stderr. Backing call: `GET /cli/org-settings`.

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia members list
records.text:
List the members of the active organization: id, email, name, role, and invitation status. The `ID`
column is there for `-o json` and `-o csv` consumers — you never need to copy it by hand.

alethia members list
alethia members list -o json
alethia members list --org org_456

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia members add
records.text:
Invite someone to the active organization. Pass their email and `--role` to run without a terminal;
with neither, the form asks for both and offers the org's own roles — including any custom role.

alethia members add teammate@example.com --role operator
alethia members add

{/* fieldspec: alethia members add */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Email Who to invite; they get an invitation at this address `[email]` — 
 Role What the invited member may do, from the org's roles `--role` — 

`--role` defaults to `member`. A scripted `alethia members add ada@example.com --no-input` keeps
that default; on a terminal the form asks, because the default is rarely what the inviter meant.

`alethia members invite` is the same command under the name of what it does. The result's `kind` is
`invitation`: the person becomes a member when they accept. `--dry-run` checks the address and
sends no invitation.

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia members remove
records.text:
Remove a member. Name them by email, or pick from the org's members; the member id still works if
you have one.

alethia members remove --email teammate@example.com --yes
alethia members remove

{/* fieldspec: alethia members remove */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Member Who to remove; name them by email rather than copying a member id `[member_id]` `--email` 

This is destructive, so it confirms first: you type the member's email. `--yes` (or `-y`) skips
the prompt and is **required** with `--no-input` — a scripted removal without it exits `9` and
removes nobody. When the CLI picks the member for you, it prints which one on stderr before it
asks. `--dry-run` names the member that would be removed and removes nobody.

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia teams list
records.text:
List the teams in the active organization, with a member count.

alethia teams list
alethia teams list --org org_456

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia teams create
records.text:
Create a team. Pass the name to run without a terminal; with no name, the form asks for one.
`--dry-run` checks the input and creates nothing. If the control plane refuses, its sentence is
printed as it sent it.

alethia teams create platform
alethia teams create

{/* fieldspec: alethia teams create */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Name What the team is called, so a list of teams is a list of purposes `[name]` —

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: alethia teams delete
records.text:
Delete a team. Name it with `--name`, or pick from the org's teams.

alethia teams delete --name platform --yes
alethia teams delete

{/* fieldspec: alethia teams delete */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Team Which team to delete; name it rather than copying a team id `[team_id]` `--name` 

Members keep their org membership but lose the grants the team carried. Destructive, so it
confirms: you type the team's name. `--yes` skips the prompt and is required with `--no-input`;
without it the command exits `9` and deletes nothing. `--dry-run` names the team that would be
deleted and deletes nothing.

records.title: Organizations, Members & Teams
records.heading: Flags
records.text:
Flag Where Description 
 ------ ------- ------------- 
 `--org ` every command (global) Operate on this org instead of the active one, for one invocation. 
 `--role ` `members add` Role for the invited member. Default `member`. 
 `--email ` `members remove` Name the member by address instead of a member id. 
 `--name ` `teams delete` Name the team instead of a team id. 
 `-y, --yes` `members remove`, `teams delete` Skip the confirmation prompt. Required with `--no-input`. 
 `--dry-run` `members add`, `members remove`, `teams create`, `teams delete` Check the input and print what would be sent, without sending it.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.text: Plan & Apply. Describe a project in alethia.yaml, preview the changes with plan, and create and deploy it with apply.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.text:
One file describes a project; two commands take it from a file to a running cluster. Nothing has
to be copied out of another command's output: the cloud account is named by its **label**, the
runner by its **name**, and every environment by the name the file gives it.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: alethia.yaml
records.text:
The manifest is the whole shape of a project — where it provisions, every environment with its
placement, and the components each environment carries:

project: boutique
cloud:
 account: prod-account # the connector's label, as `alethia connector list` shows it
 region: nbg1
environments:
 - name: prod
 stage: production
 placement: dedicated # owns the Fabric: this is the environment with a cluster
 components:
 cluster:
 node_min_size: 2
 node_max_size: 3
 - name: dev-1
 stage: development
 placement: namespace # placed onto prod's Fabric, no new cluster
 namespace: boutique-dev-1
 components:
 repositories:
 apps_destination_repo: https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-examples
 apps_path: examples/online-boutique/overlays/dev-1
 databases:
 - name: orders
 engine: postgres

 Key What it is 
 --- --- 
 `project` The project's name. Unique in the organization, so `apply` finds an existing project by it. 
 `cloud.account` The cloud account's label (or its id). Omit it to create an unlinked project. 
 `cloud.region` The region to provision into. 
 `iac.version` OpenTofu version to pin. Optional; the server defaults it. 
 `environments[].name` The environment's name. 
 `environme

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: alethia apply
records.text:
Create whatever the file declares that does not exist yet, show the plan, and deploy every
environment.

alethia apply # ./alethia.yaml, asks before applying
alethia apply --yes --no-input # in a pipeline
alethia apply --runner my-box # deploy with a named runner
alethia apply --env dev-1 # create everything, deploy only dev-1
alethia apply --yes --timeout 45m # wait at most 45 minutes for the deploys

▸ Reading alethia.yaml · boutique · hetzner/nbg1
 + project boutique
 prod dedicated + environment + cluster
 dev-1 namespace + environment + repositories + databases/orders
 1 project to create · 2 environments · 3 components
Apply these changes? Yes
 ✓ created project boutique
 ✓ added cluster in prod
 ✓ added repositories in dev-1
 ✓ added databases/orders in dev-1
▸ Deploying prod (job 4f3c2b1a-…)
 ✓ Job completed successfully
▸ Deploying dev-1 (job 8a1d0e77-…)
 ✓ Job completed successfully

✓ boutique is up.

The plan and the last line are the command's output, on stdout. Everything between them is
progress, on stderr. So a script that reads stdout gets the plan and the result and nothing else.

Running `apply` again is safe. On a project that already matches the file it creates

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: What the file leaves out is never removed
records.text:
`apply` creates and updates. It does not remove anything. An environment, a component or an add-on
that is on the server and not in the file is **unmanaged**: `plan` and `apply` list it and leave it
as it is.

 staging is on the server and not in the file — left alone (unmanaged)
 Not in the file means unmanaged: apply leaves it as it is and never removes it.

To remove an environment, destroy it with
[`alethia project destroy`](/reference/cli/project). To remove a component, use
[`alethia project component remove`](/reference/cli/project). Deleting its lines from the file does
neither.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Waiting for the deploys
records.text:
`apply` deploys each environment in file order, and waits for each one before it starts the next.
The first environment owns the cluster, so the others cannot be deployed before it.

A deploy applies a reviewed plan. So for each environment `apply` first queues a preview (a PLAN
job), waits for it, and prints how many resources it would create, update, replace and delete. The
deploy then applies exactly that plan. A preview that fails stops the run with exit `13`, and that
environment is not deployed.

▸ Previewing prod (job 2b7e91c0-…); a deploy applies a reviewed plan
 prod Plan: 14 to create, 0 to update, 0 to replace, 0 to delete.
▸ Deploying prod (job 4f3c2b1a-…)

- `--no-wait` returns once the deploys are queued. It still waits for each preview, because a
 deploy needs its plan. Every job is named in the result. `--wait=false` means the same.
- `--timeout` sets how long the whole run may take, previews included, for example
 `--timeout 45m`. When the time passes, `apply` stops waiting and exits `12`. The job that is
 running keeps running. The error names its job, the command that follows it, and the
 environments that were not deployed yet. Run `alethia apply` again when tha

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: When a deploy needs a person's approval
records.text:
A deploy or a destroy started from the CLI needs a person's approval of the plan it applies. This is
true for a device sign-in and for a service token, because the control plane cannot tell a person at
a terminal from an agent in the same shell. A person clicking deploy in the console needs no
separate approval: the click is the approval.

When the control plane answers that a deploy needs an approval, `apply` asks for one, prints the
console page where a person approves it, and waits:

⚠ This deploy needs a person's approval. Approve it at https://alethialabs.io/approvals/6b21d8f4-… — the page must show plan 2b7e91c0-… with a digest starting a1b2c3d4.
Waiting for approval 6b21d8f4-… to be decided (expires 2026-12-01T10:00:00Z)...

The approval page shows the same eight digest characters. Check that they match before you approve:
that is how you know you approve the plan the command showed you. Once it is approved, `apply`
queues the deploy with the approval and carries on.

- **Rejected:** `apply` exits `5` and nothing is deployed.
- **Expired, or superseded** by a newer plan or a change to the environment: `apply` exits `7`. Run
 it again to ask for a new approval.
- **`--no-wait

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: alethia approve
records.text:
Open the console page where a person approves a deploy or a destroy that the CLI asked for.

alethia approve 6b21d8f4-0c5e-4a93-9f27-3d81b6e5c704 # opens the page in your browser
alethia approve 6b21d8f4-0c5e-4a93-9f27-3d81b6e5c704 --no-browser # prints the page, to send to whoever approves

 Argument or flag Required Description 
 --- --- --- 
 `[approval-id]` No The approval id the deploy or destroy printed. Omit it on a terminal and you are asked for it. 
 `--no-browser` No Print the page instead of opening it. 

`approve` never approves anything. It sends nothing to the control plane, so neither a stored CLI
credential nor an agent that holds one can approve its own request. The decision is made only in a
signed-in console session.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Exit codes of apply
records.text:
Code Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `0` Done. Without `--no-wait`, every deploy finished. 
 `1` The file does not exist or is not valid. 
 `2` The file cannot be applied as written. This is the code `alethia plan` gives the same file; see [Exit codes](#exit-codes). 
 `5` A person rejected the approval a deploy asked for. 
 `7` The approval expired, or a newer plan or change superseded it. 
 `9` Nobody could confirm and `--yes` was not passed, or a deploy is waiting for a person's approval and the command did not wait. 
 `12` `--timeout` passed. The preview or the deploy is still running. 
 `13` A preview or a deploy finished and failed, or was cancelled. `alethia jobs logs` with the job's id shows why. 
 `130` You stopped the wait with Ctrl+C. 

Any other code is one of the CLI's general exit codes: for example `4` when you are not signed
in, `7` when the server refuses a change because of a conflict, and `11` when the control plane
cannot be reached.

An environment's `lifecycle` is set once, when the environment is created. Nothing changes it after
that: not `apply`, and not the console. A file that leaves `lifecycle` out means `persistent`. If the
file says a different lifecycle than the s

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Changing a component
records.text:
Edit a field of a component that already exists, and `plan` and `apply` show the change and make
it. Each row starts with a mark:

 Mark Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `+` It does not exist yet. `apply` creates it. 
 `~` It exists, and at least one field the file declares has a different value on the server. `apply` changes those fields. 
 `=` It exists, and every field the file declares already matches. `apply` sends nothing for it. 

Under each `~` row, one line names each changed field with the server's value and the file's value.
Here the file raises `max_capacity` of the `orders` database in `prod` from `4` to `8`:

▸ Reading alethia.yaml · boutique · hetzner/nbg1
 prod dedicated = environment = cluster ~ databases/orders
 ~ databases/orders max_capacity: 4 → 8
 dev-1 namespace = environment = repositories
 0 projects to create · 0 environments · 0 components · 1 component to update

`(unset)` means the server has no value for that field.

- **A field you leave out is never cleared.** `apply` compares only the fields the file names, and
 sends only the ones that changed. This is true for every kind: a named component such as a
 database, and a one-per-environment kind such as `cluster`.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: When the server changes first
records.text:
`apply` changes a component only if the server still holds the copy that `apply` read. There is no
saved plan file: `apply` reads every component again, computes the changes against that read, and
then makes them. Two rules protect that read.

**A component changed after the read is not overwritten.** `apply` sends the component's revision
(its `updated_at`) with each change. If someone changed the component in the meantime, for example
in the console or with another `apply`, the server refuses the change. `apply` then names each
setting that changed on the server:

 ✗ databases/orders in prod was not updated: databases/orders changed on the server after
 `alethia plan` read it: max_capacity: 4 → 16; re-run `alethia plan` to see the difference
 against the server's copy now, then apply again

Run `alethia plan` again, decide which value you want, and then run `alethia apply`. A component
that was removed after the read is refused in the same way. `apply` does not create it again.

**A component is not changed while its environment is deploying or being destroyed.** The server
refuses every change that `apply` makes to an existing component while one of these is unfinished
for that

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Setting and removing a provider_config key
records.text:
A component's `provider_config` holds its template knobs, the same ones the console's **Advanced**
section sets. `plan` and `apply` treat it **key by key**, not as one value:

 databases:
 - name: orders
 engine: postgres
 provider_config:
 rds_backup_retention_period: 14 # set this key
 rds_performance_insights: null # remove this key

- A key you write is set to the file's value.
- A key you write as `null` is removed. `plan` shows it as a change only while the server still
 holds the key, so the removal shows once and then settles.
- A key you do not write is kept, and shows no change. A key set in the console stays set.
- `provider_config` itself must be a mapping. A whole `provider_config: null`, or an empty
 `provider_config:`, is refused before anything is sent, because the server refuses it. To remove
 every key, write each one as `null`.

`apply` sends only the keys that changed. The keys a component accepts depend on its cloud;
[Setting template knobs](/reference/cli/project#setting-template-knobs) explains how to find them.

`apply` changes the component's **settings**. It does not tell you whether the next deploy replaces
the cloud resource. To see that, read the OpenTo

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Add-ons
records.text:
An environment can declare the [catalog add-ons](/reference/cli/addons) it runs. `plan` shows what
would change, and `apply` makes it so. This file declares two environments. `staging` runs
external-dns pinned to chart version `1.14.5` with two settings, and kube-prometheus-stack with a
Helm values file. `prod` runs loki at the catalog's default version:

project: boutique
cloud:
 account: prod-account
 region: nbg1
environments:
 - name: prod
 stage: production
 placement: dedicated
 addons:
 - id: loki # no version: the catalog's default version
 settings:
 retentionDays: 30
 - name: staging
 stage: staging
 placement: namespace
 namespace: boutique-staging
 addons:
 - id: external-dns
 version: 1.14.5 # pin the chart version
 settings:
 provider: cloudflare
 domainFilter: staging.boutique.example.com
 - id: kube-prometheus-stack
 settings:
 retentionDays: 7
 values_file: helm/kps-staging.yaml # relative to alethia.yaml

`helm/kps-staging.yaml` is an ordinary Helm values file, next to `alethia.yaml` in the repository:

grafana:
 replicas: 2
prometheus:
 prometheusSpec:
 resources:
 requests:
 memory: 2Gi

 Key What it is 
 --- --- 
 `id` The add-on's catalog id. Required. An id t

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Where a values file can come from
records.text:
The fence is the folder that holds `alethia.yaml`, not the files that Git tracks. `apply` sends any
file inside that folder that `values_file` names. This includes a file that a CI step writes into
the workspace, such as a kubeconfig or a credentials file. If `alethia.yaml` names that file,
`apply` sends its contents to the server as the override.

Keep each values file committed, and review it as you review `alethia.yaml`. Do not name a file
that a pipeline step creates.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Keep and clear
records.text:
Each key means what the same flag of [`alethia addon enable`](/reference/cli/addons) means, because
`apply` sends the same request:

 You write `apply` does 
 --- --- 
 nothing for a key keeps what is stored: the pin, the mode, each setting, the override 
 `version: 1.14.5` pins the chart version 
 `version: ""` or `version: null` removes the pin, so the catalog's default version applies 
 `settings: { key: value }` sets that one setting and keeps the others 
 `settings: { key: null }` resets that setting to the add-on's default 
 `values` or `values_file: path` replaces the whole stored override 
 `values_file: ""` or `values: null` removes the override

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: What plan shows
records.text:
Add-ons get one line per environment, with the same marks as components. Under it, one line names
each changed field. Here staging's external-dns runs the catalog's default version and an older
domain filter, kube-prometheus-stack's values file changed, and reloader in `prod` is enabled on
the server but not in the file:

▸ Reading alethia.yaml · boutique · hetzner/nbg1
 prod dedicated = environment
 add-ons = loki
 add-on reloader is enabled on the server and not in the file — left alone (unmanaged)
 staging namespace = environment
 add-ons ~ external-dns ~ kube-prometheus-stack
 ~ external-dns settings.domainFilter: boutique.example.com → staging.boutique.example.com
 ~ external-dns version: (catalog default) → 1.14.5
 ~ kube-prometheus-stack values: changed (6 lines)
 0 projects to create · 0 environments · 0 components · 0 add-ons to enable · 2 to change

**A plan never shows what an override says.** A values file can be any file in the repository,
and a plan is printed into CI logs. So the `values` line says only `changed (N lines)`, with N the
line count of the new override, or `removed`. It shows no hash either: a short hash of a value
such as a password can be guessed offli

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: What apply never does
records.text:
- **It never disables an add-on.** An add-on that is enabled on the server and not in the file is
 listed as unmanaged and keeps running. Disable one with
 [`alethia addon disable`](/reference/cli/addons).
- **It never takes a secret from the file.** `alethia.yaml` is committed to git, so a secret setting
 in it is refused before anything is sent. The refusal names the setting. Set a secret with
 `alethia addon enable --set =…` or in the console. `apply` keeps a stored secret as it
 is, and `plan` never prints a secret's value.

 
 **A secret for an environment that `apply` creates.** The file cannot carry a secret, and
 `alethia addon enable --env ` needs the environment to exist. So the first `apply` installs
 the add-on without it: external-dns on a token provider such as Cloudflare comes up and cannot
 write DNS records yet. Set the token once the environment exists, here from an environment
 variable so it stays out of your shell history, and deploy again:

 alethia apply --yes
 alethia addon enable external-dns --project boutique --env staging --set apiToken="$CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN"
 alethia apply --yes
 
 The second `apply` leaves the token as it is. On a workload-identity pr

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: alethia up
records.text:
The whole first run in one command: sign in, attach nothing (see below), write the manifest, apply
it. Every step is skipped when it is already done, so it resumes wherever the last run stopped.

alethia up # asks for what it needs
alethia up --project boutique --region nbg1 --cloud-account prod-account --yes --no-input

 Step Skipped when 
 --- --- 
 the control-plane URL and the login this machine has a live credential 
 a cloud account one is connected — **otherwise `up` stops**, see below 
 a runner a runner that takes the account's cloud is online, or a managed fleet takes the deploy — **otherwise `up` stops**, see below 
 `alethia.yaml` this directory has one 
 the apply never; that is the point 

With the manifest already present, an account connected and a runner available, `alethia up`
**is** `alethia apply`.

 
 `up` cannot attach a cloud account for you. Each cloud has its own keyless flow with its own
 arguments — `alethia connector aws gcp azure hetzner` — so `up` stops and names them
 rather than growing a fifth version that would drift from the four.
 

 
 `up` cannot start a runner for you either: a runner is a process that somebody has to start. When
 nothing would

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: alethia plan
records.text:
The same comparison, with the writes left out: what `apply` would create, what it would change
(field by field, as in [Changing a component](#changing-a-component)), what already matches, and
anything it would refuse. Nothing is written and no job is queued.

alethia plan
alethia plan --file staging.yaml --output json
alethia plan --detailed-exitcode

{/* fieldspec: alethia plan */}

 Field What it is Set without the form 
 ------------------ -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------- 
 Manifest The alethia.yaml to plan (default: ./alethia.yaml) `--file` 
 Detailed exit code Exit 0 with no changes, 2 with changes, 3 with problems (1 is an error). Default: 0 unless the plan has problems (2) `--detailed-exitcode` 

The per-environment OpenTofu plan runs inside every deploy. To queue one on its own, for a
pipeline that gates on it, use [`alethia project preview`](/reference/cli/project).

A plan never contains a removal. What is on the server and not in the file is listed as unmanaged:
see [What the file leaves out is never removed](#what-the-file-leaves-out-is-never-removed). In
`--output

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Exit codes
records.text:
A plan has **problems** when the file asks for something `apply` cannot do: a stage, placement or
lifecycle that differs from an existing environment, or an add-on setting that `apply` refuses to
send. `apply` refuses such a file before it writes anything. The exit code of `plan` tells you so
first, and a pipeline can stop on it when the pull request opens instead of at `apply`.

By default, `plan` answers one question: does `apply` accept this file?

 Code Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `0` `apply` accepts the file. There can be changes. 
 `1` The file does not exist or is not valid. 
 `2` The plan has problems. `apply` refuses the file. 

A plan with changes and no problems exits `0`, so a pipeline that runs `plan` and then `apply`
keeps working.

With `--detailed-exitcode`, the code also says whether there is anything to apply. This is the
Terraform convention. Problems win over changes, because a plan with both cannot be applied:

 Code Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `0` No changes and no problems. 
 `1` The file does not exist or is not valid. 
 `2` Changes, and no problems. 
 `3` The plan has problems. `apply` refuses the file. 

In both tables, any other code is one of the CLI's general exit code

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Problems in --output json
records.text:
Each environment in `environments` lists its problems in `problems`, one sentence each. An
environment without problems has no `problems` key. This is a plan with one problem; the `manifest`
key, which repeats the file as read, is left out:

{
 "project_id": "4b1d2c9e-7f3a-4e55-9c1d-2a6f0b8e1c37",
 "environments": [
 {
 "name": "production",
 "stage": "staging",
 "placement": "dedicated",
 "action": "unchanged",
 "id": "9e2f4a10-3c6b-4d8e-a1f7-5b0c6d2e8f94",
 "components": null,
 "problems": [
 "the file says stage staging, the server has production — a stage cannot be changed from here; edit it in the console or the file"
 ],
 "deploy": true
 }
 ]
}

A script can list every problem with `jq`:

alethia plan --output json jq -r '.environments[] .name as $env .problems[]? "\($env): \(.)"'

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Run plan on every pull request
records.text:
This GitHub Actions job fails a pull request when `alethia.yaml` cannot be applied. `plan` reads
the add-on values files the manifest names, so list their directory under `paths` too (here
`values/`); otherwise a pull request that changes only a values file skips the check. It passes when
the file has changes that `apply` accepts. It signs in with a service token in the `ALETHIA_TOKEN`
secret; `alethia token create --name ci gh secret set ALETHIA_TOKEN` makes one:

name: alethia plan
on:
 pull_request:
 paths:
 - alethia.yaml
 - values/** # the add-on values files alethia.yaml names, if it names any
jobs:
 plan:
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - name: Install the Alethia CLI
 run: 
 curl -fsSL https://get.alethialabs.io sh
 echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
 - name: Plan
 env:
 ALETHIA_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.ALETHIA_TOKEN }}
 run: alethia plan --no-input

To also see whether the file differs from the server, use `--detailed-exitcode` and read the code
yourself. `0` means the file matches what the server has. It does not mean `apply` does nothing:
`apply` deploys every environment again, even when nothing differs. A step stops on the first
non-zero

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Start from an existing project
records.text:
A project that you built in the console has no `alethia.yaml` yet.
[`alethia export`](/reference/cli/configuration#alethia-export) writes one from what the project has
now, so you can manage the project from git from that point on.

 
 

Write the file. This example takes every environment of the project; you can also export one of
them.

alethia export shop --all --out alethia.yaml

 
 

Plan it. The file describes what the project already has, so there is nothing to do:

alethia plan

▸ Reading alethia.yaml · shop · aws/eu-west-1
 prod dedicated = environment = cluster = databases/orders
 add-ons = cert-manager = external-dns
 staging namespace = environment = databases/orders
 0 projects to create · 0 environments · 0 components

 
 

Commit `alethia.yaml`. From now on, edit the file and run `alethia apply` — in a pipeline,
`alethia apply --yes --no-input`.

 
 

`export` writes only the values that Alethia publishes as plain, non-secret settings, so a secret
that Alethia stores is never written. It cannot recognize a password typed into an ordinary
setting, so review the file before you commit it. See
[What is written, and what is left out](/reference/cli/configuration#what-is-

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: One environment at a time
records.text:
`plan` and `apply` work on the whole file. To queue one job for one environment, use the `project`
commands. They are described on the [project page](/reference/cli/project):

- `alethia project preview` queues the OpenTofu plan of one environment.
- `alethia project deploy` deploys one environment from a reviewed plan: the one you name, or a
 preview it makes and shows you first.
- `alethia project destroy` tears one environment down.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: alethia project destroy
records.text:
Queue a DESTROY job for one environment. The Runner runs `tofu destroy` and tears down every
resource of that environment; the console guide's
[destroy workflow](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#destroy-an-environment) says what is kept and what is lost.
`alethia apply` never does this: removing an environment from `alethia.yaml` leaves it running.

alethia project destroy --project boutique --env dev-1 # asks you to type the project's name
alethia project destroy --project boutique --env prod --cascade --wait # prod and every environment on its cluster

The flags, the confirmation and the result are on the
[project page](/reference/cli/project).

A destroy from the CLI needs a person's approval too, given against the plan the environment's
current state was deployed from. It is asked for, shown and waited for the same way as a deploy's
(see [When a deploy needs a person's approval](#when-a-deploy-needs-a-persons-approval)). With
`--no-wait` the command exits `9` with the page; run the same destroy again once it is approved. A
`--cascade` destroy cannot be approved this way: start it from the console.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Destroying an environment that other environments run on
records.text:
A `dedicated` environment owns its cluster. `namespace` and `vcluster` environments placed on that
cluster run inside it, and their own teardown needs the cluster to still exist. So while any of them
is live, destroying the `dedicated` environment is **refused**, and the error names each one:

Environment "prod" owns the cluster that 2 other environments are still placed on:
dev-1 (namespace, ACTIVE), staging (vcluster, FAILED). ...
Re-run with --cascade to see every environment it would destroy and confirm

An environment that was never applied (`DRAFT`) or is already `DESTROYED` does not count. Destroying
a `namespace` or `vcluster` environment is never refused for this reason.

Either destroy the listed environments first, or pass `--cascade`. It prints what it will destroy,
then asks:

Will destroy, in order: dev-1 (namespace), staging (vcluster, failed), prod (dedicated, owns the cluster)

The order is enforced by the Console, not by timing: the DESTROY of `prod` stays `QUEUED`, and no
Runner can start it, until no live environment is left on its cluster. If the destroy of `dev-1` or
`staging` fails, `prod` keeps waiting. `--wait` stops at the failed job and names the two ways

records.text: alethia up --project boutique --region nbg1 --cloud-account prod-account --yes --no-input

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: The whole project from its file, unattended
records.text: alethia apply --yes --no-input

alethia project preview --project boutique --env prod --runner eu-box --wait
alethia jobs get --latest --project boutique --type PLAN

records.title: Probe Commands
records.text: Probe Commands. Inspect a project's cluster-alive probes — the "is it still up?" day-2 signal per environment.

records.title: Probe Commands
records.text:
The `probes` group (alias `probe`) lists the latest **cluster-alive probe** per environment — the
"is it still up?" half of day-2, alongside [drift](/reference/cli/drift)'s "has it diverged?". A
`PROBE_CLUSTER` job dials each environment's cluster API server; this shows the most recent result.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. `probes list` calls `/cli/projects/ /probes`
with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operates on the **active organization**, which you
change with `alethia org switch`. Pass `--org ` to scope a single invocation to a different
organization — it is refused with `403` if you are not a member of it.

records.title: Probe Commands
records.heading: alethia probes list
records.text:
List a project's latest per-environment cluster probes.

alethia probes list
alethia probes list --project my-project
alethia probes list -p my-project -o json

Name the project with `--project`; omit it at a terminal and you are asked which project to read,
from the ones you have.

{/* fieldspec: alethia probes list */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Project Whose environments to report the latest cluster probe for `--project` 

Columns: **Environment**, **Reachable** (`● up`, `○ down`, or `— never probed`), **Message** (why
unreachable, when down), **Probed** (when the last probe ran, to the minute in UTC). Every
environment is listed; one that has never been probed shows `never probed` rather than being
hidden.

Environment Reachable Message Probed
production ● up — 2026-01-01 00:00
staging ○ down dial tcp: timeout 2026-01-01 00:00
dev — never probed — —

Add `-o json` for the raw probe objects — the `probed_at` there is the wire's unrounded RFC 3339
timestamp, not the table's rendering; `-o csv` for the rows. Backing call:
`GET /cli/projects/ /probes`.

records.title: Probe Commands
records.heading: Output and exit codes
records.text:
The result is the only thing the command writes on stdout, and it writes nothing there when it
fails. A failure exits with the code of its kind, and stderr says what happened and what to run
next:

 Exit Meaning on this page 
 ------ ---------------------- 
 `4` You are not signed in, or the session has expired 
 `5` You are not permitted to read this project 
 `6` The project or environment that you named does not exist 
 `9` `--project` was left out and nothing can ask for it (`--no-input`, a pipe, or `-o json`) 

The codes mean the same on every command of the CLI.

records.title: Probe Commands
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Drift Commands](/reference/cli/drift) — the divergence half of day-2.
- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Project Commands
records.text: Project Commands. Create, inspect, design, deploy and destroy projects from the CLI.

records.title: Project Commands
records.text:
Projects are infrastructure configurations (an *app* that owns one or more environments). The CLI
can both **read** projects (`list`, `get`) and **author** them — create a project, manage its
environments, and CRUD its component resources — so the whole project lifecycle is scriptable.

All authoring commands operate on the **active organization** (set via `alethia org switch`), or on
the organization named by the global `--org ` for a single invocation — which is refused with
`403` if you are not a member of it. Every command accepts the global
`-o, --output ` flag.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: What every command on this page writes
records.text:
**The result is on stdout and everything else is on stderr.** A table, a card or a JSON document is
the result. A progress line, a queued-job notice, a warning and an error are not, so
`alethia project list --output json` can be piped into a parser in every case.

**A command that changes something returns one result.** With `--output json` it has the same keys
on every command:

{
 "id": "4f3c2b1a-9d6e-4a3b-8c17-5e2f1a9b7c04",
 "kind": "project",
 "action": "queued",
 "job": { "id": "0b7e6c55-2f0a-4d0e-9a3b-6c1d2e3f4a5b", "type": "DEPLOY" },
 "dry_run": false,
 "object": {}
}

`action` is `created`, `updated`, `deleted`, `queued` or `unchanged`. `job` is `null` when the
command queued nothing. `object` is the record, or what the command did in detail.

**`--dry-run` sends nothing.** `create`, `preview`, `deploy`, `destroy`, `env add`,
`component add` and `component remove` take it. The command resolves and checks every input,
prints the same result with `"dry_run": true` and the request under `object.request`, and makes
no change. It never asks for a confirmation, because there is nothing to confirm.

**A refusal exits with the code of its kind.** stdout stays empty. stderr carrie

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Two rules that hold for every command on this page
records.text:
**Nothing has to be copied out of another command's output.** Every reference takes the name you
already know: `--project` takes a project's name *or* its id, `--cloud-account` takes a cloud
account's label *or* its id, and `--env` takes an environment's id, name or stage, where an exact
name wins over a stage ([precedence](#components-belong-to-an-environment)). Omit one on a terminal
and you are asked, from a picker of what actually exists.

**Every question has a flag.** The interactive paths below exist so you do not have to assemble
anything by hand — they never let you say something a flag cannot. After a run that asked you
questions, the CLI prints the exact command that reproduces it, so what you answered once can be
committed to a repository:

Same result, without the questions:
 alethia project create boutique --region eu-west-1 --cloud-account prod-account

The one thing a flag cannot say is a list of environments, so a run that declared an environment
matrix through the form prints back the `alethia.yaml` its answers add up to — the file
[`alethia apply`](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply) reads. So `--no-input` always works, and so does a
pipe.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project list
records.text:
List all projects in the active organization.

alethia project list
alethia project list --output json

An organization with no projects prints nothing on stdout. A note on stderr names the two commands
that make one: `alethia up` and `alethia project create`.

On a terminal this is the shared navigable table (sort, filter, quit); piped or with
`--output json csv` it is a plain projection.

 Column Description 
 ------ ---------- 
 Project Project name 
 Env The default environment's stage 
 Status Provisioning status 
 Provider Cloud provider 
 Region Cloud region 
 Cost Estimated monthly cost 
 Updated Last change 

**Status**, **Provider**, **Region** and **Cost** are rendered for a person: the status carries a
glyph and is folded to lower case, the provider is upper-cased, an unset provider or region is `—`,
and a project the wire sent no status for reads as `draft` — an inference that tells a reader the
project has not been applied yet, rather than leaving a blank that looks like a broken table.

Under `-o csv` a script gets the values instead: each is the wire value, and each is an **empty
cell when the wire sent nothing** — including the status, because handing a script a st

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project get
records.text:
Print a project's full configuration.

alethia project get boutique
alethia project get --project boutique --output json
alethia project get boutique --open
alethia project get # asks which project

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[name]` No Project name (positional). Omit it on a terminal to pick from a list. 
 `--project` No The same project name, as a flag. Pass the argument or the flag, not both. 
 `--open` No Also open the project in the web console. (Long-only — `-o` is the global `--output` flag.) 

 
 `get` looks a project up by **name**, so the picker returns a name and refuses one that two
 projects share — that lookup answers a duplicate with whichever project is older, and quietly
 printing another project's region, cluster endpoint and apps repo is worse than an error. Every
 other command takes `--project`, which resolves a name **or** an id.
 

Shows the full project configuration including:
- Project name, provider, region, environment
- Status and estimated monthly cost
- Component summary (network, cluster, databases, caches, etc.)
- Cloud identity reference

The command prints the project and asks nothing afterwards. `--

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project create
records.text:
Create a new project in the active organization.

alethia project create # asks for everything, prints the file back

or say it all at once:

alethia project create boutique --region eu-west-1 --cloud-account prod-account

or from the manifest in the current directory, which also declares the environment matrix:

alethia project create --file alethia.yaml

The file in the current directory is read even when `--file` is not passed, and the command prints
the line naming it. A script that must not be steered by whatever `alethia.yaml` happens to be in
the tree passes `--no-manifest`.

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[name]` Yes* Project name (positional). *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--region` Yes* Cloud region to provision into. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--cloud-account` No Cloud account to link, by its **label** or its id. Asked for on a terminal when omitted; a project may be created with none. 
 `--stage` No Initial environment stage: `development` (default), `staging`, `production` 
 `--iac-version` No OpenTofu version to pin (defaults server-side) 
 `--placement-mode` No Placement of the default environment

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Node shape
records.text:
Without `--instance-type` or `--node-size`, the project's cluster gets the catalog's default machine
type for its cloud: `t3.large` on AWS, `e2-standard-2` on Google Cloud, `Standard_D2s_v5` on Azure
and `cpx22` on Hetzner. Pass one of the two flags to choose the node yourself:

alethia project create boutique --region eu-west-1 --cloud-account prod-account --instance-type t3.xlarge
alethia project create boutique --region eu-west-1 --cloud-account prod-account --node-size 4x16

The shape applies to every `dedicated` environment, because only a dedicated environment provisions
a cluster. A `namespace` or `vcluster` environment runs on the cluster of the environment it is
placed on. The two flags are mutually exclusive, and a create where no environment is `dedicated`
refuses them. To change the shape later, set the cluster's `instance_types` with
`alethia project component add --kind cluster`, which updates the existing cluster.

The created project prints as a card. With `--output json` it is one result whose `id` is the
project's id and whose `object` is the project. When anything was asked for, the
`alethia project create` line that would produce the same project without the que

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Clouds
records.text:
A project's cloud is the cloud of the account that you link with `--cloud-account`. This release
offers AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Hetzner. The control plane refuses a project on any other cloud
with one sentence, for example `DigitalOcean is not available in this release.` The command prints
that sentence and exits `8`. Link an account on an offered cloud and run the command again.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The environment matrix
records.text:
Every environment and **how each is placed onto a Fabric** is declared in `alethia.yaml`, under
`environments:`. The first entry is the default environment and owns the Fabric it provisions, so
it defaults to `dedicated`; later entries default to `namespace` and share that Fabric.

project: shop
cloud:
 account: prod-account
 region: eu-west-1
environments:
 - name: prod
 stage: production
 - name: dev
 stage: development
 namespace: boutique-dev
 - name: staging
 stage: staging
 placement: vcluster

That is **one** cluster hosting three environments. With no manifest and no terminal you get the
default Production + Preview pair instead; on a terminal you are asked for each environment in
turn — name, stage, placement, namespace — and then shown the file your answers add up to, to
save as `alethia.yaml`.

A stage or a placement outside the allowed set is refused locally, naming the whole set, rather
than coming back as a `400`. The file's full reference, components included, is on
[Plan & Apply](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply#alethiayaml).

 
 Placement is the flag with a bill attached. Each `dedicated` environment is a separate cluster with
 its own OpenTofu state; `namespace` and

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project preview · deploy · destroy
records.text:
Queue a `PLAN`, `DEPLOY` or `DESTROY` job for one environment of a project.

- `preview` works out what a deploy would change, with a cost estimate. It changes nothing in your
 cloud account.
- `deploy` creates or updates the environment's cloud resources. A deploy applies a reviewed plan:
 without `--plan-job-id` or `--latest-plan` it previews the environment first, waits for that
 plan, prints what it would change, asks, and then deploys exactly that plan. See
 [Deploying without a plan reference](#deploying-without-a-plan-reference).
- `destroy` tears them down. This cannot be undone.

alethia project preview --project boutique --env dev-1 --runner eu-box --wait
alethia project deploy --project boutique --env dev-1 --latest-plan --wait
alethia project destroy --project boutique --env dev-1

Omit `--project` on a terminal and you are asked which project; omit the runner and you are
asked which one (or "Any available"). With no terminal, a job with no runner named goes to any
available runner.

 Flag preview deploy destroy Description 
 ------ --------- -------- --------- ------------- 
 `--project` ✓ ✓ ✓ Project by **name** or id. Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--projec

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The result and the job
records.text:
Each command prints the job it queued. With `--output json` the result's `job` is the job, and
`object.jobs` lists every job with its `status`:

alethia project deploy --project boutique --env dev-1 --yes --output json

Without `--wait` the command returns when the job is queued. With `--wait` it returns when the job
finishes, and the exit code is the verdict: `0` for a job that succeeded, `13` for one that failed
or was cancelled, and `12` when `--timeout` passed first. A job that succeeded can still record
warnings, for example an add-on that did not sync. With `--wait` they are printed on stderr, and
each entry in `object.jobs` carries them as a `warnings` array. The array is empty when there are
none, or when the command did not wait. An error names the job, so
`alethia jobs logs` can pick it up.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Deploying without a plan reference
records.text:
A deploy always applies a reviewed plan, and the control plane refuses a `DEPLOY` that names
none. So `alethia project deploy` with neither `--plan-job-id` nor `--latest-plan` makes the plan
itself:

1. It queues a `PLAN` job for the same project, environment and runner.
2. It waits for that job to finish, as `--wait` does.
3. It prints the plan on stderr: the job, its verify verdict, its cost estimate, and how many
 resources it would create, update, replace and delete.
4. It asks before it deploys. `--yes` skips the question; with `--no-input` and no `--yes` the
 command exits `9` before it queues the preview.
5. It queues the `DEPLOY` of exactly that plan.

A preview that fails or is cancelled stops the command: it exits `13`, names the `PLAN` job, and
deploys nothing. A preview still running when `--timeout` passes exits `12`. Read why with
`alethia jobs logs `.

alethia project deploy --project boutique --env dev-1 --yes --wait

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Confirming a deploy or a destroy
records.text:
`deploy` asks before it queues the `DEPLOY`. The question names the project, the environment and the
plan. `destroy` asks you to **type the project's name**, because a destroy cannot be undone and a
name has to be read before it is typed. Anything else that you type destroys nothing.

With `--no-input`, in a pipe, or when an agent runs the command, nothing can ask. Both commands
then require `--yes`, and without it they exit `9` and queue nothing.

Destroying a `dedicated` environment while `namespace` or `vcluster` environments are still placed
on its cluster is refused, naming them. Destroy them first, or pass `--cascade` — see
[`alethia project destroy`](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply#alethia-project-destroy). To read what a
cascade takes with it without destroying anything, add `--dry-run`:

alethia project destroy --project boutique --env prod --cascade --dry-run

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: A deploy or a destroy that needs a person's approval
records.text:
A deploy or a destroy started from the CLI, with a device sign-in or a service token, needs a
person's approval of its reviewed plan. A deploy is approved against the plan it applies. A destroy
is approved against the plan the environment's current state was deployed from.

When the control plane answers that the job needs an approval, the command asks for one and prints
the console page where a person approves it, with the first eight characters of the plan's digest:

⚠ This deploy needs a person's approval. Approve it at https://console.example.com/approvals/6b21d8f4-0c5e-4a93-9f27-3d81b6e5c704 — the page must show plan 2b7e91c0-5d1a-4f3e-8c2b-7a9d0e1f2a3b with a digest starting a1b2c3d4.

The page shows the same eight characters. Check that they match before you approve. The command
waits for the decision, bounded by `--timeout`, and then queues the job with the approval. Nothing
is queued before that.

- A rejected approval exits `5`. An expired or superseded one exits `7`; run the command again to
 ask for a new approval.
- `--no-wait`, or agent mode, prints the page and exits `9` without waiting. Once the approval is
 approved, run the same `deploy` with `--plan-job-id` and t

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The old names: project plan and project apply
records.text:
`alethia project preview` was `alethia project plan`, and `alethia project deploy` was
`alethia project apply`. The names changed because `alethia plan` and `alethia apply` are different
commands: they read an `alethia.yaml` file.

The old names still run. They are not listed in `--help`, and each prints one line on stderr that
names the new command. `project apply` queues without a confirmation, as it always did, so a script
that calls it keeps working. Move a script to `project deploy --yes`.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Deploying the plan you just reviewed
records.text:
`--latest-plan` resolves the project's own most recent `PLAN` job, so a review-then-deploy pass
never moves a uuid between two commands:

alethia project preview --project boutique --env prod --wait
alethia project deploy --project boutique --env prod --latest-plan --wait

It prints which job it chose before it queues anything. Three things it deliberately does **not**
do:

- It is **opt-in**. Without it (or `--plan-job-id`) the deploy previews the environment first and
 applies that plan ([Deploying without a plan reference](#deploying-without-a-plan-reference)).
 The control plane refuses a deploy whose plan did not succeed, whose configuration moved since
 the plan was taken, or that something else ran on the environment after; the Runner applies the
 plan only when its digest matches the one that was reviewed.
- It resolves `PLAN` jobs **only**. The project's most recent job is as likely to be the `DEPLOY`
 that followed the plan.
- It takes the most recent `PLAN` **whatever its status**, and refuses when that is not `SUCCESS`,
 naming the job and its status. Skipping past a plan that is still running would apply an older
 one you never asked for.

When there is no `PLAN` job t

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project design apply
records.text:
The declarative counterpart to `project component add`. The imperative commands are what you narrate
one step at a time; a design document is what a repository commits and CI replays. Both write the same
tables.

bash

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The document, as it is now
records.text: alethia config export -p shop --out shop.json

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: See what would change — writes NOTHING
records.text: alethia project design apply -p shop -e dev -f shop.json --dry-run

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Apply it
records.text: alethia project design apply -p shop -e dev -f shop.json

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Or send it to the staged-changes tray for review instead
records.text: alethia project design apply -p shop -e dev -f shop.json --stage

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: From a pipe
records.text:
cat shop.json alethia project design apply -p shop -f -

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `-f`, `--file` Yes* Design document path, or `-` for stdin. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `-p`, `--project` Yes* Project name or id. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `-e`, `--env` No Environment id, name or stage; an exact name wins over a stage. Omit for the project's default. 
 `--dry-run` No Print the changes that would be made and write nothing. 
 `--stage` No Stage the change for review instead of applying it. 
 `-y`, `--yes` No Confirm an apply whose plan **removes** a component. Required with `--no-input` only in that case. 

Both `--dry-run` and a real apply print one row per component with the action taken:

3 change(s) would be made in dev:
 UPDATE databases orders
 CREATE caches sessions
 DELETE storage_buckets receipts

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The gate is on the plan, not on the command
records.text:
An apply can **delete**: a kind the document omits is a kind the environment loses. So the
confirmation appears exactly where that happens, and nowhere else.

- A plan that only **adds or updates** applies unprompted, including under `--no-input`. A design
 document is what a repository commits and CI replays, and a pipeline that adds a cache does not
 need a human in it.
- A plan that **removes** a component prints what would go, then confirms. Under `--no-input` it
 requires `-y`, `--yes`.

To decide which it is, a real apply asks the server for its own `--dry-run` first, so the prompt
names the components rather than asking in the abstract:

This apply would DELETE 1 component(s) in dev:
 DELETE storage_buckets receipts

If that check cannot be read at all, the apply is **refused** rather than run blind — `--yes`
applies without it.

An apply whose plan removes a component, with no `--yes` and nothing to ask, exits `9` and writes
nothing.

 
 `--yes` on a `design apply` is not a blanket "this command is destructive" switch. It opts *that
 invocation* into removing components. Leaving it on a pipeline permanently means every later
 replay may remove components too; if a replay is

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project env
records.text:
A project owns N independently-provisionable environments. The project is named with `--project`
(its name **or** id); omit it on a terminal and you are asked.

bash

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: List a project's environments
records.text: alethia project env list --project boutique

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Add one, answering the same four questions the --env tuple asks
records.text: alethia project env add --project boutique

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Or say it outright
records.text: alethia project env add staging --project boutique --stage staging

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: As a vcluster on a named Fabric, with its own destination namespace
records.text:
alethia project env add staging --project shop --stage staging \
 --placement-mode vcluster --fabric shared --namespace boutique-staging

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: One that provisions its OWN cluster
records.text:
alethia project env add prod --project shop --stage production --placement-mode dedicated

 Command Flags Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `env list` `--project` List the project's environments (default first) 
 `env add [name]` `--project` `--stage` `--region` `--placement-mode` `--fabric` `--namespace` `--lifecycle` Add an environment (name is slugified; region inherits the project's when omitted) 

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `--project` Yes* Project name or id. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--stage` No `development` (default), `staging`, `production` 
 `--placement-mode` No `namespace` (default), `vcluster`, `dedicated` 
 `--namespace` No ArgoCD destination namespace for a shared placement (default: derived from the name) 
 `--fabric` No Fabric to place onto, by name (default: the one the project's default environment is on) 
 `--region` No Region (inherits the project's when omitted) 
 `--lifecycle` No `persistent` (default) or `ephemeral` 
 `--dry-run` No `env add` only: check the input and print the request. Nothing is added. 

An **added** environment defaults to `namespace` placement on the Fabric the project's

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project component
records.text:
One uniform group authors **all** of a project's component resources. The project is named with
`--project`, and the environment with `--env`.

**Which kinds exist is published by the server, and `component kinds` is how you read it.** This
page used to list them, and that list drifted: it named thirteen while the server accepted fourteen.
A kind has one of two cardinalities — **singleton** (one per project *per environment*, name-less) or
**multi** (named, many per environment) — and `kinds` prints each with its own, so the answer to
"does this one need a `--name`" comes from the same place as the list itself.

bash

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: List the supported kinds
records.text: alethia project component kinds

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: List a project's components (optionally filter by --kind and/or --env)
records.text: alethia project component list --project boutique --kind databases

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: with the kind's own fields to pick from
records.text: alethia project component add --project boutique

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Or say it outright. Multi kind → --name required
records.text:
alethia project component add --project boutique --kind databases --name main \
 --set engine=postgres --set port=5432 --set iam_auth=true

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Configure the cluster singleton (--name ignored; upserts)
records.text:
alethia project component add --project boutique --kind cluster \
 --set 'cluster_version="1.35"' --set node_min_size=2 --set 'instance_types=["t3.medium"]'

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Remove components (destructive → confirms)
records.text:
alethia project component remove --project boutique --kind databases --name main
alethia project component remove --project boutique --kind network

 Command Flags Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `component kinds` — List the component kinds the server publishes, with each one's cardinality. Needs a session — the answer is the server's, not a built-in list 
 `component list` `--project` `--kind` `--env` List components (all kinds, or one) 
 `component add` `--project` `--kind` `--name` `--env` `--set` Create a component 
 `component remove` `--project` `--kind` `--name` `--env` `-y`, `--yes` Delete a component (confirms) 

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `--project` Yes* Project name or id. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--kind` Yes* Component kind. Optional on `list`, where it filters. *Asked for on a terminal for `add` and `remove`. A kind this CLI's cached list does not hold is still authorable — the picker offers it verbatim and the server decides. 
 `--name` Yes for multi kinds Component name. Ignored by singleton kinds, which upsert. *Asked for on a terminal by `add` and `remove`, as a picker over the components that ex

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Components belong to an environment
records.text:
A component is scoped to one **environment**, not to the project as a whole — so two environments
can hold the same kind with different configuration. `--env` takes an environment id, name or stage.
When one value matches more than one environment, the id wins, then an exact name, then a stage. Among
stage matches, the default environment wins. So `--env staging` selects the environment named
`staging`, even when the default environment is at stage `staging`:

bash

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: dev and staging deploy DIFFERENT overlays of the same repo
records.text:
alethia project component add --project shop --env dev --kind repositories \
 --set apps_destination_repo=https://github.com/acme/shop --set apps_path=overlays/dev

alethia project component add --project shop --env staging --kind repositories \
 --set apps_destination_repo=https://github.com/acme/shop --set apps_path=overlays/staging

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Inspect one tier at a time
records.text:
alethia project component list --project shop --env staging

What `--env` defaults to differs by verb, deliberately:

- **`add` and `remove`** default to the project's **default environment**, so a single-environment
 script needs no `--env` at all.
- **`list`** defaults to **every** environment. Narrowing a read silently would hide rows you did
 not ask to hide.

 
 `remove` deletes from **one** environment — the one you named, or the default. It never touches a
 sibling environment's copy. The confirmation names both the component and the tier
 (`Deletes the databases main configuration in staging`), and so does the success line
 (`Removed databases main in staging`).

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The --set field setter
records.text:
`--set key=value` is repeatable and generic. Each value is parsed as JSON when it can be, else taken
literally — so numbers, booleans, and arrays are typed correctly:

--set port=5432 # number
--set iam_auth=true # boolean
--set instance_types='["t3.medium"]' # array
--set 'node_size={"vcpu":4,"memory_gb":16}' # object
--set engine=postgres # string
--set 'cluster_version="1.31"' # string that would otherwise parse as a number

Quote a value that looks like a number but is a string field — `cluster_version=1.31` coerces to the
number `1.31`, which the server refuses.

A cluster is sized one of two ways. `node_size` is a size that works on any cloud: the deploy picks
the closest machine type in the catalog for the cluster's cloud. `instance_types` pins a machine type.
Setting one clears the other in the same write, and a single `add` that sets both fails.

`capacity_type` chooses how the nodes are bought: `on_demand` (the default) or `spot`. Spot nodes cost
less, but the cloud can take a node back at short notice. Each cloud applies `spot` to its own node
pool setting:

 Cloud What `spot` changes 
 --- --- 
 AWS The managed node group runs on Spot. 
 GCP The node pool runs on Spot V

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Setting template knobs
records.text:
A component's `provider_config` field sets the template's own variables: the same knobs as the
**Advanced** section of the component's card on the canvas. Examples are the GKE private endpoint,
the AKS Spot pool and the EKS volume type. Pass it as a JSON object with `--set`:

alethia project component add --project boutique --kind cluster \
 --set 'provider_config={"gke_enable_private_endpoint":true,"gke_disk_type":"pd-ssd"}'

In `alethia.yaml`, write it as a nested mapping under the component:

environments:
 - name: prod
 components:
 cluster:
 node_min_size: 2
 provider_config:
 gke_enable_private_endpoint: true
 gke_disk_type: pd-ssd
 databases:
 - name: orders
 engine: postgres
 provider_config:
 cloud_sql_high_availability: true

**Which keys you can set depends on the project's cloud and the component.** The server checks each
key against the template for that cloud. It refuses a key it does not accept, and the error lists
every key that you can set. To find the keys, send one you know is wrong:

provider_config key(s) not settable for cluster on gcp: gke_private_endpoint (not a variable of this template).
Settable keys for cluster on gcp: external_dns_service_account_email,

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.text: Promotion Commands. Inspect environment promotions — status, approval tally, and approval slots.

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.text:
The `promotion` group (aliases `promotions`, `promo`) reads a project's **environment promotions** —
moving a source environment's proven design into a target environment, gated by that environment's
[protection rules](/reference/cli/protection).

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These subcommands call
`/cli/projects/ /promotions[/…]` with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on
the **active organization**, which you change with `alethia org switch`. Approving, rejecting, or
cancelling a promotion stays in the console.

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.heading: alethia promotion list
records.text:
List a project's promotions, newest first.

alethia promotion list
alethia promotion list --project my-project
alethia promotion list -p my-project -e production
alethia promotion list -p my-project -o json

{/* fieldspec: alethia promotion list */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Project Whose promotions to list `--project` 
 Target environment Show only promotions INTO this environment, by id, name or stage (an exact name wins over a stage) `--env` 

Columns: **ID**, **Source**, **Target**, **Status**, **Created**. Backing call:
`GET /cli/projects/ /promotions`.

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.heading: alethia promotion get
records.text:
Show one promotion's status, approval tally, and approval slots.

alethia promotion get
alethia promotion get --project my-project
alethia promotion get 8f3c1a2b -p my-project

A promotion has no name, so there is nothing to type but its id — which is why **you do not have
to**. Run `promotion get` with no argument at a terminal and you are shown the project's
promotions and pick one; `--env` narrows that list exactly as it narrows `promotion list`. Given an
argument, an unambiguous **id prefix** is enough: `8f3c1a2b` resolves as readily as the full UUID.

{/* fieldspec: alethia promotion get */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Project Which project the promotion belongs to `--project` 
 Promotion The promotion to open, by id or id prefix; omit it to choose from the list `[promotion]` 

Renders a summary card (source → target, status, **approvals** `N/M`, initiator, created, any
error) followed by the approval slots (status, approver, required role, decided-at). The per-gate
evaluation detail and full config diff stay in the console. Add `-o json` for the full object.

The card is written for a person, and `-o csv` gives a script the values: the stat

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.heading: Output and exit codes
records.text:
The result is the only thing the command writes on stdout, and it writes nothing there when it
fails. A failure exits with the code of its kind, and stderr says what happened and what to run
next:

 Exit Meaning on this page 
 ------ ---------------------- 
 `4` You are not signed in, or the session has expired 
 `5` You are not permitted to read this project 
 `6` The project or environment that you named does not exist 
 `9` `--project` was left out and nothing can ask for it (`--no-input`, a pipe, or `-o json`) 

The codes mean the same on every command of the CLI.

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.heading: See also
records.text:

- [Staged Commands](/reference/cli/staged) — an environment's pending canvas changes.
- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Protection Commands
records.text: Protection Commands. Inspect a project's promotion protection rules — the gates that guard deploys into each environment.

records.title: Protection Commands
records.text:
The `protection` group (alias `protect`) lists the **promotion protection rules** configured per
environment: the gates that must pass before a promotion deploys into that environment.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. `protection list` calls
`/cli/projects/ /protection` with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operates on the
**active organization**, which you change with `alethia org switch`. Pass `--org ` to scope a single invocation to a different
organization — it is refused with `403` if you are not a member of it.

records.title: Protection Commands
records.heading: alethia protection list
records.text:
List a project's per-environment protection rules.

alethia protection list
alethia protection list --project my-project
alethia protection list -p my-project -o json

Name the project with `--project`; omit it at a terminal and you are asked which project to read,
from the ones you have.

{/* fieldspec: alethia protection list */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Project Whose environments' promotion gates to read `--project` 

Columns: **Environment**, **Predecessor** (predecessor stage must be deployed + in-sync),
**Verify** (Elench verify must pass), **Approval** (a human must approve), **Approvers** (minimum
approver count), **Soak (min)** (minutes since the predecessor deploy), **Cost Δ** (a plan cost
delta above this USD/mo flips the promotion to pending-approval). A configured gate renders as a
check; an unset gate or limit renders as `—`. Only environments with rules configured appear.

Environment Predecessor Verify Approval Approvers Soak (min) Cost Δ
production ✓ ✓ ✓ 2 30 $100.00
staging — ✓ — — — —

Every one of those renderings is for a person reading a column. Under `-o csv` a script gets the
values instead: a gate is `true` or `false`

records.title: Protection Commands
records.heading: Output and exit codes
records.text:
The result is the only thing the command writes on stdout, and it writes nothing there when it
fails. A failure exits with the code of its kind, and stderr says what happened and what to run
next:

 Exit Meaning on this page 
 ------ ---------------------- 
 `4` You are not signed in, or the session has expired 
 `5` You are not permitted to read this project 
 `6` The project or environment that you named does not exist 
 `9` `--project` was left out and nothing can ask for it (`--no-input`, a pipe, or `-o json`) 

The codes mean the same on every command of the CLI.
