records.title: Standards & Protocols
records.heading: How to read these pages
records.text:
Each page has the same three parts:

1. **What the standard is** — one or two paragraphs, no marketing.
2. **How Alethia implements it** — the real files, routes, functions, env vars, and tables.
3. **The authoritative spec** — the IETF RFC, OASIS document, or `openid.net` reference.

For the security model in prose, see [concepts/security](/concepts/security); for the authorization
layer (roles, grants, the PDP), see [access control](/concepts/access-control).

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.text: JWT, JWS & JOSE. Where Alethia uses JSON Web Tokens and signatures — Better Auth sessions, HS256 CLI tokens, RS256 workload assertions, and the ed25519-signed Elench verify evidence receipts.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**JOSE** (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) is the family of IETF standards for representing keys,
signatures, and encryption over JSON. The two that matter here:

- **JWS** ([RFC 7515](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515)) — a JSON Web Signature: a payload plus
 a detached or compact signature, with a header naming the algorithm (`HS256`, `RS256`, `EdDSA`, …).
- **JWT** ([RFC 7519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519)) — a JSON Web Token: a set of claims
 (`sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, …) carried as a JWS. A signed JWT is verifiable and tamper-evident:
 anyone with the key (symmetric) or public key (asymmetric) can confirm the claims were not altered.

Alethia uses signed tokens in several distinct places, each with the algorithm that fits its trust
boundary. It never encrypts tokens (no JWE) — every token here is *signed*, not secret-bearing.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
Surface Format Alg Key Lifetime Code 
 --- --- --- --- --- --- 
 Console web session Better Auth session cookie (HTTP-only), backed by the `session` table — signed with `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` rolling `lib/auth/index.ts` 
 CLI access token JWT `HS256` `CLI_JWT_SECRET` 1 hour `api/auth/cli/exchange` 
 CLI refresh token JWT `HS256` `CLI_JWT_SECRET` 90 days `api/auth/cli/exchange` 
 Cloud workload assertion JWT `RS256` `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` ≤ 600s `lib/oidc/issuer.ts` 
 MCP access token OAuth 2.1 token (OIDC provider) — Better Auth `mcp()` plugin short `lib/auth/index.ts` 
 Verify evidence receipt detached ed25519 signature over canonical JSON `EdDSA` / ed25519 `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY` per-apply `packages/core/verify` 

 
 The **web session is not a JWT** in this build — there is no `jwt()` plugin. It is a Better Auth
 signed, HTTP-only session cookie referencing a `session` row (validated by Next.js middleware). The
 genuine JWT/JWS surfaces are the CLI tokens, the workload assertions, and the MCP tokens. The verify
 receipt is a JOSE-adjacent EdDSA signature, described below.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: CLI tokens (HS256)
records.text:
`apps/console/app/api/auth/cli/exchange/route.ts` mints access/refresh JWTs with the `jose` library
(`new jose.SignJWT(...).setProtectedHeader({ alg: "HS256" })`). Claims: `sub` = profile id, `email`,
`type` ∈ {`access`, `refresh`}, `iss`/`aud` set to placeholder `urn:example:*` values, and `exp` of
1h / 90d respectively. `/api/auth/cli/refresh` verifies the refresh token
(`jose.jwtVerify`, matching `iss`/`aud`), rejects any token whose `type !== "refresh"`, and issues a
new 1-hour access token. See [device code](/reference/standards/device-code) for the full flow.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: Workload assertions (RS256)
records.text:
The [workload-identity](/reference/standards/workload-identity) issuer signs its federation assertions RS256 —
the widest-compatible alg for AWS/GCP/Azure token exchange — and publishes the public key at
`/api/oidc/jwks` so clouds verify independently. Key rotation is supported by publishing a second
(previous) key while the primary rolls over.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: Elench verify receipts (ed25519)
records.text:
The [Elench](/concepts/elench) verify gate emits a per-apply **evidence receipt** — a precise, honest record of
what was checked, against which plan, under which control set (`packages/core/verify/receipt.go`). The
receipt binds to the exact plan via `plan_sha256` and pins `tofu_version` / `provider_versions` /
`catalog_version`. When `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY` is set (a base64 64-byte ed25519 private key,
`packages/core/verify/signing.go`), `Sign()` produces a `SignedReceipt`: a detached **ed25519**
([RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032)) signature over the receipt's canonical JSON bytes,
plus `algorithm: "ed25519"` and a short `key_id` (`KeyID` = first 8 bytes of SHA-256 of the public
key). `Verify()` recomputes the canonical bytes and checks the signature — any tampering fails.

 
 **Root-of-trust honesty (from the code's own comments).** Signing is *additive evidence*, not a
 precondition — an unset key attaches an **unsigned** receipt rather than blocking the apply. And a
 signature from Alethia's runner only proves "Alethia asserted this". For a receipt to mean something
 to a customer's auditor, sign with a customer-controlled key and/or anchor the signature

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [RFC 7519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519) — JSON Web Token (JWT).
- [RFC 7515](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515) — JSON Web Signature (JWS).
- [RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032) — EdDSA (Ed25519).

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.text: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE. Console social sign-in over OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) with PKCE (RFC 7636), implemented by Better Auth — GitHub/Google natively, GitLab/Bitbucket via the generic OAuth plugin.

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**OAuth 2.0** ([RFC 6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749)) is the authorization framework
that lets a user grant an application access to a resource without sharing a password. The web flow
Alethia uses is the **authorization-code grant**: the app redirects the user to the provider's
authorization endpoint, the provider redirects back with a short-lived `code`, and the app exchanges
that code at the token endpoint for an access token.

**PKCE** ([RFC 7636](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636), "Proof Key for Code Exchange") hardens
that exchange against code-interception. The client generates a random `code_verifier`, sends its
SHA-256 hash (`code_challenge`) on the authorization request, and presents the raw verifier at token
exchange — so a stolen `code` is useless without the verifier.

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
The [Console](/reference/glossary) delegates web sign-in to **Better Auth** (in-process, Drizzle
adapter). The auth instance is built in `apps/console/lib/auth/index.ts`; the single catch-all route
`apps/console/app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts` serves every Better Auth endpoint (authorization start,
callback, token exchange). Better Auth drives the authorization-code + PKCE handshake — the console
never hand-rolls the flow.

Four social providers are registered, in two ways:

 Provider Registration Scopes requested 
 --- --- --- 
 GitHub native `socialProviders.github` `repo` (+ Better Auth's `read:user`/`user:email` defaults) 
 Google native `socialProviders.google` provider defaults 
 GitLab `genericOAuth` plugin (self-hosted base URL) `read_api read_user read_repository read_registry openid profile email` 
 Bitbucket `genericOAuth` plugin `account repository` 

Native GitHub/Google use Better Auth's built-in provider configs. GitLab and Bitbucket go through the
`genericOAuth` plugin (`import { genericOAuth } from "better-auth/plugins"`), configured with explicit
`authorizationUrl` / `tokenUrl` / `userInfoUrl` in `genericOAuthConfigs`. Each provider is registered
**only when its c

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: Where the token lands
records.text:
On callback, Better Auth exchanges the code (with PKCE) and creates a session — an HTTP-only cookie
backed by the `session` table. Next.js middleware validates it on every request; the
[PDP](/concepts/access-control/architecture) then resolves the active org and sets `app.current_org` for the
coarse Postgres [RLS](/concepts/security) tenant guard. See
[JWT / JWS](/reference/standards/jose) for the token formats and [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc) for enterprise SSO.

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: The MCP authorization server
records.text:
Alethia also *acts as* an OAuth 2.1 authorization server for its Model Context Protocol endpoint. The
`mcp()` plugin (also in `lib/auth/index.ts`) lets remote MCP clients register dynamically and obtain
an access token that `/api/mcp` resolves into a PDP-scoped actor — no new authority beyond the token
owner's normal scope.

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [oauth.net/2](https://oauth.net/2/) — the OAuth 2.0 landing page and flow overview.
- [RFC 6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) — The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework.
- [RFC 7636](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636) — Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE).

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.text: OpenID Connect. Enterprise SSO with Alethia as the OIDC Service Provider — Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, AWS IAM Identity Center and any OIDC IdP, via @better-auth/sso.

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**OpenID Connect (OIDC)** is a thin identity layer on top of [OAuth 2.0](/reference/standards/oauth2). Where
OAuth 2.0 answers *"is this app allowed to act?"*, OIDC answers *"who is this user?"* — the IdP
returns a signed **ID token** (a JWT) with verified identity claims (`sub`, `email`, group/role
claims), and the Relying Party verifies it against the IdP's published JWKS. It is the protocol behind
"sign in with your company account".

Alethia plays two OIDC roles, kept strictly separate:

- **Relying Party / Service Provider** for enterprise SSO — it *consumes* a customer's IdP so members
 sign in with their corporate identity (this page).
- **Identity Provider** for keyless cloud federation — it *is* an OIDC issuer that clouds trust. That
 is a different subsystem; see [workload identity](/reference/standards/workload-identity).

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
Enterprise SSO is an [Enterprise](/editions)-gated capability contributed by the `@alethia/ee` module
(`ee/src/index.ts`) through the `getAuthPlugins()` seam in `apps/console/lib/auth/plugins.ts`. It wraps
the **`@better-auth/sso`** plugin. Alethia is always the **Service Provider** — it never runs an IdP
of its own for user login (no Hydra, no Alethia-as-IdP).

Each [organization](/reference/glossary) registers its own provider (rows in the `ssoProvider` table,
scoped by `organizationId`), so different orgs can federate different directories. Supported IdPs
include Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, AWS IAM Identity Center, OneLogin, and Ping — any
standards-compliant OIDC provider. The server actions in `apps/console/app/server/actions/sso.ts`
manage provider CRUD and report each row's protocol (`oidc` `saml` `unknown`) from which config
block is present.

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Domain verification and JIT provisioning
records.text: Two safeguards gate first sign-in:

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Domain proof
records.text:
Registration is bound to domain ownership. `@better-auth/sso` is configured with
`domainVerification: { enabled: true, tokenPrefix: "alethia-sso" }` — the customer publishes a DNS
`TXT` record at `_alethia-sso- `. Until the domain is verified, sign-in through that
provider is rejected and no email-domain account-linking is trusted.

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Entitlement gate
records.text:
A custom `alethia-sso-entitlement-guard` middleware blocks `POST /sso/register` unless the target org
holds the `sso` entitlement — so a non-Enterprise admin cannot register a provider by calling the API
directly. The UI shows the upsell instead.

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Just-in-time member provisioning
records.text:
On first successful SSO sign-in, the user is provisioned into their org with
`organizationProvisioning.defaultRole: "member"` (least-privileged). The
[PDP](/concepts/access-control/architecture) then authorizes them exactly like any other
[member](/guides/access/members-and-invitations) — mapping better-auth's `member` to Alethia's
viewer-scoped access.

 

 
 **Honest current state.** SSO users are always provisioned as least-privileged members — automatic
 **IdP group-claim → Alethia role** mapping (owner/admin/operator/viewer) is a documented follow-up,
 not yet wired. Directory-driven provisioning/deprovisioning (SCIM) is **not implemented**; see
 [SAML & SCIM](/reference/standards/scim-saml).
 

For the operator-facing setup (fields per protocol, the register flow), see
[access control → SSO](/guides/access/sso).

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [openid.net — How OpenID Connect works](https://openid.net/developers/how-connect-works/).
- [OpenID Connect Core 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html) — the specification.

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.text: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0. Enterprise directory federation — SAML 2.0 SSO is implemented (Enterprise, Service Provider) with documented hardening follow-ups; SCIM 2.0 provisioning is NOT implemented (just-in-time provisioning only).

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.text:
Two enterprise directory standards, at two different maturities. Read the status on each honestly —
one is live, one is roadmap.

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**SAML 2.0** (Security Assertion Markup Language, OASIS) is the long-standing XML protocol for
enterprise SSO. The Identity Provider (IdP) issues a digitally-signed XML **assertion** about the
user; the Service Provider (SP) validates the signature against the IdP's X.509 certificate and logs
the user in. It predates OIDC and is still the default in many enterprise directories.

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
Alethia is the **Service Provider** — same posture as [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc). SAML providers are
registered per [organization](/reference/glossary) via the `@better-auth/sso` plugin (`ee/src/index.ts`,
[Enterprise](/editions)-gated). SAML config is stored in the `ssoProvider.samlConfig` column; the
server actions in `apps/console/app/server/actions/sso.ts` parse it to surface the IdP entry point and
a **SHA-256 fingerprint of the signing certificate**, and classify each row's protocol as
`oidc` `saml` `unknown` (a row with neither config is reported `unknown` rather than mislabelled).
Registration collects the IdP entity ID, SSO entry-point URL, and X.509 signing certificate (see
[access control → SSO](/guides/access/sso)).

Domain verification (DNS `TXT` at `_alethia-sso- `) and the same
`alethia-sso-entitlement-guard` gate apply to SAML exactly as to OIDC, and users are provisioned
just-in-time as least-privileged members.

 
 **Documented hardening follow-ups (from `ee/src/index.ts`).** The SAML integration ships with two
 standup items still open: enabling `algorithms.onDeprecated: "reject"` (reject deprecated signature
 algorithms) and turning on `InResponseTo` vali

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**SCIM 2.0** (System for Cross-domain Identity Management, [RFC 7644](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644)
protocol + [RFC 7643](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7643) schema) is the REST standard for
**automatic** user/group provisioning and *de*-provisioning. A directory (Okta, Entra) pushes
create/update/delete against the SP's `/scim/v2/Users` and `/scim/v2/Groups` endpoints, so access is
granted and — critically — **revoked** the moment HR changes the directory, with no sign-in required.

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: Reality in Alethia
records.text:
SCIM is **not built**. There is no `/scim/v2` endpoint. Membership is populated only by **just-in-time
provisioning** — a user becomes a member the first time they successfully sign in through SSO, and is
never automatically deprovisioned by the directory.

This is stated honestly in the product itself: the console SSO settings
(`apps/console/components/settings/sso/sso-manager.tsx`) render a plain note that *"automatic user
provisioning/deprovisioning from your IdP isn't available yet — SSO users are provisioned
just-in-time on first sign-in"*, with a "talk to us" link. The code comments record that an earlier
UI advertised a `/scim/v2/ ` URL that never existed; that fake card was removed. The plan
catalog lists SCIM as *"coming soon"*.

 
 Do not represent SCIM as available. If a deployment's compliance posture depends on **automatic
 deprovisioning** (offboarding removing access without an admin action), that requirement is **not
 met today** — plan around JIT provisioning and manual member removal
 ([members & invitations](/guides/access/members-and-invitations)).

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [OASIS — SAML 2.0 Core](https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/v2.0/saml-core-2.0-os.pdf).
- [RFC 7644](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644) — SCIM 2.0 Protocol · [RFC 7643](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7643) — SCIM 2.0 Core Schema.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.text: Security & Compliance. The real security controls behind Alethia — tenant isolation via Postgres RLS, keyless cloud credentials, the fail-closed verify gate, least-privilege connector roles, audit logging, and the state proxy — mapped to the standards, with an honest SOC 2 posture.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.text:
This page maps Alethia's **real, shipped** controls to the standards in this section. Every control
below has code evidence. The compliance framing is deliberately conservative — see the SOC 2 note at
the end.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Tenant isolation — coarse Postgres RLS
records.text:
Every tenant-owned table is scoped by `org_id`, and Postgres **Row-Level Security** enforces the
boundary at the database. After authentication, the [PDP](/concepts/access-control/architecture) resolves the
active [organization](/reference/glossary) and sets `app.current_org` via `set_config`; RLS policies
key on that setting, so a query can only ever see its own org's rows even if application code forgets a
`WHERE`. This is *coarse* isolation (org-level), complemented by the fine-grained PDP for
role/resource authorization. See [concepts/security](/concepts/security) and
[access control](/concepts/access-control).

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Keyless cloud credentials — zero stored secrets
records.text:
Alethia stores **no** static cloud credentials. All four managed clouds federate keylessly through the
Alethia OIDC issuer ([workload identity](/reference/standards/workload-identity)); the only durable private key
is the issuer's own signing key, held on the control plane and never shared. Revocation is the
customer deleting the trust in their own account — there is nothing to leak from Alethia's side.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Fail-closed verify gate — Elench
records.text:
On a real apply the [runner](/concepts/runner) runs the [Elench](/concepts/elench) `verify` gate between `tofu plan` and
`tofu apply` (`provisioner.RunDeployV2` over `packages/core/verify`). It is **fail-closed**: a hard
control failure (keyless / least-privilege / OIDC-subject checks) blocks the apply unless an
authorized, time-boxed `verify.Override` waives it — and the waiver is recorded in the evidence
receipt. The report is forwarded on `execution_metadata["verify_result"]` and rendered in the Console
Plan tab. Evidence receipts are ed25519-signable ([JOSE](/reference/standards/jose)).

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Least-privilege connector roles
records.text:
The cloud roles Alethia assumes are scoped down from cloud-admin to the minimum needed to provision
and inspect — not blanket administrative access — narrowing blast radius even within a federated
session.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Runner holds no storage credentials — the state proxy
records.text:
The runner never receives object-storage keys. `tofu` state is read and written through the Console
**state proxy** (`backend "http"` → `/api/jobs/{id}/state`, authenticated by a per-job token in
`TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`). A compromised runner cannot reach the state bucket directly. The runner images
also ship **CLI-free** (no bundled `aws`/`gcloud`/`az`); cluster tokens are minted in-process.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Audit / activity log
records.text:
Membership and authorization-relevant actions (invites, removals, role changes, policy decisions) are
written to the org **activity log** (`recordActivity` / `enforceDecision`, surfaced at
[access control → activity log](/guides/access/activity-log)). It gives a per-org trail of who did
what.

 
 **Known honest limitation.** The activity/audit log today has no dedicated RLS policy or
 write-once (WORM) retention guarantee — it is an application-level trail, not yet a tamper-evident
 store. Note this when scoping evidence requirements; it is a tracked hardening item, not a shipped
 guarantee.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Control-to-standard map
records.text:
Control Backing standard Evidence 
 --- --- --- 
 Web sign-in [OAuth 2.0 + PKCE](/reference/standards/oauth2) `lib/auth/index.ts`, Better Auth 
 Enterprise SSO [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc) · [SAML 2.0](/reference/standards/scim-saml) `ee/src/index.ts`, `@better-auth/sso` 
 CLI auth [Device grant](/reference/standards/device-code) · [JWT](/reference/standards/jose) `api/auth/cli/*` 
 Keyless cloud access [Workload identity](/reference/standards/workload-identity) `lib/oidc/issuer.ts`, `lib/cloud-providers/session/*` 
 Tamper-evident apply evidence [ed25519 / EdDSA](/reference/standards/jose) `packages/core/verify` 
 Tenant isolation Postgres RLS (`org_id`) `app.current_org` + RLS policies

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: SOC 2 posture — read this carefully
records.text:
Alethia is **built to support SOC 2** — the controls above map to the Security and Confidentiality
Trust Services Criteria (least-privilege access, no stored credentials, tenant isolation, change
verification, audit trail). This is **SOC 2 readiness / control mapping**, and nothing more.

 
 Alethia is **not SOC 2 certified**, **not SOC 2 compliant**, and no SOC 2 report has been issued.
 SOC 2 is an attestation performed by an independent auditor over an observation period; **no such
 formal audit has been performed and no report exists yet.** Anyone stating otherwise is wrong. The
 accurate phrasing is "designed for SOC 2 readiness" / "controls mapped to SOC 2 criteria".
 

For the security model in prose, see [concepts/security](/concepts/security).

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text: - [AICPA — SOC 2](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance/audit-and-assurance-greater-than-soc-2) — what a SOC 2 report is (and requires).

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.text: Cloud Workload Identity. Keyless cloud connectors — one Alethia OIDC issuer federates into AWS (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity), GCP (Workload Identity Federation), and Azure (federated identity). No static cloud secrets are ever stored.

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**Workload identity federation** lets a workload prove *what it is* to a cloud without holding a
long-lived cloud key. The workload obtains a short-lived, signed **OIDC token** from an issuer the
cloud trusts, presents it to the cloud's token exchange, and receives temporary cloud credentials in
return. Trust is established once (the cloud is configured to trust the issuer's URL, its published
JWKS, and a specific `sub`/`aud`); after that every access is a fresh, expiring assertion. The static
attack surface — access keys, service-account JSON, client secrets — disappears.

Each major cloud has its own exchange built on the same OIDC primitive:

- **AWS** — STS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` against an IAM OIDC identity provider.
- **GCP** — Workload Identity Federation (STS token exchange into a workload identity pool).
- **Azure** — a federated identity credential on an Entra ID app (client-assertion grant).

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
The control plane **is its own OIDC issuer**, purpose-built for machine federation and nothing else
(`apps/console/lib/oidc/issuer.ts`). It mints short-lived **RS256** JWTs and publishes the matching
public material so any cloud can verify them:

 Property Value 
 --- --- 
 Issuer `${APP_URL}/api/oidc` 
 Discovery `/api/oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration` 
 JWKS `/api/oidc/jwks` 
 Signing alg `RS256` (widest cloud-federation compatibility) 
 Subject (`sub`) `alethia-connector` (single, stable, non-secret) 
 Max token TTL 600 seconds 
 Signing key `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` (PKCS8, vault-held) `+ ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY_PREVIOUS` for zero-downtime rotation 

`mintWorkloadToken()` produces a per-cloud-scoped assertion (audience set per provider); the same
issuer serves both the [Console](/reference/glossary) (server-side inventory/health) and the
[runner](/concepts/runner) (provisioning). **No platform cloud account and no stored customer secret exists
anywhere on the Alethia side** — revocation is the customer deleting the trust in their own cloud.

 api/oidc RS256] --> mint sub=alethia-connector TOK[Short-lived JWT]
 TOK --> AWS[AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity]
 TOK --> GCP[G

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.heading: Per-cloud exchange
records.text:
`apps/console/lib/cloud-providers/session/aws.ts`. The customer's IAM role trusts the Alethia issuer
**directly** as an IAM OIDC provider, so the console/runner federate straight in via
`AssumeRoleWithWebIdentityCommand` (`@aws-sdk/client-sts`) presenting a freshly minted assertion.
`AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` is an unauthenticated STS action — **no platform AWS account, no
`ExternalId`, no stored key**. Session ≈ 1 hour (`DurationSeconds: 3600`); each caller re-assumes the
role (mints a fresh assertion) when it needs credentials — the session itself is not refreshed in place.

 
 

`apps/console/lib/cloud-providers/session/gcp.ts` + `apps/console/lib/cloud-providers/gcp-wif.ts`. A direct-OIDC Workload Identity
Federation config exchanges the Alethia-minted JWT for a GCP access token. The audience encodes the
pool/provider:
`//iam.googleapis.com/projects/ /locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/ /providers/ `.
Connection validation asserts the audience contains `workloadIdentityPools` (`connections.ts`).

 
 

`apps/console/lib/cloud-providers/session/azure.ts`. Each customer creates a **User-Assigned Managed
Identity** in their **own** subscription with a **federated-identity cred

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [OpenID Connect Core 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html) — the token format clouds verify.
- [AWS — `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.html) and [creating an IAM OIDC provider](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_providers_create_oidc.html).
- [GCP — Workload Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation).
- [Azure — Workload identity federation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/workload-id/workload-identity-federation).

records.title: Configuration
records.text: Configuration. Set the .env keys of a self-hosted Alethia bundle — domain, client-IP header, sign-in providers, storage — and rotate its instance secrets.

records.title: Configuration
records.text:
Configure a self-hosted instance by editing `/opt/alethia/.env`, then applying the change. The
installer has already set the domain and generated every instance secret. Compose wires the
internal service addresses, so you do not set those.

To apply a change, recreate the services from `/opt/alethia`:

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/selfhost/docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Domain and client IP
records.text:
Key What it does 
 --- --- 
 `ALETHIA_DOMAIN` The domain Caddy gets a TLS certificate for. Empty: plain HTTP on port 80. 
 `ALETHIA_ACME_EMAIL` The contact address for Let's Encrypt. 
 `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`, `BETTER_AUTH_URL` The public origin, for example `https://alethia.example.com`. Set both when the domain changes. 
 `ALETHIA_TRUSTED_IP_HEADER` The header that carries the client's IP address. Default: `cf-connecting-ip`. 

The console counts sign-in attempts per client IP, and reads that IP from one header. The bundled
Caddy overwrites `cf-connecting-ip` with the real client address, so the default is correct. If you
put another proxy in front of the app, set `ALETHIA_TRUSTED_IP_HEADER` to a single-value header that
the proxy overwrites, and keep the app unreachable except through it. In production, sign-in answers
`503` when the header is missing or does not hold one valid IP address.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Sign-in providers
records.text:
Email sign-in always works. Each OAuth provider you configure adds a button to the sign-in page.

 Provider Keys Callback URL to register 
 --- --- --- 
 GitHub `GITHUB_CLIENT_ID`, `GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET` `https:// /api/auth/callback/github` 
 Google `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` `https:// /api/auth/callback/google` 
 GitLab `GITLAB_APPLICATION_ID`, `GITLAB_SECRET` `https:// /api/auth/oauth2/callback/gitlab` 
 Bitbucket `BITBUCKET_KEY`, `BITBUCKET_SECRET` `https:// /api/auth/oauth2/callback/bitbucket` 

To send sign-in codes by email, see [Email](/self-host/email).

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Database and object store
records.text:
The Compose bundle always uses its own Postgres and SeaweedFS. Compose sets their addresses, and a
value in `.env` does not override them. To use a managed Postgres, or S3 or R2, install with the
[Helm chart](/self-host/helm#use-a-managed-database-or-object-store).

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Other optional keys
records.text:
Key What it turns on 
 --- --- 
 `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` The assistant. 
 `INFRACOST_API_KEY` Cost estimates. 
 `HCLOUD_TOKEN`, `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN`, `CIVO_TOKEN` Token clouds for the bundled runner. 
 `NEXT_PUBLIC_CONNECTOR_ASSETS_ORIGIN` Serves the connector setup scripts from another public origin. Default: your console. 
 `ALETHIA_LICENSE_KEY` Enterprise. See [Enterprise setup](/self-host/enterprise-setup). 

`.env.example` in the repository lists every key, with a comment for each.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Instance secrets
records.text:
The installer generates 13 instance secrets. `deploy/selfhost/secrets.manifest` lists them with the
command that makes each one. You never type them:

- A first install generates all of them. A later run adds any that are missing and never changes one
 that is set.
- Compose refuses to start when one is empty, and names it. The `preflight` service refuses a
 template placeholder.

Back up `.env`. Without `ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, the connector secrets and alert-channel
webhooks stored in the database cannot be decrypted.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Rotate a secret
records.text:
sh /opt/alethia/deploy/selfhost/rotate-secret.sh ALETHIA_CRON_SECRET

The script writes a new value to `.env` and restarts the services that read it. `--list` prints
every name. Some secrets need more, and the script does it:

 Secret What else the script does 
 --- --- 
 `ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY` Keeps the old key as `ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY_ ` and re-encrypts every stored secret with the new one, with no downtime. Delete the old key from `.env` after you check your connectors. 
 `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` Keeps the old key as `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY_PREVIOUS`, so tokens it signed still verify. Delete that key after 24 hours. 
 Database passwords Changes the role's password in Postgres first, then writes `.env`. 
 Storage keys Recreates the object store with the new identity. 

For any other secret, sessions and tokens signed with the old value stop being accepted. Rotating
`BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` signs everyone out.

records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Email](/self-host/email)
- [Upgrade and back up](/self-host/upgrading)
- [Managed runner fleet](/self-host/managed-provisioning): the `FLEET_*` and `HCLOUD_*` keys.

records.title: Email
records.text: Email. Send sign-in codes and notifications from a self-hosted Alethia through an SMTP server or AWS SES, from sending subdomains with SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

records.title: Email
records.text:
Make a self-hosted console send email. Until you do, it writes sign-in codes and every other email
to its log, so a new install works without email.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- A domain whose DNS you control.
- Either an SMTP service (Postmark, Mailgun, SES SMTP, or Mailpit for testing), or an AWS account
 with SES production access. A new SES account is in the sandbox and can mail only verified
 addresses.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Choose the sending addresses
records.text:
Send each kind of mail from its own subdomain, so a spam complaint about one kind does not stop
sign-in codes from arriving. Your root domain keeps your own mailboxes and sends no app email.

 Mail Subdomain Key Example 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Sign-in codes, verification `auth.` `AUTH_EMAIL_FROM` `Alethia ` 
 Invitations, job notifications `mail.` `EMAIL_FROM` `Alethia ` 

`EMAIL_FROM` falls back to `AUTH_EMAIL_FROM` when it is not set. Quote both values in `.env`.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Send through SMTP
records.text:
1. Verify both subdomains with your SMTP provider. It gives you the SPF and DKIM records to add.
2. Set these keys in `/opt/alethia/.env`:

 Key What it does 
 --- --- 
 `SMTP_HOST` The server. Setting it selects SMTP. 
 `SMTP_PORT` Default `587`. 
 `SMTP_USER`, `SMTP_PASS` Credentials, if the server needs them. 
 `SMTP_SECURE` TLS from the first byte. Default: `true` on port 465, otherwise `false`. 
 `AUTH_EMAIL_FROM`, `EMAIL_FROM` The addresses above. 

3. Apply the change: run `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/selfhost/docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d`
 from `/opt/alethia`.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Send through AWS SES
records.text:
1. In the SES console, in one region, create a domain identity for `auth.example.com` and for
 `mail.example.com`.
2. Turn on Easy DKIM for each identity, and add the three CNAME records SES shows.
3. Set a custom MAIL FROM domain for each (for example `bounce.auth.example.com`), and add the MX and
 SPF records below.
4. Request production access.
5. Give the console permission to send: an IAM role on the VM with `ses:SendEmail` and
 `ses:SendRawEmail`, or an IAM user with those permissions and its keys in `.env`.
6. Set the keys and apply the change as in the SMTP steps:

 ALETHIA_SES_REGION=eu-west-1
 ALETHIA_SES_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... # only without an IAM role
 ALETHIA_SES_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... # only without an IAM role
 AUTH_EMAIL_FROM="Alethia "
 EMAIL_FROM="Alethia "
 
Setting `ALETHIA_SES_REGION` selects SES. `AWS_REGION` selects it too when `ALETHIA_SES_REGION` is
not set.

records.title: Email
records.heading: DNS records for SES
records.text:
Record Host Type Value 
 --- --- --- --- 
 DKIM, three of them ` ._domainkey. ` CNAME ` .dkim.amazonses.com` 
 MAIL FROM `bounce. ` MX `10 feedback-smtp. .amazonses.com` 
 MAIL FROM SPF `bounce. ` TXT `v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all` 
 DMARC, once `_dmarc.example.com` TXT `v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com` 

Start DMARC at `p=none`. Move to `p=quarantine`, then `p=reject`, once the reports are clean.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Stop mailing addresses that bounce
records.text:
Optional. SES can report bounces and complaints, so the console stops mailing those addresses:

1. Create an SES configuration set for each kind of mail, and set `ALETHIA_SES_AUTH_CONFIG_SET` and
 `ALETHIA_SES_GENERAL_CONFIG_SET`.
2. Publish `Bounce` and `Complaint` events from both to one SNS topic.
3. Set `ALETHIA_SES_EVENTS_TOPIC_ARNS` to the topic's full ARN (comma-separated for more than one).
 Do this before the next step: without it, the console refuses every message with `503`.
4. Subscribe `https:// /api/webhooks/ses` to the topic over HTTPS.

A permanent bounce or a complaint puts the address on a suppression list, and later sends skip it.
The OpenTofu stack in `infra/email-ses/` creates all of the SES pieces on this page; read its
`README.md` before you apply it to your domain.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Which transport is used
records.text:
`EMAIL_PROVIDER` (`smtp` or `ses`) chooses the transport. Without it, SMTP wins when `SMTP_HOST` is
set, then SES. Any other value stops the console with an error. `EMAIL_PROVIDER=resend`, or a
`RESEND_API_KEY` with nothing else set, is also an error: Resend support was removed.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Request a sign-in code from the console. It arrives from your `auth.` address; check the spam folder
on the first send. If it does not arrive, read the console's log: it shows the SMTP or SES error, or
the line `[email] no provider configured` when no transport is set.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.text: Enterprise setup. Turn on the Enterprise edition of a self-hosted Alethia with a licence key, and optionally the OpenFGA engine and SSO.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.text:
Turn a self-hosted instance from Community into
 Enterprise . The published console image already contains the Enterprise
code. A licence key turns it on. What each edition includes is in the
[feature matrix](/editions/feature-matrix).

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- A self-hosted instance running the published images. See [Install on a VM](/self-host/install).
- A licence key from Alethia Labs. It is a signed token.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Add the key
records.text:
Set the key in `/opt/alethia/.env`:

ALETHIA_LICENSE_KEY=

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Restart the console
records.text:
From `/opt/alethia`:

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/selfhost/docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d app

The console checks the licence's signature offline, against keys built into the image. It sends
nothing to Alethia Labs.

 
 

The database tables for organizations, teams and SSO are already there: the `migrate` service
applies every migration on each start.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Optional: use OpenFGA
records.text:
Enterprise runs on the built-in Postgres authorization engine. To use the
[OpenFGA engine](/concepts/access-control/openfga) instead:

1. Start it:

 docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/selfhost/docker-compose.selfhost.yml --profile enterprise up -d openfga
 
2. Create a store, and note the `id` in the answer:

 curl -X POST http://localhost:8082/stores -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"name":"alethia"}'
 
3. Set `OPENFGA_API_URL=http://openfga:8080` and `OPENFGA_STORE_ID= ` in `.env`, and restart the
 console as above.

On start, the console writes the authorization model and copies your existing grants into OpenFGA.
With either key empty, the Postgres engine stays in use.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Optional: register an SSO provider
records.text:
In **Settings → Single Sign-On**, register your identity provider over
[OIDC or SAML](/guides/access/sso).

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
- The organization switcher and **Settings → Members**, **Teams** and **Roles** are available.
- Invite a second member, and accept the invitation. See
 [Members and invitations](/guides/access/members-and-invitations).
- In **Settings → Access**, grant a role and add a deny exception, then check that it applies. See
 [Grants and scopes](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes).

If none of this appears, the licence did not verify. A licence that is missing, expired, or signed by
another key grants nothing, and the console runs as Community. The console still starts.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: What happens when the licence ends
records.text:
A licence keeps working for a grace period after its end date: 30 days, unless the licence states
another period. No restart is needed for either change. After the grace period, the instance goes
back to Community behaviour. No data is deleted. Members already in an
organization keep their data, and Enterprise-only operations stop until a valid licence is set.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Licensing](/editions/licensing): entitlements and how the licence is checked.
- [Access control](/concepts/access-control)

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.text: Run untrusted code on the fleet. Turn on the per-job container sandbox on a managed runner fleet, prove it on a canary pool, then allow bring-your-own charts and IaC.

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.text:
Turn on the container sandbox before your fleet runs code your users wrote, such as bring-your-own
Helm charts. Alethia's own templates do not need it.

Each job then runs in a nested rootless Podman container. It sees only an allowlisted set of
environment variables and its own processes, and reaches the network only through a proxy that
allows listed domains. It cannot reach the cloud metadata address `169.254.169.254`.

The sandbox cannot be tested in CI, so prove it on one real VM before you rely on it.

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- A working fleet. See [Managed provisioning](/self-host/managed-provisioning).
- SSH access to the fleet's VMs (`HCLOUD_SSH_KEYS`).

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.heading: Turn on the sandbox, without egress enforcement
records.text:
Set on the console and restart it:

FLEET_SANDBOX_CONTAINER=1
FLEET_EGRESS_PROXY_IMAGE=ubuntu/squid@sha256: # default ubuntu/squid:latest; pin a digest
FLEET_EGRESS_EXTRA_DOMAINS=charts.example.com # optional, comma-separated

New VMs get the proxy, a network with no other route out, and the container backend. Leave
`FLEET_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED` unset: until it is set, managed jobs refuse to run in the container.
That proves the container starts before you trust its network.

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.heading: Prove it on a canary VM
records.text:
On a new fleet VM, every check must pass:

- `podman run --rm true`, as the `runner` user, succeeds.
- Inside the nested container, `/proc/1/environ`, `$ALETHIA_RUNNER_TOKEN` and the storage and
 registration secrets cannot be read, and only the container's own processes are visible.
- `curl --max-time 3 http://169.254.169.254/` from the container times out, with the proxy
 variables set and unset.
- Through the proxy, an allowed domain (your console, `registry.opentofu.org`) answers, and
 `example.com` is refused with `403`. With `HTTPS_PROXY` unset, a direct request fails.

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.heading: Enforce egress
records.text:
Set `FLEET_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED=1` and restart the console. On the canary, run a real plan and
deploy, and check that both finish.

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.heading: Roll out and allow bring-your-own code
records.text:
1. Optional: set `FLEET_SANDBOX_ENFORCE_MANAGED=1`. A pool without the container backend then refuses
 managed jobs instead of running them unsandboxed.
2. Set `ALETHIA_BYO_HELM_ENABLED=true` to let users attach their own charts.

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
A user attaches a chart and its safety scan finishes. On the VM that ran the job, the job's process
runs inside a Podman container, and the proxy's log shows the job's requests.

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.heading: If nested Podman fails
records.text:
Nested rootless Podman on the ARM Hetzner kernel is the part most likely to fail. Try, in order:

1. Set the storage driver in `storage.conf` to `vfs`. It is slower and more robust.
2. Add `--cap-add SETUID --cap-add SETGID` to the outer container, for `newuidmap`.
3. Move to a VM type that runs microVMs, such as Kata Containers. This is a larger change.

Until the canary passes, keep `ALETHIA_BYO_HELM_ENABLED` off. Alethia's own templates run as before.

records.title: Run untrusted code on the fleet
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Isolated execution](/concepts/isolated-execution)
- [Bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac)

records.title: Helm chart
records.text: Helm chart. Install the self-hosted Alethia bundle on a Kubernetes cluster with the Helm chart, with the bundled or a managed Postgres and object store.

records.title: Helm chart
records.text:
Install Alethia on a Kubernetes cluster you already run. The chart deploys the console, the docs, a
runner, and optionally Postgres and SeaweedFS, behind one Ingress: the console at `/`, the docs at
`/docs`.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- A cluster with x86 nodes. The images are `linux/amd64` only, so every pod has the node selector
 `kubernetes.io/arch=amd64`.
- An Ingress controller. The defaults match ingress-nginx.
- A default StorageClass, for the bundled Postgres and object store.
- cert-manager with a `ClusterIssuer`, for automatic TLS.
- A clone of the repository, `helm`, and `openssl`.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Generate the instance secrets
records.text:
The chart does not generate secrets. Generate the same set the VM installer makes, from the clone:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs.git && cd alethialabs
(umask 077; : > secrets.env; . deploy/selfhost/secrets.sh; fill_required_secrets secrets.env >/dev/null)

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Write a values file
records.text:
DOMAIN=alethia.example.com
(umask 077; . ./secrets.env; {
 echo "domain: $DOMAIN"
 echo "postgres: { password: \"$ALETHIA_DB_PASSWORD\", appPassword: \"$ALETHIA_APP_DB_PASSWORD\" }"
 echo "objectStore: { accessKey: \"$ALETHIA_STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY_ID\", secretKey: \"$ALETHIA_STORAGE_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY\" }"
 echo "secrets:"
 echo " cliJwtSecret: \"$CLI_JWT_SECRET\""
 echo " betterAuthSecret: \"$BETTER_AUTH_SECRET\""
 echo " extraEnv:"
 echo " NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL: \"https://$DOMAIN\""
 echo " BETTER_AUTH_URL: \"https://$DOMAIN\""
 grep -vE '^(CLI_JWT_SECRET BETTER_AUTH_SECRET)=' secrets.env sed -E 's/^([A-Z0-9_]+)=(.*)$/ \1: "\2"/'
} > alethia-values.yaml)

`secrets.extraEnv` becomes environment variables of the console and the runner. Add OAuth and
email keys there too: see [Configuration](/self-host/configuration) and [Email](/self-host/email).

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Install the chart
records.text:
helm install alethia deploy/helm/alethia \
 --namespace alethia --create-namespace \
 -f alethia-values.yaml

Then point your domain's DNS record at the Ingress controller's external address.

 
 

Keep `secrets.env` and `alethia-values.yaml` in a secret store, and delete them from disk.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
kubectl -n alethia get pods

The console, docs, runner, Postgres and SeaweedFS pods are `Running`. The console pod ran two init
containers first: `wait-for-postgres` and `migrate`. Open `https:// ` and sign in. Until email
is set up, the sign-in code is in the console's log: `kubectl -n alethia logs deploy/alethia-alethia-console`. Resources are named
` -alethia- `.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Use a managed database or object store
records.text:
Turn off the bundled services and point the chart at yours:

helm install alethia deploy/helm/alethia -f alethia-values.yaml \
 --set postgres.enabled=false \
 --set postgres.host=db.internal --set postgres.user=alethia --set postgres.database=alethia \
 --set objectStore.enabled=false \
 --set objectStore.endpoint=https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com

`postgres.password` is the schema owner's password. `migrate` creates the `alethia_app` role with
`postgres.appPassword`. For a managed store, set `ALETHIA_STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and
`ALETHIA_STORAGE_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` in `secrets.extraEnv` to that store's credentials.

To manage the Kubernetes Secret yourself, set `secrets.existingSecret= `. It must hold
`ALETHIA_DATABASE_URL`, `ALETHIA_APP_DATABASE_URL`, `ALETHIA_APP_DB_PASSWORD`,
`ALETHIA_STORAGE_ENDPOINT`, `CLI_JWT_SECRET`, `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` and every key you would put in
`extraEnv`.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Upgrade
records.text:
helm upgrade alethia deploy/helm/alethia --reuse-values --set image.tag= 

The `migrate` init container runs on every rollout, so the schema moves before the new console
serves. Back up the database first; see [Upgrade and back up](/self-host/upgrading#what-to-back-up).

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Key values
records.text:
Value Default What it does 
 --- --- --- 
 `domain` `alethialabs.io` The Ingress host. Always set it. 
 `image.tag` `latest` One tag for every Alethia image. 
 `nodeSelector` `kubernetes.io/arch: amd64` Set to `{}` once multi-arch images exist. 
 `postgres.enabled`, `objectStore.enabled` `true` `false` uses your own service. 
 `ingress.className` `nginx` The Ingress class. 
 `ingress.trustedIpHeader` `x-real-ip` The client-IP header the Ingress overwrites. 
 `ingress.tls.clusterIssuer` `letsencrypt-prod` The cert-manager issuer. 

With another Ingress controller, set `ingress.trustedIpHeader` to a single-value header that
controller overwrites with the client address. In production, sign-in answers `503` when the header
is missing or invalid.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Configuration](/self-host/configuration): every key you can add to `extraEnv`.
- [Scaling out](/self-host/scaling-out): run more console replicas.

records.title: Self-host
records.text: Self-host. Run the whole Alethia platform on your own VM or Kubernetes cluster, then configure, upgrade and back it up.

records.title: Self-host
records.text:
A self-hosted Alethia is one Docker Compose bundle: the console, the docs, Postgres, an
S3-compatible object store (SeaweedFS), a runner, and Caddy for HTTPS. It runs on a VM in any cloud
or on your own hardware, and needs no managed database or object store.

records.title: Self-host
records.heading: Choose how to install
records.text:
Path Use it when Page 
 --- --- --- 
 Installer You have a Linux VM and a domain. One command. [Install on a VM](/self-host/install) 
 One-click You want AWS or Azure to create the VM from a template. [One-click deploy](/self-host/one-click) 
 OpenTofu You want the VM, its firewall and a Cloudflare Tunnel as code. [OpenTofu per cloud](/self-host/terraform) 
 Helm You already run Kubernetes. [Helm chart](/self-host/helm) 

The one-click templates run the same installer. The Helm chart deploys the same images.

records.title: Self-host
records.heading: Then
records.text:
1. [Configure](/self-host/configuration) sign-in providers, storage and the client-IP header.
2. [Set up email](/self-host/email), so sign-in codes reach your users.
3. [Upgrade and back up](/self-host/upgrading) on a schedule.

Optional: [turn on Enterprise](/self-host/enterprise-setup), [run more console
replicas](/self-host/scaling-out), or [run a managed runner
fleet](/self-host/managed-provisioning) that provisions into your users' clouds.

records.title: Self-host
records.heading: What is in the bundle
records.text:
Service Role 
 --- --- 
 `app` The console: web app and API 
 `preflight` Checks that every instance secret is set and is not a placeholder, then exits 
 `migrate` Applies database migrations, then exits. `app` starts after it. 
 `docs` These docs, at `/docs` 
 `blog` News and changelog, at `/news` 
 `postgres` The database 
 `seaweedfs` Object storage for OpenTofu state and plan files 
 `runner` Runs plan and apply jobs, with the credentials you give it 
 `caddy` The only service with open ports (80 and 443). Gets TLS certificates. 
 `pgweb` Optional database browser (`tools` profile) 
 `openfga` Optional authorization engine for Enterprise (`enterprise` profile) 

The bundle is AGPL-3.0, except the `ee/` directory. See [Licensing](/editions/licensing).

records.title: Install on a VM
records.text: Install on a VM. Install the self-hosted Alethia bundle on a Linux VM with one command, with automatic HTTPS for your domain.

records.title: Install on a VM
records.text:
Install Alethia on one Linux VM. The installer generates every secret, pulls prebuilt images and
starts the stack.

records.title: Install on a VM
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- A Linux VM with an x86-64 CPU, 2 or more vCPU, 8 GB of memory (4 GB is the minimum) and 25 GB of
 disk. The images are built for `linux/amd64` only.
- `git`, `openssl` and `curl` on the VM. The installer adds Docker and the Compose plugin if they are
 missing.
- A domain whose `A` (or `AAAA`) record points at the VM, and ports 80 and 443 open. Without a
 domain, the console serves plain HTTP on port 80, which is enough for a test.
- Outbound access to `ghcr.io`, `github.com` and the clouds you will deploy into.

records.title: Install on a VM
records.heading: Run the installer
records.text:
curl -fsSL https://get.alethialabs.io/self-host \
 DOMAIN=alethia.example.com ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com sh

The installer clones the repository to `/opt/alethia`, writes `/opt/alethia/.env` with a generated
value for every instance secret, and records `ALETHIA_VERSION=latest`. To pin an image tag, add
`ALETHIA_VERSION= `. To install somewhere else, add `ALETHIA_DIR= `.

records.title: Install on a VM
records.heading: Wait for the stack
records.text:
The installer runs a preflight check, pulls the images and starts the stack. It prints
`Alethia is starting at https://alethia.example.com`. Caddy gets a TLS certificate on the first
request, which can take a minute.

records.title: Install on a VM
records.heading: Sign in
records.text:
Open the URL and sign in with your email. No email provider is set yet, so the console writes the
code to its log instead of sending it:

cd /opt/alethia
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/selfhost/docker-compose.selfhost.yml logs app grep '\[email\]'

records.title: Install on a VM
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
cd /opt/alethia
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/selfhost/docker-compose.selfhost.yml ps

`app`, `postgres`, `seaweedfs`, `runner`, `docs`, `blog` and `caddy` are `running`. `preflight` and
`migrate` have exited with code 0. In the console, **Runners** lists the bundled runner as online.

If the installer stops with `has an instance secret that is not usable`, it names the variable and
the command that replaces it. Nothing was started.

records.title: Install on a VM
records.heading: Install from a clone instead
records.text:
To read the files first, clone the repository and run the same script:

git clone https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs.git /opt/alethia
cd /opt/alethia
DOMAIN=alethia.example.com ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com sh deploy/install.sh

Do not start the stack with `docker compose up` before the installer has written `.env`: compose
refuses to start while any instance secret is empty, and names it.

records.title: Install on a VM
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Configuration](/self-host/configuration): sign-in providers, storage, and the client-IP header.
- [Email](/self-host/email): send sign-in codes instead of logging them.
- [Upgrade and back up](/self-host/upgrading).

records.title: Keyless cloud connectors
records.text: Keyless cloud connectors. What a self-hosted instance needs so that users can connect AWS, GCP and Azure without keys, and how to rotate the issuer key those clouds trust.

records.title: Keyless cloud connectors
records.text:
Let your users connect AWS, GCP and Azure accounts with no stored key. Each instance is its own
OpenID Connect (OIDC) issuer. A user's cloud trusts that issuer, and Alethia exchanges a short-lived
signed assertion for cloud credentials when it needs them. You do not need a cloud account of your
own. How the trust works on each cloud is in [Security](/concepts/security#the-alethia-oidc-issuer-workload-identity).

Hetzner, DigitalOcean and Civo are not keyless: the user pastes an API token, which Alethia stores
encrypted. They need nothing on this page.

records.title: Keyless cloud connectors
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` is set. The installer generates it.
- `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` is an `https://` address that the internet can reach. AWS, GCP and Azure
 fetch the issuer's public keys from it.

The issuer is ` /api/oidc`. Its discovery document is at
`/api/oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration`, and its public keys at `/api/oidc/jwks`.

records.title: Keyless cloud connectors
records.heading: Check that the issuer is reachable
records.text:
From a machine outside your network:

curl -fsS https://alethia.example.com/api/oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration
curl -fsS https://alethia.example.com/api/oidc/jwks

Both return JSON. Then open **Connectors** in the console: the AWS, GCP and Azure cards offer
**Connect**.

If the console instead says the instance cannot serve a keyless connect, it names one reason:

 Reason Fix 
 --- --- 
 no issuer signing key Set `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY`. Run the installer again to generate it. 
 no public URL configured Set `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`. 
 the URL is not HTTPS Give the instance a domain with TLS. See [Install on a VM](/self-host/install). 
 a private or local address Publish the console on a public address, or use a token cloud or a [self-operated runner](/guides/runners/self-operated) that holds its own cloud credentials.

records.title: Keyless cloud connectors
records.heading: What the user does
records.text:
The user runs a setup script or OpenTofu module in their own account, which trusts your issuer, and
pastes the result into the console. See [Connect AWS](/guides/connectors/aws),
[Connect GCP](/guides/connectors/gcp) and [Connect Azure](/guides/connectors/azure). On Azure the
federated credential names issuer ` /api/oidc`, subject `alethia-connector` and
audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange`.

 
 Every user connection trusts your issuer's URL. If `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` changes, every user must
 run their setup again.

records.title: Keyless cloud connectors
records.heading: Rotate the issuer signing key
records.text:
The signing key is the trust root for every keyless connection, so rotate it with an overlap:

1. Run the rotation script:

 sh /opt/alethia/deploy/selfhost/rotate-secret.sh ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY
 
 The old key moves to `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY_PREVIOUS`. The issuer publishes both keys and
 signs with the new one.

2. Wait at least 24 hours, so every cloud refreshes its copy of the keys and every old assertion has
 expired.
3. Delete `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY_PREVIOUS` from `.env`, and restart the console.

No change is needed in your users' clouds.

records.title: Keyless cloud connectors
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Managed provisioning](/self-host/managed-provisioning): run the jobs on a runner fleet you operate.
- [Cloud credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials): how the runner uses the credentials.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.text: Managed provisioning. Run a fleet of Hetzner runner VMs that your instance scales by queue depth, so your users' plan and deploy jobs run without a runner of their own.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.text:
Run the jobs for your users. Your instance creates runner VMs on Hetzner Cloud, each one claims a
job, signs in to the user's cloud with that job's own short-lived credential, runs OpenTofu, and
streams the log and the state back. Users never run a runner.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.heading: How a job runs
records.text:
1. A user connects a cloud and starts a plan or a deploy.
2. Every 60 seconds the scaler compares the queue with each pool, and creates a Hetzner VM when a
 pool needs one. The VM pulls `ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner- ` and registers with a
 one-time token that expires.
3. The runner claims the job. It gets a credential for the user's cloud (keyless on AWS, GCP and
 Azure; the user's API token on Hetzner) and a credential for that job's OpenTofu state. State
 goes through the console; the VM never holds a storage key.
4. The job ends, and the VM takes the next job or is removed. A VM runs one job at a time by
 default.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- A working install with a public HTTPS address. See [Install on a VM](/self-host/install).
- Keyless connectors working, if you offer AWS, GCP or Azure. See
 [Keyless cloud connectors](/self-host/managed-cloud-connectors).
- A Hetzner Cloud project for the fleet, and an API token for it. Keep it apart from any project a
 user connects.
- Permission to manage the fleet. Pools appear only on a self-managed instance, and no licence
 gates them there.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.heading: Set the fleet keys
records.text:
Add to `/opt/alethia/.env`, then restart the console:

 Key Default What it does 
 --- --- --- 
 `FLEET_PROVIDER` `manual` `hcloud` turns the fleet on. `manual` turns it off. 
 `HCLOUD_TOKEN` none The fleet project's API token. Required. 
 `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN` `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` The address the VMs call back to. 
 `HCLOUD_SSH_KEYS` none Hetzner SSH key IDs, comma-separated, for emergency access. 
 `HCLOUD_SERVER_TYPES` `cax21,cpx31` Server types to try, in order. 
 `HCLOUD_IMAGE` `ubuntu-24.04` The VM's operating system image. 
 `FLEET_RUNNER_IMAGE_TAG` `latest` The runner image tag the VMs pull. 
 `FLEET_RUNNER_SLOTS` `1` Jobs one VM runs at the same time. 
 `FLEET_MAX_TOTAL_INSTANCES` none A ceiling on VMs across all pools. 
 `FLEET_BOOT_GRACE_SECONDS` `180` How long a new VM is safe from scale-down.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.heading: Check the runner images
records.text:
Each cloud you offer needs its runner image at the tag you set:

for c in aws gcp azure hetzner; do
 docker manifest inspect ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner-$c:latest >/dev/null && echo "runner-$c OK"
done

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.heading: Create one pool per cloud
records.text:
Open **Runners** in the console and select **Add pool**. Choose the cloud, the number of VMs to keep
warm, the maximum, and the Hetzner locations. The scaler reads pools on every pass, so no restart is
needed. A paused pool gets no new VMs.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
For each cloud you offer:

1. Connect a test account, and create a project with a small cluster.
2. Run a plan. A server named `fleet- -…` appears in the fleet's Hetzner project, and shows in
 **Runners** as online. The plan finishes with its verification result.
3. Deploy, then destroy. The destroy also deletes the job's OpenTofu state.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.heading: If something fails
records.text:
Symptom Cause and fix 
 --- --- 
 The VM boots and never registers Its registration token expired during a slow image pull. Raise `FLEET_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS` (default `3600`) or `FLEET_BOOT_GRACE_SECONDS`. After 5 failed boots in 30 minutes, the pool pauses itself. 
 The VM cannot pull `runner- ` The tag is not published for that cloud. Repeat the image check. 
 The plan fails to sign in to the cloud The user's setup is missing, or the issuer is not reachable. See [Keyless cloud connectors](/self-host/managed-cloud-connectors#check-that-the-issuer-is-reachable). 
 No VM is created `FLEET_PROVIDER` is not `hcloud`, `HCLOUD_TOKEN` is empty, or the pool is paused or at its maximum.

records.title: Managed provisioning
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Run untrusted code on the fleet](/self-host/fleet-sandbox): the container sandbox that bring-your-own charts and IaC need.
- [Runners](/guides/runners): the runners users register themselves.

records.title: One-click deploy
records.text: One-click deploy. Launch the self-hosted Alethia bundle on AWS or Azure from a template button, with no local tooling.

records.title: One-click deploy
records.text:
Create a VM on AWS or Azure from a template. The VM runs the [installer](/self-host/install) on
first boot, so you get the same bundle as every other path.

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- An AWS account that can create EC2 instances, security groups and Elastic IPs, or an Azure
 subscription where you can create a resource group.
- An SSH key: an EC2 key pair name on AWS, or a public key on Azure.
- Optional: a domain. Create its DNS record after the deploy, pointing at the public IP the template
 outputs.

Both templates create an x86 VM (AWS `t3.medium`, Azure `Standard_D2s_v5`) running Ubuntu 24.04, with
ports 22, 80 and 443 open.

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: Deploy on AWS
records.text:
1. Select **Launch Stack**.
2. Fill in the parameters: `KeyName` is required. `Domain`, `AcmeEmail`, `InstanceType`,
 `AllowedSshCidr` and `VolumeSize` are optional. `AllowedSshCidr` defaults to `0.0.0.0/0`, so
 narrow it to your own address range.
3. Create the stack, and read `PublicIp` from its **Outputs**.

The template is
[`deploy/oneclick/aws-cloudformation.yaml`](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/main/deploy/oneclick/aws-cloudformation.yaml).
From the AWS CLI:

aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name alethia \
 --template-file deploy/oneclick/aws-cloudformation.yaml \
 --parameter-overrides Domain=alethia.example.com AcmeEmail=you@example.com KeyName=my-key \
 --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: Deploy on Azure
records.text:
1. Select **Deploy to Azure**.
2. Fill in `sshPublicKey`, and optionally `domain`, `acmeEmail`, `adminUsername`, `vmSize` and
 `location`.
3. Create the deployment, and read `publicIp` from its **Outputs**.

The template is
[`deploy/oneclick/azure-arm.json`](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/main/deploy/oneclick/azure-arm.json).
From the Azure CLI:

az deployment group create --resource-group alethia-cp \
 --template-file deploy/oneclick/azure-arm.json \
 --parameters domain=alethia.example.com acmeEmail=you@example.com \
 sshPublicKey="$(cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub)"

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: Add a domain later
records.text:
With the domain left empty, the console serves plain HTTP at the public IP. To add HTTPS, point the
domain's DNS record at the IP, SSH to the VM, set `ALETHIA_DOMAIN`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` and
`BETTER_AUTH_URL` in `/opt/alethia/.env`, and run `sh /opt/alethia/deploy/install.sh` again.

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Open `http:// ` or your domain. The sign-in page loads. First boot takes a few minutes
while Docker installs and the images pull. Then follow [Sign in](/self-host/install#sign-in).

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Install on a VM](/self-host/install): what the installer does.
- [Configuration](/self-host/configuration) and [Email](/self-host/email).

records.title: Scaling out
records.text: Scaling out. Run several console replicas of a self-hosted Alethia behind one ingress, with no message broker.

records.title: Scaling out
records.text:
Run more than one console container, for throughput or so that one restart does not take the
console down. The replicas need nothing beyond the bundled Postgres.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- A working install. See [Install on a VM](/self-host/install).
- Memory for each extra replica. The Helm chart requests 512 MiB for each; give it more under load.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Add replicas
records.text:
From `/opt/alethia`:

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/selfhost/docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d --scale app=3

Caddy sends requests to every `app` container. On the Helm chart, set `console.replicas` instead.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Why no broker is needed
records.text:
- **Live updates.** Job logs, support messages and runner wake-ups reach the browser over
 Server-Sent Events. Each replica listens to Postgres `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` itself, so an event written
 through any replica reaches the browsers connected to every replica.
- **Rate limits.** The counters are in Postgres, so all replicas count against the same limit, and a
 restart does not reset them.
- **Stored state.** Every replica uses the same database and object store.

The compose file also defines a `redis` service in the `scale-out` profile. Nothing in the current
release uses it, so do not start it.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/selfhost/docker-compose.selfhost.yml ps app

Three `app` containers are `running`. Open a job's log in two browsers: both show new lines as the
job writes them.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Helm chart](/self-host/helm)
- [Configuration](/self-host/configuration)

records.title: AWS
records.text: AWS. Provision the control-plane VM on an x86 EC2 instance with OpenTofu, behind a Cloudflare Tunnel, with admin access through SSM.

records.title: AWS
records.text:
Provision an EC2 instance for the control plane with `infra/cp-aws`. It has no open port: web
traffic comes through a Cloudflare Tunnel, and you reach a shell through SSM Session Manager. Read
[OpenTofu per cloud](/self-host/terraform) first.

records.title: AWS
records.heading: What it creates
records.text:
- An EC2 `t3.large` (2 vCPU, 8 GB) running Ubuntu 24.04, with an encrypted 60 GB gp3 root volume and
 IMDSv2 required. It runs in the account's default VPC, with a public IP for outbound traffic only.
- A security group with no inbound rules.
- An IAM role and instance profile with only `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`.
- The Cloudflare Tunnel, and proxied CNAME records for the apex and `www`.

At the default region `eu-west-1`, on demand, this costs about $72 a month (Infracost). A
`t3.medium` costs about half, with 4 GB of memory.

records.title: AWS
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- AWS credentials for the target account. Use a short-lived source, such as
 `aws sso login --profile `, instead of an access key.
- The Cloudflare token, zone ID and account ID.

records.title: AWS
records.heading: Apply
records.text:
cd infra/cp-aws
cp backend.hcl.example backend.hcl
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars # cloudflare_*, domain, aws_region
tofu init -backend-config=backend.hcl
tofu plan -out=tfplan
tofu apply tfplan

Variables you may change: `instance_type` (must be x86), `root_volume_size`, `aws_region`.

records.title: AWS
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Open a shell on the instance. No SSH port is needed:

aws ssm start-session --target 

`/opt/alethia` holds the repository.

records.title: Azure
records.text: Azure. Provision the control-plane VM on an x86 Gen2 Azure VM with OpenTofu, behind a Cloudflare Tunnel, with admin access through run-command.

records.title: Azure
records.text:
Provision an Azure VM for the control plane with `infra/cp-azure`. It has no inbound rule: web
traffic comes through a Cloudflare Tunnel, and you run commands through the Azure control plane.
Read [OpenTofu per cloud](/self-host/terraform) first.

records.title: Azure
records.heading: What it creates
records.text:
- A `Standard_D2s_v5` (2 vCPU, 8 GB, x86 Gen2) running Ubuntu 24.04, with a 30 GB StandardSSD OS
 disk, Trusted Launch (secure boot and vTPM), a system-assigned managed identity, and boot
 diagnostics for the Serial Console.
- A resource group, a virtual network and a subnet.
- A network security group with no inbound rules.
- A Standard public IP, for outbound traffic only.
- The Cloudflare Tunnel, and proxied CNAME records for the apex and `www`.

At the default location `westeurope`, on demand, this costs about $90 a month (Infracost).

records.title: Azure
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- An Azure subscription, and Contributor on it. Sign in with `az login` instead of a
 service-principal secret.
- The Cloudflare token, zone ID and account ID.

records.title: Azure
records.heading: Apply

cd infra/cp-azure
cp backend.hcl.example backend.hcl
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars # location, cloudflare_*
az login
tofu init -backend-config=backend.hcl
tofu plan -out=tfplan
tofu apply tfplan

Variables you may change: `vm_size` (must be x86 Gen2, for Trusted Launch), `os_disk_size`,
`location`.

records.title: Azure
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Run a command on the VM, or open its Serial Console:

az vm run-command invoke -g -n alethia-cp --command-id RunShellScript --scripts 'ls /opt/alethia'
az serial-console connect -g -n alethia-cp

records.text: GCP. Provision the control-plane VM on an x86 Compute Engine instance with OpenTofu, behind a Cloudflare Tunnel, with SSH only through IAP.

records.title: GCP
records.text:
Provision a Compute Engine VM for the control plane with `infra/cp-gcp`. Web traffic comes through a
Cloudflare Tunnel, and SSH is open only to Google's Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP). Read
[OpenTofu per cloud](/self-host/terraform) first.

records.title: GCP
records.heading: What it creates
records.text:
- An `e2-standard-2` (2 vCPU, 8 GB) running Ubuntu 24.04, with a 30 GB `pd-balanced` boot disk,
 Shielded VM (secure boot and vTPM), and its own least-privilege service account.
- A firewall rule that allows SSH only from the IAP range `35.235.240.0/20`.
- An ephemeral external IP, for outbound traffic only.
- The Cloudflare Tunnel, and proxied CNAME records for the apex and `www`.

At the default region `europe-west4`, on demand, this costs about $57 a month (Infracost).

records.title: GCP
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- A GCP project with the Compute Engine and IAP APIs turned on.
- Application Default Credentials: `gcloud auth application-default login`. Do not use a
 service-account key file.
- The Cloudflare token, zone ID and account ID.

records.title: GCP
records.heading: Apply
records.text:
cd infra/cp-gcp
cp backend.hcl.example backend.hcl
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars # gcp_project, gcp_region, gcp_zone, cloudflare_*
tofu init -backend-config=backend.hcl
tofu plan -out=tfplan
tofu apply tfplan

Variables you may change: `machine_type` (must be x86), `boot_disk_size`, `gcp_region`, `gcp_zone`.

records.heading: Check that it worked

gcloud compute ssh alethia-cp --zone --tunnel-through-iap
